comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule. DHS's finding that the rule has no federalism implications.

1. DHS's own analysis says public schools are state entities
In its small-entity analysis, DHS counts 1,044 public institutions among the 2,478 schools that recommended OPT in 2022-2024. It excludes all of them because they "are run by states." Footnote 137 says DHS "found that the schools were state-run colleges and universities." Its UMRA section says the rule "exceeds the $100 million expenditure threshold in the first year." Its reliance discussion names "state and local governments" as OPT employers. Yet the Executive Order 13132 section says the rule would not "impose substantial direct compliance costs on State and local governments." DHS cannot treat these schools as arms of the state to avoid a small-entity finding and then treat them as something else to avoid a federalism finding.

2. The cost is direct and paid from state budgets
The fee is not an indirect market effect. The proposed rule makes the school the payer: $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including STEM OPT. Footnote 134 says the full amount must be paid before the recommendation issues. When the school is a state university, a state entity writes the check from state-controlled funds. That is the kind of direct compliance cost section 6(b) of E.O. 13132 addresses. Where such a rule is not required by statute, the order bars it unless federal funds cover the cost or the agency consulted state and local officials early and publishes a federalism summary impact statement. No statute requires a $70,000 OPT fee. DHS provides no funds; the fees go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. It did no consultation and published no statement.

3. "Voluntary" does not cure the problem
DHS may argue that OPT recommendations are voluntary, since DSOs "are not required to recommend." But the UMRA section DHS chose to include already concludes the rule crosses the threshold. And a public university that stops recommending eligible students is not saving money. DHS concedes OPT "may contribute to increased enrollment and associated revenue." The real choice is between paying the fee and losing enrollment and tuition. Either way, the state budget pays.

4. State budget rules were never considered
DHS acknowledges that an institution "may have to alter its budget that was prepared without consideration of" the fee. It says schools may pass the cost to F-1 students, "all students," or employers. At many public universities, budgets depend on legislative appropriations, and resident tuition is set or capped by a governing board or the legislature. A school may lack legal authority to add a new charge on short notice. DHS proposes an effective date 60 days after the final rule. It does not ask whether that fits state fiscal years, appropriation cycles or tuition-setting rules. It says it "is unable to estimate" the budgeting and transaction costs.

5. The state-level numbers exist but were not shown
DHS projects $12.4 billion in annual fees in its primary estimate and annualized costs up to $8.2 billion. It knows which public schools recommended OPT and how many students each recommended. It could estimate each state's exposure. It did not. Instead, the UMRA section says only that "state and private sector entities make the cost-benefit decisions" about OPT. That is a description of the choice, not an analysis of its cost.

6. Consultation would have surfaced better options
State higher-education agencies and public university systems run their own compliance and audit offices. Early consultation could have produced options that address fraud without billing state treasuries, such as employer-side checks at the Form I-983 stage or shared site-visit data. DHS invites comments now, but section 6(b) calls for consultation early in the process of developing the proposed regulation, not after publication.

7. Requests
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. If DHS pursues any OPT fee, it should first: (a) consult state and local officials under E.O. 13132 section 6(b) and UMRA section 204; (b) publish a federalism summary impact statement with estimated fee exposure for each state's public institutions; (c) reconcile its RFA, UMRA and federalism findings on whether public schools are state entities; and (d) exempt public institutions, or defer their obligation until the first state fiscal year that begins after the effective date.

PUBLIC COMMENT ON THE PROPOSED RULE REGARDING OPT FEES
Re: Comments in Opposition to the Proposed Assessment of a $100,000 Mandatory Fee on Optional Practical Training (OPT) Applicants
Dear Desk Officer / Regulatory Affairs Division,
This public comment is submitted to respectfully register strong opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $100,000 fee on Optional Practical Training (OPT) participants. While regulatory cost-recovery and oversight measures are recognized administrative priorities, the imposition of an exorbitant financial barrier of this scale creates profound, unintended, and highly destructive ramifications across domestic higher education, corporate investment structures, and long-term national competitiveness.
The economic and legal flaws of the proposed rule are articulated across three primary domains:
1. Severe Impairment of Global Educational Competitiveness and Institutional Revenue
The proposed $100,000 fee fundamentally alters the value proposition of domestic higher education for international scholars.
Market Diversion: Post-study work authorization via OPT is an integral component of the international education framework. Imposing a cost-prohibitive threshold will systematically divert prospective talent to competitor nations (such as the UK, Canada, Australia, and EU member states) that maintain viable post-graduation employment pathways.
Institutional Fiscal Strain: The resulting decline in international student enrollment will inflict substantial financial harm on higher education institutions. Because international students largely pay non-subsidized tuition, this fee policy threatens institutional revenue streams that directly support campus infrastructure, domestic student financial aid, and critical scientific research programs.
2. Risk of Capital Flight, Supply Chain Realignment, and Tax Base Erosion
The proposal creates unpredictable regulatory volatility in the domestic labor market, compelling corporate restructuring away from domestic jurisdictions.
Offshoring of Operations: Multinational and high-growth technology enterprises facing policy instability and artificial labor costs in the domestic market are increasingly incentivized to establish or expand regional headquarters, R&D facilities, and operational hubs in Europe and Asia.
Fiscal Losses: The physical relocation of early-career global talent and supporting business units will diminish domestic payroll tax contributions, corporate tax receipts, and local economic multiplier effects, ultimately undermining federal and local revenue generation.
3. Loss of High-Skilled Human Capital and Perceived Xenophobic Regulatory Shift
The rule signals a systemic policy pivot toward isolationism and regulatory hostility, eroding the nation's core innovation advantage.
Brain Drain: Depriving domestic industry of top-tier STEM and advanced-degree graduates weakens critical innovation ecosystems. Emerging industries reliant on highly technical labor will suffer immediate talent shortages.
Chilling Effect on Foreign Direct Investment (FDI): Beyond the quantitative financial burden, the policy conveys an impression of arbitrary, protectionist regulatory enforcement. This qualitative shift dissuades foreign entrepreneurs, scholars, and investors from establishing roots or deploying venture capital locally, compromising long-term technological supremacy.
Conclusion and Regulatory Recommendation
The proposed $100,000 OPT fee imposes disproportionate economic hardship, destabilizes institutional educational revenues, and incentivizes corporate capital flight without advancing any compelling statutory objective. Accordingly, the agency is strongly urged to withdraw this proposed fee rule in its entirety or significantly amend the regulatory impact analysis to consider viable, non-disruptive alternatives.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the proposed $100,000 OPT fee, citing severe negative impacts on competitiveness.

**Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees**

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation, including STEM OPT extensions.

As an international student who has invested significant time, financial resources, and effort into pursuing higher education and professional development in the United States, I am deeply concerned about the consequences of this proposal for international students, American universities, and the U.S. economy.

**First, the proposed fees are extraordinarily disproportionate and would effectively eliminate OPT opportunities for many qualified students.** Although the fees would formally be imposed on educational institutions, universities may pass these costs on to students or employers, or simply decline to support OPT applications. A $70,000 fee is far beyond the financial means of most students and would transform a long-established educational training opportunity into a privilege accessible primarily to the wealthy.

**Second, the proposal would undermine America's ability to attract and retain international talent.** International students contribute substantially to American universities, local communities, and the broader economy. Many pursue degrees in STEM, business, engineering, and other fields that support innovation and economic growth. OPT provides an important bridge between academic education and practical professional experience. Imposing such prohibitive fees would discourage talented students from choosing the United States and encourage them to pursue education and employment in countries with more accessible post-graduation opportunities.

**Third, the proposal creates significant uncertainty and unfairness for students who have already made educational and career commitments under the existing regulatory framework.** Students have selected universities, paid tuition, and planned their academic and professional futures with the reasonable expectation that OPT would remain accessible subject to established eligibility requirements. Introducing such substantial financial barriers without adequate protection for currently enrolled students would disrupt these legitimate expectations and potentially cause severe financial and professional harm.

**Finally, I respectfully question whether imposing extraordinary fees is a proportionate or effective approach to addressing fraud.** If the Department's objective is to strengthen program integrity, more targeted enforcement, employer verification, institutional oversight, and investigation of fraudulent activities would better address misconduct without penalizing the overwhelming majority of students who comply with immigration regulations.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee increases. At a minimum, I ask the Department to consider substantially lower, evidence-based fees, meaningful exemptions or financial hardship protections, and comprehensive transition relief for students already enrolled in U.S. educational programs.

The United States has long benefited from attracting ambitious international students who contribute their knowledge, skills, and productivity to American society. Policies that make legitimate practical training financially inaccessible risk weakening that competitive advantage.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they are disproportionate and harm students and the U.S. economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jacob Mathai
comments.commentText:
I am a U.S. citizen and a fifth-year PhD candidate and graduate worker in the Department of Immunobiology at Yale University. I study how the RAG recombinase, the enzyme that assembles antibody and T-cell receptor genes, evolved from ancient transposable elements, using biochemistry and structural biology. I am submitting this comment in my personal capacity. I am the kind of U.S. worker this proposed rule says it protects, and I believe it would harm me, my colleagues, and American science. I am writing to oppose the fees proposed at [8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)], [8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)], and [8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)]. I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.
1. Impact on my research and lab environment. Academic biomedical research depends on trainees. Graduate students and postdocs run most of the experiments in U.S. research labs, and many of them are international. In my lab, I work with 11 different graduate and postdoctoral workers, 8 of whom are working under visas. My own projects have depended on my international postdoctoral colleagues who brought skills and expertise that I did not possess. During my graduate education, I aimed to develop my expertise in protein purification, biochemistry, cryo-EM, bioinformatics, and computational biology. These international colleagues taught me these essential techniques, and my training would not be possible without their support and mentorship. These same colleagues were supported by an F1 visa during their graduate education in the US and the OPT and the STEM OPT extension supported their seamless transitions from their graduate studies towards postdoctoral positions. OPT and the STEM OPT extension let my colleagues finish their projects, publish, and develop their expertise so they can support my training and help me become a strong mentor and leader in the scientific fields of my interest. The proposed fee is $70,000 for a first OPT recommendation. That is more than the NIH’s own FY2026 NRSA stipend for a first-year postdoc ($63,480) and more than twice the NIH minimum predoctoral stipend ($29,364). Many universities and nonprofit research institutes cannot pay a fee of this size for every trainee. Where the fee is passed on, very few trainees will be able to afford to pay it. The predictable result is that projects are abandoned partway through and labs lose people they spent years training, along with the federal research money already invested in them.
2. Impact on academia and my career. DHS argues that OPT competes with U.S. workers. Academic research does not work that way. Research positions are created by grants, and grants are won by productive labs. When a lab loses trained scientists partway through a project, it publishes less, competes worse for funding, and hires fewer people, U.S. citizens included. As I move into postdoctoral work and, I hope, eventually run my own lab, my career will depend on joining and later building teams that can recruit the best scientists anywhere. This rule would shrink that pool and shift it toward people who can afford the fee rather than people with the most scientific promise. It would not make room for me. It would weaken the labs I hope to work in.
3. Impact on universities’ ability to recruit. International students compare U.S. programs against programs in other countries. In 2024, temporary visa holders earned 38% of U.S. science and engineering doctorates (NSF NCSES, Survey of Earned Doctorates). For many students, being able to gain training and work experience after graduation is part of why they choose a U.S. program. Countries competing for this talent offer post-study work pathways with no fee of this kind. Adding $70,000 to $100,000 to the cost of U.S. practical training would steer top applicants toward those countries before they ever apply here.
4. Impact on society and U.S. standing. The rule does not formally bar anyone from OPT, but at these prices it would end OPT for most participants. DHS states its goal is to fight fraud. Yet the fee applies equally to accredited research universities and to the “visa mills” DHS describes, so it does nothing to separate fraud from legitimate training. These fees do not act as a measure to mediate fraud, instead it will simply push trained scientists out of the United States after American institutions have worked and paid to educate them. These scientists will not be able to give back to the institutions and academic systems that have supported their training and these talented scientists will go onto to make their discoveries and new entrepreneurial ventures elsewhere. These fees will contribute to the brain drain that is currently occurring in the US. These fees will contribute to a loss of important talent and source of mentorship and training in the US academic system. If fraud is the concern, DHS should use enforcement aimed at the institutions committing it, not a flat fee on every student.

For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposal because it risks damaging America’s own economic interests. The United States attracts students from around the world, educates them at its universities, and then benefits when employers can hire those graduates. Making that last step prohibitively expensive would give competing countries an opportunity to recruit talent trained here.
The consequences would extend well beyond international students. If fewer students choose American universities, institutions could lose tuition revenue, putting pressure on research budgets, academic programs, and jobs. Local businesses would also lose spending on housing, food, transportation, and other services.
For American companies, especially startups and smaller businesses, these fees could make qualified graduates unaffordable to hire. Restricting access to talent could delay projects, raise recruitment costs, and encourage companies to expand teams overseas. Universities and research groups could face similar obstacles.
Protecting American workers is a legitimate goal, but this proposal could weaken the institutions and businesses that create American jobs. Target fraud and labor violations directly instead of imposing a financial barrier that risks driving education revenue, talent, and innovation out of the United States.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees harm the economy, universities, and businesses by driving talent away.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by James Farquhar
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposal to add these fees to the OPT program on the grounds listed below. For context, I am a University faculty member who trains students. Many of these are US. Some of these are international. Some of the international students have applied for and worked with the OPT program. The ones that have worked with the OPT program have been among the best and the brightest that I have worked with. While I do not work in Oil and Gas, these students have interestingly gone into that business. One subsequently took a job where he has contributed patents valued in the hundreds of millions to billions of dollars. I have written at least some letters for their OPT applications and I would not recommend someone who is sup par to one of these companies. The reason is simple. IF I recommend a subpar candidate, it will damage the chances of any future candidates I write letters for. This is part of the process of filtering out poor quality candidates. It is part of the process and it is where the focus should be if there are concerns about the system not working to bring the best and brightest to the US. Caliber and intellect does not follow nationality, race, or economic situation. However, those factors can affect how someone approaches and solves problems and this is important for business and research. This is the reason why I support OPT. It is also the reason why I argue that putting in a blanket disincentive like adding a high across the board cost, instead of tightening up the program to focus on quality is the wrong way to go. My views and some questions that should be addressed are enumerated below.
(1)Adding a charge is not a good way to improve the impact of OPT on the economy and to address the less poorly qualified OPT participants. It will shut down a program that has been highly successful in making contributions to the US workforce and economy without targeting the issue of quality of the participants.
(2)The goal of OPT as I understand it is to bring the best and brightest to the US research and business enterprise. It can also be beneficial to the economic strength of our country. This means making selections based on merit and capability without handouts to subpar, sub-quality workers/researchers. Adding a charge does not address the issue of worker quality and benefit of these workers to the US economy, it just puts in place a barrier to all participants and as a result will reduce the number of high quality workers contributing to the US economy. The program has checks and procedures for selection and those should be strengthened. If those are not working (for instance if inferior international students/workers are supplanting superior US students/workers) then there is a problem that should be fixed by changing the selection process not by changing the charge structure.
(3)What is unclear to me is adding the charges is a way to make money and then the question is does the money made by the government offset the money lost by the businesses and people with the loss of the quality workforce. This has not been addressed sufficiently.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states opposition to the proposed fees, arguing they act as a blanket disincentive for talented students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to formally submit my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to levy an unprecedented $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) authorizations and an additional $30,000 fee for subsequent STEM extensions. This extreme fee structure represents a multi-thousand percent escalation over historical baselines, effectively operating as a administrative ban on post-graduation professional training for the vast majority of international graduates from American research institutions.
Beyond its catastrophic financial impact on students and universities, this proposed rule exposes a glaring, counterproductive contradiction in current federal policy: the administration cannot aggressively champion the deregulation of the domestic artificial intelligence sector while simultaneously engineering prohibitive blockades against the high-skilled human capital required to build it.
The administration has repeatedly stated that maximizing domestic computing power, slashing regulatory red tape, and fast-tracking massive infrastructure projects—such as the multi-hundred-billion-dollar compute campuses—are vital national security imperatives necessary to outpace foreign adversaries. Yet, this strategy overlooks a fundamental economic reality: advanced hardware, energy grids, and deregulated regulatory frameworks are entirely inert without human intelligence. The rapid scaling of next-generation AI systems, advanced cryptography, and semiconductor design demands an extraordinary concentration of specialized STEM talent—specifically in advanced machine learning, quantum computing, and systems engineering.
For decades, the OPT and STEM OPT extension programs have served as the United States' most successful mechanism for retaining top-tier, globally recruited minds educated at premier American universities. Forcing these graduates, or their sponsoring academic institutions and employers, to absorb up to $100,000 in arbitrary fee assessments directly undermines the domestic technology pipeline.
The hypocrisy of this dual approach is stark. On one hand, the government intervenes in federal courts to shield AI developers from regulatory friction and uses emergency declarations to build data centers. On the other hand, it weaponizes the immigration bureaucracy to artificially choke off the supply of highly skilled technical experts who operate those very systems. You cannot accelerate the engine of technological progress while systematically starving it of fuel.
By imposing these massive costs, the policy introduces severe market friction and imposes an immense financial tax on innovation. The predictable macroeconomic outcome will not be the protection of domestic labor, but rather the forced migration of the world’s brightest researchers and engineers to competing global tech hubs in Europe, Canada, or Asia, where high-skilled immigration pathways are actively incentivized.
Furthermore, the brief 30-day public comment window provided for a regulatory shift of this magnitude is wholly inadequate. It violates the spirit of the Administrative Procedure Act by preventing universities, economic analysts, and industry stakeholders from fully quantifying the long-term structural damage this rule will inflict on American competitiveness.
Because this proposal is logically inconsistent with broader national strategic goals, economically counterproductive, and deeply damaging to the domestic technology ecosystem, I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to immediately withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed exorbitant OPT fees, arguing they act as a ban on post-graduation training.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a PhD student working on an impactful research & technology to improve the healthcare in the US. I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment shows that the fraud evidence in Sec. IV.A does not support the fees and that targeted enforcement fits the problem better.

The rule would require schools to pay $70,000 before a DSO first recommends a student for any OPT and $30,000 for each later recommendation, including STEM OPT (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). The fees go to the general Treasury. Fraud is DHS's main justification (Sec. IV.A, 91 FR 64570-72).

1. Anecdotes, not analysis. The record is one 2020 conviction of a shell-company operator, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story on about a dozen suspected shell companies, 2025 site visits in Northern Virginia, and a May 2026 ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp (91 FR 64570-71, nn.60-74). DHS gives no fraud rate, no trend, no audit, and no data in the docket.

2. The "10,000" figure is inconsistent. The text says an investigation found more than 10,000 students working for highly suspect employers (91 FR 64571, n.67). Footnote 56 says the same video showed 10,000 highly suspected employers. These are different claims. Suspicion is not a finding, and DHS reports no confirmed cases.

3. Even at face value it is about 3 percent: 3.4 percent of the 289,938 OPT and STEM OPT participants DHS's analysis counts for 2024, or 2.8 percent of the 360,078 its preamble counts. DHS would charge the other 97 percent.

4. The fraud is employer fraud; the fee ignores employers. Every specific finding (shell companies, empty buildings, residential worksites, "phantom employees," employer clusters sharing staff) concerns employers (91 FR 64571). Yet initial OPT needs no employer (91 FR 64569), the fee is "not tied to a specific employer," and changing employers triggers no fee or review (91 FR 64577). A student whose school paid $70,000 can move to a shell employer the next week unchecked.

5. A fee would not have stopped DHS's examples. The 2020 scheme sold false offer letters to at least 2,693 people "in exchange for a fee" (91 FR 64570); such schemes can simply raise their price. The foreign-agent case turned on lying to the U.S. Army, not inability to pay (n.62). On Sept. 14, 2026, a federal court faulted DHS's duration-of-status rule for resting on a few anecdotes the rule would not have prevented (Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, D. Mass. No. 1:26-cv-13799). The same flaw recurs here.

6. Existing tools work. Site visits, HSI investigations and prosecutions found every case DHS cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS cites, found OPT oversight had improved; ICE has implemented five of its seven recommendations and partly implemented the rest (91 FR 64570 n.56; 64572 n.81). ICE began DSO fraud training in November 2025 (n.81) and reports no results before turning to a fee.

7. DHS's diagnosis calls for resources the fee does not supply. The Ombudsman report DHS quotes blames compliance resources that have not kept pace with the program (91 FR 64571). About 60 field representatives cover some 6,186 schools (id.). OPT grew 21 percent from 2023 to 2024 (160,627 to 194,554), not "exponentially" (id.). That is a staffing problem, and the fee funds no staff (91 FR 64576).

8. The fee ignores compliance history. A school with a clean record pays the same $70,000 as a visa mill.

9. Fraud is real and should be prosecuted. The question is fit: the fee falls on everyone except the employers where the fraud was found.

RECOMMENDATIONS
- Withdraw the rule.
- Place in the docket the data behind the "10,000" figure, state whether it counts students or employers, and report confirmed cases.
- Extend risk-based site visits to post-completion OPT employers; require prompt employer reporting and E-Verify for initial OPT; use the address, ownership and payroll signals HSI identified to flag employer clusters.
- Act against noncompliant schools under existing SEVP authority (8 CFR 214.3-214.4).

CONCLUSION
DHS's own evidence shows employer fraud caught by existing enforcement. A fee on every student's school, untied to any employer and funding no enforcement, does not address that problem at all. DHS should withdraw the rule and target fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule due to lack of valid fraud evidence.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Sec. IV.B - DHS misreads its own data and the labor-market evidence

I am a PhD Student working in improving the healthcare sector through my research contributions. I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment shows that the worker-protection rationale in Sec. IV.B rests on inconsistent figures and on evidence that does not measure OPT.

The rule would require schools to pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including STEM OPT (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). Sec. IV.B says the fees protect U.S. workers (91 FR 64572-74).

1. One number to justify the rule, another to price it. The preamble says STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of about 92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, citing 165,524 participants in 2024 (91 FR 64573). That counts everyone active at any time in 2024 in a 24-month program. DHS's impact analysis uses 95,384 STEM OPT participants in 2024 to compute fees (Sec. VII.A.3). On that basis STEM OPT is near the 2016 projection and about 12 percent above the 85,000 annual H-1B cap, not "nearly double." DHS does not say what the 2016 projection measured. An agency may not rest a rule on figures it contradicts without explanation (Encino Motorcars v. Navarro, 579 U.S. 211 (2016)).

2. The labor claims are borrowed. Every labor statistic in Sec. IV.B comes from Proclamation 10973 on the H-1B program: unemployment of recent computer-science graduates, growth of all foreign-born STEM workers since 2000, and a 2017 study of 2001 data (nn.84, 91-93, 111-112). None measures OPT. DHS's accounting statement lists the rule's effects on wages and growth as "N/A" (Table 1, 91 FR 64580). DHS cannot claim to protect wages while declining to estimate any wage effect.

3. The study DHS cites concludes the opposite. Bound, Khanna and Morales modeled H-1B computer scientists in 1994-2001, before STEM OPT existed. They estimate U.S. computer scientists' 2001 wages would have been 2.6-5.1 percent higher without immigration, but find it raised overall U.S. welfare and U.S. workers' incomes (0.2-0.3 percent), lowered IT prices, and raised IT output 1.9-2.5 percent. DHS quotes the side effect and omits the conclusion.

4. Research on OPT itself finds gains for U.S. workers. A February 2026 study of the 2016 STEM OPT expansion found growing employment gains for native high-skilled and STEM workers and more firm creation (Kwon, Lee and Monras, UPF Economics Working Paper 1940). An NFAP analysis found more OPT approvals relative to U.S. workers associated with lower U.S. STEM unemployment (Zavodny, March 2019). DHS addresses neither. BLS data, as reported, show unemployment in computer and math occupations falling from 3.9 percent (Sept. 2025) to 3.3 percent (Sept. 2026).

5. DHS reverses its 2016 findings without evidence. In 2016 DHS found that education, exchange and STEM innovation benefit the economy and U.S. workers (91 FR 64573, quoting 81 FR 13040). Contrary new findings require a reasoned explanation (FCC v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502, 515-16 (2009)). DHS offers belief.

6. FICA is set by Congress, not changed by the fee. The payroll-tax exemption is statutory (26 U.S.C. 3121(b)(19)) and also covers CPT and on-campus work (n.108). A fee paid by a school leaves every employer's FICA savings unchanged. DHS counts possible FICA gains as a benefit but ignores income taxes OPT workers pay.

7. Protections exist; DHS does not verify them. STEM OPT employers attest on Form I-983 that students will not replace U.S. workers and will be paid commensurately, and DHS may verify by site visit (nn.53-54). DHS's complaint is that it rarely verifies (91 FR 64573). That calls for verification, not a fee.

8. "Circumvention" is DHS's own design. DHS gives no data on how many OPT participants later obtain H-1B status or displace U.S. hires. Its cap-gap rules, expanded in 2024, exist to carry OPT workers into H-1B status (91 FR 64568-69).

- Withdraw the Sec. IV.B rationale or support it with OPT-specific wage and employment analysis.
- Reconcile the 165,524 and 95,384 figures and state what the 2016 projection measured.
- Address the OPT-specific research above.
- Enforce Form I-983 attestations with risk-based site visits.

The worker-protection rationale rests on a number DHS's own analysis does not use, statistics about a different program, and a study whose conclusion runs the other way. Research on OPT itself finds U.S. workers gain. DHS should withdraw the rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Sec. IV.C - A price is not a screen, and DHS dismissed better alternatives

I am a student at a top university in US. I used my analytical skills to do some digging on the claims used to back this proposal.
TLDR: I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment shows that a fee cannot do the screening Sec. IV.C expects, creates perverse incentives, and was chosen over alternatives DHS never evaluated.

The rule would require schools to pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). DHS expects schools to recommend only "the most promising students" (91 FR 64574) and chose a fee over site visits, training plans and reporting because it is faster and cheaper for the government (91 FR 64576).

1. A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit, honesty or the value of a placement. Schemes that already sell job letters can build it into their price. An honest student without $70,000 cannot.

2. Pass-through dissolves the incentive. DHS says schools "may pass the financial obligation" to F-1 students, "all students," or employers (91 FR 64575, 64578). If someone else pays, the school bears no cost and has no new reason to screen. DHS cannot rely on pass-through to soften the burden and on school-borne cost to produce screening.

3. "All students" means American students' tuition could fund a federal levy on international students' training (91 FR 64575).

4. The gatekeepers are unequipped. DHS calls DSOs "often overwhelmed" and "not fully trained" (91 FR 64574), then makes them the screen with no training, staff or criteria, and declines to define the "genuine educational value" they should screen for (91 FR 64575).

5. The school pays before any employer exists. Initial OPT requires no job offer (91 FR 64569), so the fee is paid when there is no placement to evaluate.

6. Perverse incentives DHS does not consider:
- A shift to CPT, which the rule leaves untouched although DHS says CPT fraud has been "historically prevalent" and is growing (91 FR 64576).
- A penalty on work-study: pre-completion ($70,000), post-completion ($30,000) and STEM OPT ($30,000) total $130,000, versus $100,000 for a student who skipped training during school (91 FR 64577).
- An opening for foreign money: DHS warns adversaries may subsidize fees through gifts to schools (91 FR 64575). The rule creates the gap that invites them.

7. Unsupported assertions. DHS says the fees are "on par with" one or two years of tuition, with no data (91 FR 64575), and that the fee "serves as a clear signal to the public" (91 FR 64576). Signaling cannot justify a $109 billion charge.

8. Alternatives dismissed for convenience. DHS rejects site visits, training plans and reporting because a fee "can be implemented quickly" and needs no "significant additional resources" (91 FR 64576). Those tools uncovered every fraud case DHS cites, and GAO-19-297 found oversight improving. DHS estimates neither the cost nor the effectiveness of any alternative, and calls the fee only "a crucial first step" (id.), conceding it is not enough. Administrative ease is not a reasoned choice among alternatives (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983)).

9. "Schools can decline to recommend students" (91 FR 64578) is the design: OPT restricted by price instead of by a rule that says so and justifies it.

SUGGESTIONS
- Withdraw the fee.
- If DHS wants schools to screen, define criteria, fund DSO training, and use SEVP's authority over noncompliant schools (8 CFR 214.3-214.4).
- Evaluate, with cost and effectiveness estimates, risk-based site visits and training plans for post-completion OPT employers.
- If any charge survives, exempt pre-completion OPT.

A price cannot do the screening DHS describes, and DHS's own pass-through provision ensures it will not. The tools that found the fraud DHS cites remain available. DHS should withdraw the rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Secs. III.A and IV.C - The fee is a tax Congress has not authorized

I am a working professional interested in pursuing law major. I analysed the rule and here are my conclusions:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment shows that the charge is a tax that DHS lacks authority to impose.

Schools would pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). The money would go to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302; DHS concedes no statute lets ICE keep it (91 FR 64576). DHS relies on the "time and conditions" power in INA 214(a) (91 FR 64567).

1. The charge has every feature of a tax. It is set to deter, not to recover a cost. It buys no service. It goes to general revenue. Its amount was chosen to "closely align with the H-1B fees," not from any cost study (91 FR 64575). DHS projects $74.6-144.3 billion in transfers over ten years (91 FR 64579).

2. Congress authorizes immigration fees to recover costs. INA 286(m), 8 U.S.C. 1356(m), allows fees that recover the full cost of adjudication services. Congress funded SEVIS through a separate fee (8 U.S.C. 1372(e)), and DHS's 2019 SEVP fee rule set fees to recover program costs (84 FR 23930). The user-fee statute, 31 U.S.C. 9701, ties charges to the value of a service. DHS invokes none of these.

3. INA 214(a) is not a taxing power. Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), upheld OPT as a condition of stay; it says nothing about revenue. Narenji v. Civiletti, 617 F.2d 745 (D.C. Cir. 1979), upheld a reporting requirement. A charge exceeding the value of a service to the payer is a tax (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). Congress may delegate taxing power, but it must do so (Skinner v. Mid-America Pipeline Co., 490 U.S. 212 (1989)).

4. INA 274A(h)(1) does not help. DHS cites it (91 FR 64575), but it requires limits on employment to be stated on work documents. It says nothing about fees.

5. The scale demands clear authorization. A levy of this size, reshaping a program used by about 280,000 students a year, is a question of vast economic significance (West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022)). DHS's reading of INA 214(a) gets no deference (Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)).

6. A court has called the fee this one copies a tax. On June 8, 2026, the District of Massachusetts held the $100,000 H-1B payment a tax and vacated its implementing policy (State of California et al., D. Mass. No. 1:25-cv-13829); the First Circuit declined to stay that ruling on July 24, 2026. On Sept. 30, 2026, the Northern District of California vacated the agency policies implementing that fee and its renewal, faulting them for ignoring alternatives and reliance interests (Global Nurse Force v. Trump). DHS benchmarks this fee to the H-1B fee (91 FR 64575) without mentioning any of these rulings.

7. "Without the fees, OPT may close" is a non sequitur. DHS says three times it "may shut down the program entirely" without the fees (91 FR 64572, 64574). None of the money reaches OPT oversight (91 FR 64576). The fee works only by reducing participation. If DHS means to restrict OPT, it must propose that directly and justify it.

8. Anticipated responses. A D.C. district court upheld the H-1B fee in the Chamber of Commerce case, now on appeal, but rested on the President's statutory power over entry, which this rule does not invoke. Calling the charge a "deterrent" does not help: a charge untied to cost, designed to suppress an activity, and paid into general revenue is what the Massachusetts court called a tax.

ADVICE
- Withdraw the rule.
- Any OPT-related fee should be cost-based, set under a statute that authorizes it, and retained for SEVP compliance.
- If DHS claims taxing authority, identify the statute and explain why it reaches a $109 billion levy.

DHS concedes it cannot keep the money, admits the amount was copied from a fee a court has called a tax, and identifies no statute authorizing revenue of this scale. DHS should withdraw the rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Sec. VII.A - The regulatory impact analysis cannot support the rule

I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment shows that the cost-benefit analysis in Sec. VII.A is unreliable.

Schools would pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). DHS estimates annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion, transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion, and ten-year transfers of $109.4 billion (primary), and monetizes no benefit (91 FR 64579-80).

1. No monetized benefits against billions in costs. Executive Orders 12866 and 13563, which DHS says apply, require a reasoned finding that benefits justify costs (91 FR 64579).

2. The cost cap is circular. DHS values lost OPT at only the unpaid fee, because if OPT is worth more, "affected parties could collectively cost share to preserve OPT" (91 FR 64588-89). That is not conservative:
- much of OPT's value goes to people who never pay: taxpayers, local economies, U.S. co-workers and firms;
- initial OPT needs no employer (91 FR 64569), so no employer exists to share the cost;
- students cannot borrow $70,000 against a job they do not have;
- the cap keeps measured losses small whatever their true value.

3. The participation scenarios are unexplained. The high scenario assumes no decline. The low scenario keeps 88,374 initial and 74,088 STEM OPT participants a year (Sec. VII.A.3), implying 84 percent pay another $30,000 for STEM OPT, though DHS's data show about 56 percent continue with no fee (id.).

4. DHS ignores evidence on fee response. DHS matched this fee to the $100,000 H-1B fee (91 FR 64575). As reported, the 2026 proclamation renewing that fee said employers paid it for only about 700 people, and DHS's own H-1B fee rule reported a 91.2 percent drop in initial H-1B petitions. A recent paper estimates a $100,000 practical-training charge could cut OPT up to 84 percent for bachelor's and 99 percent for master's graduates (Clemens, IZA DP 18933).

5. Enrollment losses are acknowledged, then dropped. DHS concedes schools unable to fund the fees may lose enrollment revenue (Sec. VII.A) but never estimates it. International students contributed about $43.8 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 378,000 jobs in 2023-24 (NAFSA data). On Sept. 14, 2026, a federal court found DHS's duration-of-status rule likely arbitrary partly because DHS treated unquantified enrollment losses as zero (Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, D. Mass. No. 1:26-cv-13799). This NPRM repeats the error. See Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Transfers are not free. DHS treats $8.7-16.9 billion a year from schools as costless, with no analysis of who ultimately pays through higher tuition, program and research cuts, or the domestic students DHS says may be charged (91 FR 64575).

7. Lost tax revenue is ignored. DHS counts possible FICA gains (Table 1) but not the income and payroll taxes lost when OPT workers leave.

8. The accounting statement contradicts the rule. Table 1 lists effects on wages, growth, and state, local and tribal governments as "N/A" (91 FR 64580), though the rule's purpose is wage protection and 1,044 public institutions would pay (Sec. VII.B). Its first listed benefit, enforcing the INA's "unlawful presence" provisions, has no evident connection to a training fee.

9. The paperwork estimate is implausible: 5 minutes per DSO response to confirm a $70,000 payment (PRA section), while budgeting, accounting and audit burdens go unquantified (Table 1).

RECOMMENDATIONS
- Withdraw the rule.
- Any reproposal should monetize benefits; ground participation scenarios in evidence, including the H-1B fee response; value lost OPT at its social value; quantify enrollment, tax and research losses; analyze who bears the transfers; and publish the underlying data.

DHS monetizes no benefit, caps costs by assumption, picks participation figures without evidence, and omits enrollment losses a court has already faulted it for ignoring. The analysis cannot support a $109 billion rule. DHS should withdraw it.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and argues the cost-benefit analysis is unreliable.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Secs. V.A and VI - Reliance interests, and the per-degree-level fee alternative

I am a student working on a startup to improve the healthcare and legal sector by making their services affordable to the Americans. I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment addresses DHS's treatment of reliance interests (Sec. VI) and responds to its request for comment on charging the initial fee again at each degree level (Sec. V.A).

Schools would pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including the STEM extension (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). DHS concludes that reliance interests are "speculative" and outweighed (91 FR 64577-79).

1. About 280,000 people a year rely on OPT. DHS calls reliance "speculative" because only about 20 percent of 1.4 million F-1 students used OPT in 2024 (91 FR 64578). That is about 280,000 people who chose programs, borrowed money and planned careers around a benefit offered for decades. On Sept. 14, 2026, a federal court faulted DHS for dismissing similar concerns as "speculative" without analysis (Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, D. Mass. No. 1:26-cv-13799).

2. Current students and workers pay at once. DHS's model assumes everyone recommended in Year 1 pays $70,000, including students already on OPT who seek the STEM extension (Sec. VII.A.3). They are in the U.S., employed, on training plans DHS approved. DHS concedes current students are in a different position from prospective ones (91 FR 64578 n.124), then treats them the same.

3. "Never intended to provide a pathway to employment" contradicts DHS's own history. DHS's preamble traces student practical-training employment to 1947 regulations (91 FR 64568 n.24). The D.C. Circuit upheld OPT employment as a lawful condition of F-1 status (Washington Alliance v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (2022)). DHS publishes a STEM Designated Degree Program List that schools build programs around (91 FR 64570 n.49). An agency changing a policy with serious reliance interests must weigh them (DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1 (2020); FCC v. Fox, 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009)).

4. The alternatives DHS names are not substitutes. DHS points to H-1B after graduation and on- or off-campus work during study (91 FR 64578). H-1B is capped and allocated by lottery; OPT is how graduates stay employed while awaiting selection, which is why DHS's own cap-gap rules exist (91 FR 64568-69).

5. Employers' reliance is waved away. DHS says employers can "recruit U.S. citizens" (91 FR 64578) without asking whether qualified workers exist in the fields, regions and timelines involved, including the state and local government employers DHS itself names.

6. No recourse for errors. Refunds are available only if no EAD issues, and SEVP's decisions are "final and not appealable" (91 FR 64577). If a student loses an OPT job to a fraudulent employer, the school gets nothing back.

7. The per-degree-level alternative should be rejected. DHS asks whether to charge $70,000 again at each higher degree level (91 FR 64577). A student earning a bachelor's, master's and doctorate in the U.S. would owe $210,000 in initial fees before any $30,000 subsequent fees. It falls hardest on those who invest longest in American education, including doctoral researchers who staff U.S. laboratories. DHS identifies no fraud pattern tied to degree level.

Here are my suggestions:
1. Withdraw the rule.
2. If any fee survives, exempt every student enrolled before the final rule's effective date, including those seeking STEM extensions.
3. Reject the per-degree-level alternative.
4. Make refund decisions appealable, and allow refunds when OPT ends early through no fault of the student or school.

DHS dismisses the plans of roughly 280,000 people a year as speculative, charges current students at once, and proposes an alternative that would cost doctoral students $210,000. DHS should withdraw the rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Sec. VII.B, UMRA and E.O. 13132 - Small institutions, states and federalism

The statistics provided by the department are very misleading and not at all convincing. As an economist who is proficient in understanding basic numbers, I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. This comment shows that DHS acknowledges heavy costs on small institutions and state universities but declines to mitigate them or consult the states.

Schools would pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). DHS counts 2,478 affected schools: 1,044 public, 1,294 private non-profit and 140 for-profit (Sec. VII.B).

1. Severe impacts on small institutions. Of 1,389 small affected institutions, in the transition year 841 (60.5 percent) face costs above 1 percent of revenue and 116 (8.4 percent) above 20 percent (Sec. VII.B). Even after the transition, only 622 stay at or below 1 percent, so 767 (55 percent) exceed it (id.).

2. DHS rejects relief for the wrong reason. It declined a small-entity exemption because small entities are 56 percent of certified schools (91 FR 64576). That is why the Regulatory Flexibility Act requires DHS to analyze significant alternatives (5 U.S.C. 603(c)), not a reason to skip them. DHS did not analyze tiered fees, caps, phase-ins, or exemptions for schools with clean compliance records.

3. Small schools are not where DHS found fraud. DHS identifies no evidence that small institutions as a class drive OPT fraud. Its examples involve employers (91 FR 64571).

4. States pay, yet DHS finds no state effect. DHS sampled the 1,044 public institutions, found them state-run, and excludes them from the small-entity analysis because they are run by states (91 FR 64591-92, n.137). Its UMRA section concedes the rule exceeds the inflation-adjusted $100 million threshold ($211.36 million) in year one. Yet Table 1 lists effects on state, local and tribal governments as "N/A" (91 FR 64580), and DHS finds no federalism implications warranting a summary impact statement under E.O. 13132. DHS cannot treat these schools as arms of the state in one analysis and ignore the states in the next.

5. No consultation. E.O. 13132 sec. 6(b) bars rules with federalism implications that impose substantial direct compliance costs on states, and are not required by statute, unless the agency funds those costs or consults state and local officials early. The NPRM describes no consultation with any state official.

6. No distributional analysis. DHS does not show how costs fall by state, region or type of institution, although states and regional schools with many international students will bear far more than others.

a) Withdraw the rule.
b) If DHS proceeds, analyze and adopt small-entity alternatives: tiered fees, caps, phase-ins, and exemptions for schools with clean compliance records.
c) Prepare a federalism summary impact statement and consult state officials and their national organizations before any final rule.
d) Correct Table 1 and publish institution-level impacts by state and institution type.

DHS's own figures show severe harm to most small institutions and billions in costs to state universities, yet DHS offers no relief, no consultation and no federalism analysis. DHS should withdraw the rule.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees, cites severe financial impacts on small schools, and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I have taken lectures at one of the topmost universities including in the US. I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. At a minimum, DHS should extend the comment period to at least 60 days, correct its baseline, and place its key evidence in the docket.

Schools would pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). OMB designated the rule economically significant (91 FR 64579). Comments on the rule are due November 9, 2026; comments on its information collection are due December 7, 2026 (91 FR 64566).

1. Thirty days for a $109 billion rule. DHS allows about 30 days to comment on a rule with $109.4 billion in projected ten-year transfers, but 60 days on a paperwork burden it estimates at 5 minutes per response. E.O. 12866 sec. 6(a)(1) says the comment period should in most cases be at least 60 days; E.O. 13563 sec. 2(b) says the same.

2. DHS confuses comment with notice. DHS says the 30-day period, a delayed effective date and prospective application give students "ample time" to "depart the United States" (91 FR 64578). Time to leave the country is not time to comment on whether the rule should exist.

3. The baseline relies on a postponed rule. DHS justifies the higher initial fee partly by vetting under the Duration of Status Final Rule, 91 FR 44976, counting it among "the regulations currently in effect" (91 FR 64575 n.115). On Sept. 14, 2026, more than three weeks before this NPRM was published, a federal court postponed that rule and barred DHS from implementing it (Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, D. Mass. No. 1:26-cv-13799). The baseline is wrong, and the stated reason for the gap between the $70,000 and $30,000 fees falls with it.

4. The fee benchmark is a vacated fee. DHS set the amount to "closely align with the H-1B fees" (91 FR 64575) without disclosing that two federal district courts had vacated policies implementing the $100,000 H-1B fee and the First Circuit had declined to stay one of those rulings.

5. Key evidence is missing from the docket. The central fraud claim rests on a YouTube video cited by timestamp (91 FR 64571, nn.67-74); the underlying HSI data are not available. The public cannot test what it cannot see. Agencies must disclose the critical factual material behind a proposal (Portland Cement Ass'n v. Ruckelshaus, 486 F.2d 375 (D.C. Cir. 1973)).

6. Signs of haste. The NPRM cites Proclamation 10973 as 90 FR 46027 (Sept. 24, 2025) in one note and as "90 FR (Sept. 19, 2025)," with no page, in another (nn.84, 116). It calls the "10,000" figure students in the text and employers in footnote 56. It uses 165,524 STEM OPT participants in the preamble and 95,384 in the impact analysis. Its accounting statement lists a benefit, enforcing "unlawful presence" provisions, with no evident connection to a training fee (Table 1).

- Extend the comment period to at least 60 days from publication, to no earlier than December 7, 2026.
- Place in the docket the HSI data behind the "10,000" figure, any OPT fraud rates, the data behind the participation tables, and any analysis supporting the fee amounts.
- Correct the baseline for the postponed Duration of Status rule and disclose the H-1B fee litigation.
- After corrections, repropose with a new comment period.

A rule of this size deserves a full comment period, a lawful baseline and a public record. DHS gave none of the three. DHS should withdraw the rule or, at minimum, extend the comment period and complete the docket.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Secs. IV.B and VI - The rule works against American students, workers, research and competitiveness

I oppose the proposed OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. DHS says the fees put "the United States' interests first" (91 FR 64572). This comment shows that Americans would bear the costs.

Schools would pay $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)). DHS projects $8.7-16.9 billion a year in payments from 2,478 schools, 1,044 of them public (91 FR 64579; Sec. VII.B).

1. American students pay. DHS lets schools pass the fee to "all students" (91 FR 64575), so domestic tuition could fund a federal levy on international students' training. International enrollment also supports domestic students: one study found each additional 10 bachelor's degrees awarded to international students associated with 15 more STEM bachelor's degrees for U.S. students (Zavodny, NFAP).

2. American universities pay or shrink. International students contributed about $43.8 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 378,000 jobs in 2023-24 (NAFSA data). DHS never estimates the enrollment it would lose.

3. American workers gain from OPT. A February 2026 study of the 2016 STEM OPT expansion found growing employment gains for native high-skilled and STEM workers and new firm creation (Kwon, Lee and Monras, UPF Economics Working Paper 1940).

4. American research depends on it. NFAP estimates international students are about 75-80 percent of full-time graduate students in AI-related fields such as computer and information sciences. Many begin their research careers in U.S. labs on OPT.

5. American startups begin on OPT. Cloudflare co-founder Michelle Zatlyn has said OPT let her develop the company's business plan after graduation; the company now employs over 5,000 people (as reported).

6. Competitor nations gain. Canada, the United Kingdom and Australia offer post-study work authorization, and none charges anything close to $70,000. DHS concedes OPT is one factor in where students choose to study (91 FR 64578). Raising its price sends that talent, and the firms it would build, to competitors.

7. Taxpayers lose. Departing graduates take their income and payroll taxes and local spending with them; DHS counts none of it.

8. Security is not served. The documented fraud is employer fraud, yet the fee is not tied to any employer (91 FR 64577) and funds no enforcement (91 FR 64576). DHS warns the fee may invite foreign subsidies to schools (91 FR 64575).

9. The constitutional order suffers when an agency raises billions in revenue Congress never authorized; DHS concedes no statute lets ICE retain the money (91 FR 64576).

10. DHS's own 2016 finding was that education, exchange and STEM innovation benefit the economy and U.S. workers (91 FR 64573). DHS offers no evidence that this has changed.

- Withdraw the rule.
- Pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers and noncompliant schools.
- Before any reproposal, analyze effects on domestic students' tuition, research output, startups and U.S. competitiveness for talent.

The fraud DHS describes is real and should be prosecuted. But a rule that taxes the honest majority, leaves fraudulent employers untouched, and sends the money everywhere except enforcement serves neither American workers nor American security. DHS should withdraw it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Title/Subject: Public Comment on Proposed Rule: Optional Practical Training Fees (DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-XXXX)
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposal to charge very high new fees for the Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT extension programs. While DHS has the authority to regulate F-1 students doing temporary practical training, the argument that these extreme fees are necessary to stop fraud and improve the immigration system is wrong and unfair. This proposal should be canceled for the following five reasons:

1. Unfair Punishment for Innocent Students
The proposal punishes the vast majority of law-abiding international students for the wrongdoings of a very small number of bad actors. In a fair legal system, enforcement costs should be paid by the entities committing the fraud—such as fake staffing agencies and shell companies—not by honest students who are the victims, not the creators, of these scams.

2. Driving Away Top Talent While Failing to Stop Criminals
While the goal is to stop fraud, a $70,000 fee will actually do the exact opposite. Excellent, law-abiding students who have real job offers will be forced to give up their practical training because they cannot afford this huge amount of money. On the other hand, criminals backed by wealthy, illegal networks will easily pay this fee just to buy legal status. This rule will push away the best students while failing to stop real fraud.

3. Charging Twice for the Same Service (Double Dipping)
The government claims these fees are needed to pay for company visits and employer background checks. However, this is a form of "double dipping." Employers using the STEM OPT program must already use E-Verify, and employers sponsoring H-1B visas already pay hundreds or thousands of dollars in "Fraud Prevention and Detection Fees." Since these companies are already checked and funded through employer-paid fees, charging students tens of thousands of dollars for the same exact oversight is redundant and unfair.

4. Violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), government agency fees must be reasonably close to the actual cost of providing the service. In today's digital age, checking if a company is real by matching information with IRS tax data, Social Security Numbers (SSN), or electronic systems costs less than $10 per case. A $70,000 bill has no connection to actual administrative costs. It acts as a punishment tax designed to stop students from applying, which goes beyond what DHS is legally allowed to do.

5. Hurting the True Educational Purpose of OPT
The legal purpose of OPT is to be an extension of a student’s education; it is not a standard foreign labor program. Putting up an impossible financial wall to post-graduation training will immediately hurt the global appeal of U.S. universities. By driving top global talent to other countries, this rule will hurt America's technological innovation and economic leadership, which goes completely against the goal of keeping America competitive.
For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw this harmful proposal and instead use smart, data-driven methods to catch fraud without punishing innocent students.

Respectfully submitted,

A Concerned F-1 Student
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition to the proposed OPT fees, arguing they are unfair and punish innocent students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to levy a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) authorizations and an additional $30,000 fee for subsequent STEM extensions must be withdrawn. The imposition of a cumulative $100,000 regulatory assessment on international graduates seeking post-completion technical training constitutes an unprecedented financial barrier that operates as a de facto administrative prohibition on high-skilled workforce participation.
This proposed regulatory framework introduces a profound, counterproductive contradiction within broader federal policy objectives. While the administration prioritizes aggressive deregulation and infrastructure fast-tracking to accelerate the domestic artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced technology sectors, this rule simultaneously engineers prohibitive market friction against the specialized human capital essential to sustain those sectors. Advanced hardware, domestic compute campuses, and deregulated frameworks are entirely inert without human intelligence. The rapid scaling of next-generation machine learning, quantum computing, and cryptography requires a concentrated supply of elite technical talent. Weaponizing administrative fee adjustments to choke off the supply of highly skilled technical experts directly undermines the domestic technology pipeline.
For decades, the OPT and STEM OPT extension programs have served as the premier mechanism for retaining top-tier, globally recruited minds educated at leading American research institutions. Forcing these graduates or their prospective employers to absorb exorbitant, non-statutory upfront costs introduces artificial labor market distortions. The predictable macroeconomic consequence of this rule will not be the safeguarding of domestic labor, but rather a severe, self-inflicted contraction of the American innovation ecosystem.
Global technical talent is highly mobile. By artificially inflating the cost of domestic professional integration, this policy creates a powerful economic incentive for elite researchers and engineers to migrate to competing technological hubs in Europe, Canada, and Asia, where high-skilled immigration pathways are actively optimized. Consequently, American universities will suffer a sharp decline in global academic competitiveness, and domestic industries will face acute, structural labor shortages in critical STEM fields.
Furthermore, the allocation of a restrictive 30-day public comment window for a regulatory modification of this magnitude is procedurally deficient. Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), a 30-day timeline is wholly inadequate for universities, economic analysts, and industry stakeholders to comprehensively quantify the long-term structural and macroeconomic damage this rule will inflict on American industrial competitiveness.
An administration cannot logically seek to outpace foreign adversaries in technological innovation while systematically starving the domestic tech engine of its primary catalyst: elite human capital. Because this proposal is logically inconsistent with stated national security imperatives, economically counterproductive, and procedurally rushed, the Department of Homeland Security must immediately withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees act as an unprecedented financial barrier and must be withdrawn.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by David Reitze
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is David Reitze, and I'm the Executive Director of the NSF's LIGO Laboratory and a Research Professor of Physics at Caltech.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

LIGO Laboratory like many laboratories and universities across the US rely on bright young researchers from the US and abroad to advance our scientific mission. The imposition of a $100,000 fee for the OPT visa will essentially turn of the pipeline of talented overseas researchers because US universities do not have the financial resources to pay that fee. This will have the direct consequence of reducing the number of qualified researchers in the US and, as a result, further erode the US's scientific capabilities.

International students make up more than 1/3 of the total graduate student population in STEM fields. In 2024, approximately 165,000 foreign researchers in STEM had OPT visa (Source: SEVIS). The loss of this critical source of talent would create a void that US students would not be able to fill.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Dr. David Reitze

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yicui Ding
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation, including STEM OPT extensions.

As a prospective international graduate student interested in computer science and artificial intelligence, I believe that practical training is an essential part of higher education. The opportunity to apply academic knowledge in real-world environments is one of the major reasons international students choose to study in the United States.

First, these proposed fees would create substantial financial barriers for international students. Many students and their families already make significant financial sacrifices to afford tuition, living expenses, and other educational costs. Although the proposed fees would formally be paid by educational institutions, those costs could ultimately be passed on to students or employers. As a result, access to practical training could increasingly depend on financial resources rather than academic ability, professional qualifications, or individual merit.

Second, the proposed rule could undermine America's ability to attract talented international students. The United States has long benefited from welcoming students who contribute to academic research, technological development, and innovation. In rapidly developing fields such as artificial intelligence, computer science, and engineering, practical training provides an important bridge between university education and professional contribution. Creating such substantial financial barriers could discourage talented students from pursuing their education and careers in the United States.

Third, these fees could disproportionately disadvantage smaller universities, startups, research organizations, and students pursuing early-career opportunities. Large institutions may have greater financial resources to accommodate additional costs, while smaller organizations may struggle to support international graduates. This could reduce opportunities for students and limit the range of institutions able to benefit from their skills.

I recognize the importance of preventing fraud, maintaining immigration system integrity, and protecting American workers. However, these legitimate objectives should be pursued through targeted oversight, stronger compliance mechanisms, and effective enforcement rather than disproportionately high fees that could restrict legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and consider more proportionate, evidence-based alternatives that protect the integrity of the OPT program while preserving educational access, innovation, and opportunities for qualified international students.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,

A Prospective International Graduate Student
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees due to financial barriers and harm to students.

I support increasing OPT, H-1B, and H-4 fees, or even eliminating these visa programs altogether if necessary to combat widespread fraud and abuse. My personal experience explains why I feel this way.

A few years ago, I joined the information security team of a financial services company as a manager. The company claimed to manage hundreds of billions, potentially even a trillion dollars, in assets. Ironically, it had also recently suffered security incidents resulting in millions of dollars in losses.

After joining, I noticed that one of the senior security specialists was significantly underperforming despite claiming years of experience in the field. Eventually, this individual admitted that it was their first time doing anything related to information security and that they had never even taken a college course in the subject. This person was working on OPT. I was baffled by how they had cleared the interview process in the first place.

Unfortunately, this was just the beginning.

Nearly every resume I received was from an OPT candidate claiming experience that, based on my subsequent interactions, appeared fabricated. I am not exaggerating when I say that this was an overwhelming pattern in the resumes coming through reputed staffing firms across the NJ, PA, and NY tristate area.

How is this supposed to help a company improve its security posture when it is paying substantial salaries to people who may not have the skills or experience they claim to possess?

I never got an opportunity to hire an American citizen. Eventually, many of these OPT candidates were replaced by H-4, H-1B, and other OPT candidates who were relatives, spouses, or acquaintances of existing employees and managers. Many of these employees were current or former H-1B holders who had been waiting years for green cards. I also encountered H-1B employees running side businesses while employed full-time.

And who ended up losing their jobs during restructuring?

American citizens who had taken out student loans, worked hard in college, built careers, paid their taxes, and were trying to pay off their debts and raise families. People who followed the rules, worked hard, and simply wanted an opportunity to make an honest living.

Here is a question worth asking:

Visit the IT departments of Fortune 1000 companies across NJ, NY, PA, and TX. Look at the workforce composition and ask why, in some departments, American citizens appear so underrepresented while employees on current or former H-1B, H-4, and OPT status seem to dominate.
