comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees. This comment tests the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) in section VII.A against E.O. 12866 and OMB Circular A-4 (2003), which DHS cites in footnotes 126 and 130.

1. Once transfers are removed, one unquantified benefit is left
The RIA names three benefits: program integrity, protecting U.S. workers, and "alleviating burdens imposed on DHS tied to OPT investigations." DHS then classifies the worker effect as "transfers to other workers" and the FICA effect as "additional transfers for federal taxes collected." Footnote 130, citing A-4, says transfers "do not affect total resources available to society." By DHS's own accounting, those are not benefits. What remains is fraud deterrence, which DHS "believes" will occur, with no estimate. The investigation savings DHS claims are never estimated, though DHS holds its own enforcement cost data.

2. No break-even analysis
When benefits cannot be quantified, A-4 asks for a threshold or break-even analysis. The primary annualized cost is $4.1 billion (3 percent). DHS's largest fraud figure is "more than 10,000" students working for "highly suspect employers." Even if the fee ended every one of those cases, it would need to produce about $410,000 in benefits per case per year to break even. At the $8.2 billion high estimate, about $820,000. DHS does not state the threshold or argue it is met. E.O. 12866 section 1(b)(6) requires a reasoned determination that benefits justify costs. The RIA contains none.

3. The low scenario mixes two baselines
The high scenario uses 2024 counts: 194,554 OPT and 95,384 STEM OPT. The low scenario uses a different base. Footnote 129 multiplies the 2022-2024 average of 157,494 by 56.11 percent to get 88,374 STEM-bound initial fees, and the STEM OPT count drops to the 74,088 average. The scenario's premise is that schools keep paying for STEM-bound students. Yet it removes about 20,790 STEM-bound initial fees (56.11 percent of 194,554 is about 109,164) and 21,296 STEM extensions. Those cuts come from switching baselines, not from the fee. By my arithmetic, about $2.1 billion of the $8.07 billion annual post-transition opportunity cost is a baseline artifact. About $6.0 billion is the assumed loss of non-STEM OPT. The text also calls 88,374 "a low-end future annual OPT population," which conflicts with footnote 129. A-4 calls for one baseline, with baseline uncertainty handled through sensitivity analysis.

4. Two corners are not an uncertainty analysis
A-4 calls for a formal quantitative analysis of uncertainty for rules with annual effects of $1 billion or more. Annualized transfers here are $8.7 to $16.9 billion. DHS offers two corner cases: no behavioral change at all, or every non-STEM student dropped. It calls their midpoint the "primary" estimate without assigning any probability. There is no intermediate case, no participation elasticity and no enrollment response.

5. Alternatives are listed, not analyzed
A-4 asks agencies to compare alternatives, including more and less stringent options. DHS analyzed one fee schedule. It assigns no cost or benefit to any alternative it names: no action, a small-entity exemption, a repeat fee at each degree level, or expanded site visits and reporting. It rejects site visits because they "may require substantial time and resources," with no figure, though it priced DSO time at $50.14 an hour. It never tests a lower fee, a phased-in fee, or a cost-based fee.

6. Costs capped by assumption
DHS assumes opportunity costs are "equal to or less than the proposed fee," so its cost estimate cannot exceed the fee by construction. Refund, Treasury and bank costs are left unestimated. In Presidents' Alliance v. DHS, No. 26-cv-13799 (D. Mass. Sept. 14, 2026), the court found DHS likely acted arbitrarily in the companion Duration of Status rule partly because DHS used "no principled method" to compare costs and benefits. The court quoted the rule that "a reasoned decision would explain why any unquantified benefits cannot reasonably be quantified."

7. Request
DHS should withdraw the proposal. Any re-proposal should include an RIA that:
(a) separates benefits from transfers and estimates fraud reduction, or at least presents a break-even analysis;
(b) uses one baseline for every scenario, with baseline sensitivity shown separately;
(c) provides a probabilistic uncertainty analysis with intermediate participation and enrollment responses;
(d) prices at least one less stringent and one more targeted alternative, including a lower or cost-based fee and employer verification; and
(e) estimates the DHS investigation savings it claims as a benefit.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and critiques the economic analysis.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Benjamin Sanders
comments.commentText:
I am a PhD graduate researcher at Yale University School of Medicine, supported by an NIH/NIA fellowship, and my dissertation research focuses on Alzheimer’s disease and neurodegeneration. I work daily alongside international graduate students and postdocs, and I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.
Biomedical research depends on trained scientists staying long enough to finish projects. Neurodegeneration studies run for years and can attest to that as I am already planning to stay here in a postdoctoral role to finalize and publish my work. OPT currently allows for international PhD graduate trainees to remain in the US following completion of their PhD and continue their research as a postdoctoral associate. These international trainees contribute essential expertise in imaging, computational analysis, and clinical collaboration that would otherwise be lost if this program didn’t exist. This new proposed rule (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100) requiring an initial fee of $70,000 before recommending an F-1 student for OPT would essentially place a financial barrier that would stand in the way of research progress. DHS already acknowledges that the cost could be passed to students, if not paid by the university, and a postdoctoral position funded by an NIH training grant cannot absorb a $70,000 surcharge. In essence, universities would be left with three terrible options: absorb a cost that exceeds many trainees’ annual stipends, pass it on to students who cannot pay it, or stop recommending OPT. Each one of these removes skilled scientists from US laboratories and grinds research progress to a halt.
Nearly 300,000 international workers participate in OPT each year. I can imagine that incoming PhD graduate researchers weigh the opportunity to work after graduation when choosing where to study. If that opportunity becomes prohibitively expensive, the most talented applicants will be actively recruited by other countries who are already capitalizing on a toxic environment in the US for international workers. This includes Canada, the UK, Europe, or Asia. The US would lose researchers it trained at great public and institutional expense, and international research progress would advance leaving US research to falter and fall behind. The next biomedical advancements, and corresponding economic investment, will happen elsewhere as a result. Alzheimer’s disease affects millions of Americans, and progress against it requires the best minds available. Discouraging international scientists from staying slows the discovery of treatments, weakens the biotechnology sector and job creation, and erodes the nation’s global standing in science. For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Nadia Fereydooni
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT.

I am commenting because I have personally gone through the process this proposal would affect. I came to the US as an international student, used OPT after completing my education, and am now a lawful permanent resident. I received my green card through the National Interest Waiver process, where I had to demonstrate the substantial merit and national importance of my work to the United States.

OPT was an important part of how I got from being an international student to where I am today.

Like many international students, I invested a significant amount of money in an American education. Tuition alone was a major financial commitment. After spending years studying here, OPT gave me the opportunity to apply what I had learned in school and gain real professional experience.

I also saw OPT as an opportunity to give something back. Since graduating, I have worked, paid taxes, developed my expertise, and contributed to the U.S. economy. Eventually, I qualified for permanent residence through the National Interest Waiver process based on the importance of my work.

That contribution did not stop with my own employment. In my current role, I built a new unit within my department. As that unit has grown, I have hired more than 10 interns and over 5 full time employees over the past two and a half years. My unit has also enabled hiring over 3 American vendors/content creation companies for projects.

When I was an international student using OPT, I could not have known that years later I would help build something that would provide opportunities to American students. That is why I don't believe the value of OPT can be measured simply by looking at the first job an international graduate takes.

I understand the argument that employment opportunities in the United States should benefit American workers first. I do not dismiss that concern. American students and workers should have strong opportunities to build their careers in their own country.

But giving an international graduate a limited period of practical training does not necessarily mean taking an opportunity away from an American worker. My own experience shows why it can be more complicated than that. The opportunity I received early in my career helped me develop the experience that eventually put me in a position to help build a new area of business and create opportunities for other people, including American workers.

I am not suggesting there is never competition between international and American workers. There can be competition in any labor market, and protecting American workers is a legitimate concern. But international graduates can also build teams, develop new areas of business, pay taxes, train colleagues, and create additional opportunities for American workers.

I also understand DHS's concerns about fraud and abuse. I support enforcement against employers, schools, or individuals who misuse OPT. People who break the rules should face consequences. But a $70,000 fee does not distinguish between someone abusing the system and a student who has done everything correctly.

Most graduating students simply do not have $70,000 available for the opportunity to begin working in the field they studied. Universities cannot reasonably absorb that amount for every international graduate either. Regardless of who technically pays the fee, I worry that many legitimate students will lose access to OPT.

If there are weaknesses in OPT oversight, DHS should address them directly through employer verification, investigations, audits, and enforcement against those who violate the rules. Those approaches target misconduct rather than creating a financial barrier for everyone.

International students make enormous financial and personal commitments to study in the United States. If obtaining even a limited period of practical experience after graduation effectively requires a $70,000 payment, talented students may choose to study and build their careers elsewhere. The United States could then lose not only those students and their tuition, but also whatever they might have contributed here afterward.

My experience is only one example, but it is a real one. I came here as an international student, invested heavily in an American education, used OPT to turn that education into practical experience, followed the legal immigration process, and eventually qualified for permanent residence through the National Interest Waiver process. Today, the work I helped build is also creating opportunities for American students.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees and instead pursue targeted measures against fraud and abuse that do not make legitimate practical training financially inaccessible to students who have followed the rules.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they harm the pathway for international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Merritt Maduke
comments.commentText:
I have spent more than 35 years in the U.S. biomedical research enterprise. Now a well-published scientist, I have seen how sustained, curiosity-driven federal investment fuels discovery and trains the next generation. My trainees and I are deeply grateful for the opportunity to serve the nation, and we work hard to honor that trust.
The proposed OPT fees introduce several critical harms. First, the fees will substantially deter the progress that comes from engaging with a wide range of ideas and technical expertise. My research has been strengthened repeatedly through work with international trainees. Prohibitive fees will restrict such collaborations and sharply reduces the likelihood of innovative, creative, out of the box advances that arise only when one is open to the broadest possible array of perspectives and methods. Second, the fees will greatly diminish the United States’ ability to compete globally. If we impose restrictions on international trainees while other countries continue building vibrant, cross border scientific partnerships, we will fall behind in global competition. Third, it will remove the joy, inspiration, and goodwill that come from working with colleagues around the world. These relationships not only enrich scientific discovery but also foster international trust and stability.

While DHS has a responsibility to protect the integrity of the immigration system and prevent fraud, that responsibility must not come at the expense of the international students and researchers who are vital to U.S. scientific innovation, research excellence, and global competitiveness. Rather than imposing excessive fees without a clear justification or demonstrated connection to program costs, DHS should strengthen targeted fraud detection, improve verification of employment and training arrangements, and hold employers, intermediaries, and institutions that violate program requirements accountable. Punitive fees are not a substitute for effective oversight and risk placing an unnecessary financial burden on legitimate students, researchers, and employers who strengthen the U.S. scientific enterprise.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees will harm biomedical research, deter talent, and reduce U.S. global competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Huda Al-Zuhairi
comments.commentText:
Personal Statement on the Importance of OPT to Scientific Research

I am an international researcher who recently earned a Ph.D. in Physics, specializing in Biophysics, from the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). I am currently working as a postdoctoral researcher under Optional Practical Training (OPT), continuing my scientific research in the United States.

My research focuses on bacterial chromosome organization and segregation through single-molecule biophysics, particularly protein–DNA and protein–protein interactions. This work involves advanced experimental techniques, including single-molecule fluorescence microscopy, surface plasmon resonance, and protein purification. These studies require years of specialized training, technical expertise, and continuous scientific investigation.

OPT provides an essential opportunity for international graduates to apply their education, contribute to ongoing research, publish scientific findings, and collaborate with American scientists. It also allows universities and research institutions to retain highly trained researchers who have developed specialized skills through years of graduate study in the United States.

I am deeply concerned about the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 for initial participation and $30,000 for subsequent participation. **The initial fee exceeds the annual salary of many postdoctoral researchers, making it financially unrealistic for early-career scientists and extremely burdensome for universities and research institutions.** Many postdoctoral researchers earn significantly less than $70,000 annually, while university laboratories often operate on limited research grants. Requiring such substantial payments could prevent qualified international graduates from continuing their research, even when universities recognize the value of their scientific contributions.

As an early-career scientist, I am concerned that these changes could significantly affect my ability to continue my research and build a scientific career in the United States. They could also disrupt ongoing projects, discourage international scientific talent, and weaken research collaborations that contribute to American scientific innovation.

International researchers are not only beneficiaries of American education; we are also active contributors to scientific discovery, technological advancement, and the training of future scientists.

Protecting accessible OPT opportunities is an investment in the future of American science, innovation, and global scientific leadership.

While DHS has a responsibility to protect the integrity of the immigration system and prevent fraud, that responsibility must not come at the expense of the international students and researchers who are vital to U.S. scientific innovation, research excellence, and global competitiveness. Rather than imposing excessive fees without a clear justification or demonstrated connection to program costs, DHS should strengthen targeted fraud detection, improve verification of employment and training arrangements, and hold employers, intermediaries, and institutions that violate program requirements accountable. Punitive fees are not a substitute for effective oversight and risk placing an unnecessary financial burden on legitimate students, researchers, and employers who strengthen the U.S. scientific enterprise.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ningchen Ma
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee described in Section V.A, and I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw them.

I am an international student pursuing a master’s degree in Computer Science at Yale University, expecting to graduate in spring 2027. Before beginning this program, I worked as a software engineer at Amazon in Canada. My academic and professional interests include artificial intelligence, compilers, and computer systems. OPT would allow me to apply what I am learning through practical experience directly related to my degree.

These proposed fees would create a major barrier at the point when I am preparing to graduate and begin my career in the United States. Although schools would be responsible for paying the fees, students would still face the consequences if schools could not cover them or passed the costs along. I cannot reasonably plan my education and career around an additional $70,000 charge or assume that a university or future employer would pay it.

The proposal could also narrow the opportunities available to me. A startup, research group, or smaller employer might offer valuable training that closely matches my education but lack the resources to absorb such a cost. Access to practical training should not depend on whether a student can find an institution or employer willing to cover a fee of this size.

I understand the importance of preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. However, I ask DHS to explain how these fee amounts address specific misconduct and to consider targeted enforcement and oversight measures that do not impose such a substantial financial barrier on students following the rules.

I am also concerned about the transition period discussed in Section V.C. Students already enrolled have committed significant time and resources to their degrees. A change of this scale shortly before graduation would disrupt plans made under the existing framework. If DHS proceeds with any fee changes, it should protect currently enrolled students and provide a meaningful transition period.

Please withdraw the proposed fees and preserve an accessible OPT pathway that allows international graduates to gain relevant experience and contribute their skills to U.S. workplaces.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I. Introduction and Overview
I am writing to submit this formal public comment in strong opposition to any proposed rule or policy that would impose an additional "training fee," user surcharge, or substantial fee hike on participants and employer sponsors of Optional Practical Training (OPT) and the STEM OPT extension.

Practical training is an indispensable, integral component of higher education in the United States. Instituting cost-prohibitive fees on recent graduates, early-career researchers, and hosting institutions undermines the foundational mission of practical training, harms U.S. academic institutions, damages economic competitiveness in key STEM fields, and creates arbitrary financial barriers for high-skilled global talent.

II. Core Arguments Against the Proposed Fee
1. Incompatibility with the Nature of Practical Training as an Educational Benefit
Direct Extension of Degree Curricula: OPT is not a distinct employment-based immigrant visa; it is a regulatory continuation of F-1 student status authorized under 8 CFR § 214.2(f)(10). Experiential learning, clinical practice, and laboratory training are natural extensions of graduate and undergraduate curricula.

Double Taxation of Students: International students already make enormous financial contributions to the U.S. higher education system via full tuition, institutional administrative fees, the SEVIS I-901 fee, and standard USCIS Form I-765 application filing fees. Imposing a separate "training fee" is an unjustified financial extraction that mischaracterizes essential experiential training as a commercial luxury.

2. Disproportionate Harm to Academic Research and Early-Career Scientists
Severe Burden on Postdoctoral Scholars and Academic Labs: A substantial share of STEM OPT beneficiaries are postdoctoral researchers, clinical fellows, and research scientists at major universities and biomedical research institutes.

Depleted Research Budgets: Postdoctoral stipends are strictly bounded by federal guidelines (e.g., NIH NRSA scales) and funded through constrained academic grants. Siphoning vital grant capital into administrative training fees shifts resources away from scientific discovery, laboratory supplies, and peer-reviewed research without providing any commensurate administrative benefit.

Risk to Foundational Science: Driving early-career researchers out of U.S. laboratories directly slows down critical work in cutting-edge biotechnology, artificial intelligence, semiconductor physics, and public health.

3. Erosion of U.S. Global Competitiveness in STEM
Global Talent Diversion: The U.S. relies heavily on recruiting the world’s top minds in STEM disciplines. Competing nations—such as the United Kingdom, Canada, Germany, and Australia—continue to liberalize and streamline post-study work authorization to actively attract international researchers and engineers.

Economic Bottlenecks: Levying steep financial penalties on post-graduation training signals hostility toward skilled international contributors, accelerating "reverse brain drain" and pushing promising innovators to launch startups or pursue specialized research abroad.

4. Disproportionate Hardship on Startups, Nonprofits, and Small Businesses
Chilling Effect on Early-Stage Hiring: Large technology conglomerates can easily absorb extra administrative costs, but early-stage spin-offs, non-profit think tanks, and local educational institutions cannot.

Distortion of the Talent Market: Adding mandatory fees skews the playing field, effectively pricing small employers and startup ventures out of hiring top talent trained at U.S. universities.

5. Arbitrary Cost Structure and Lack of Regulatory Justification
Lack of Demonstrable Service Delivery: Fees charged by federal agencies must reflect the actual adjudicative and administrative cost of providing the specific service (as mandated under the Independent Offices Appropriation Act, 31 U.S.C. § 9701). The SEVIS system and standard Form I-765 fees already fully recover the administrative costs of tracking students and issuing Employment Authorization Documents (EADs).

Regulatory Exceedance: Imposing a punitive, standalone fee detached from direct processing costs exceeds statutory authority and operates as a de facto tariff on international educational exchange.

III. Conclusion and Request
For these reasons, the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS should withdraw any proposed implementation of an OPT training fee. Imposing such a fee places an unjustifiable drag on scientific innovation, damages the recruitment capacity of American universities, and harms the U.S. economy. The agency should instead focus on reducing processing backlogs, modernizing adjudications, and protecting the integrity of post-study practical training.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong opposition to the proposed OPT training fee.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As a 20-year veteran of international education, currently serving undergraduate international students at a small, private, liberal arts university in the Midwest, I am submitting this comment in opposition to DHS’s OPT Fee proposed rule with a request that it be withdrawn. Note that I have also worked with international students at a large public university and a large private university.

My opposition to the proposed OPT rule centers on a number of factors, among them:

There are less burdensome, more efficient ways of combatting fraud and improving/facilitating oversight
Disproportionate impact on small colleges and their students and harms to local economies
Stifling of innovation, particularly in STEM fields

First: For the majority of small, liberal arts colleges and universities in the United States that serve international students, paying and/or collecting a $70,000 fee to pursue OPT would simply not be possible. Due to the demographic cliff, many such colleges are already strapped for resources. Coming up with these funds for students would simply not be possible. (Note that the proposed initial OPT fee is equivalent to half of a four year degree at my institution.) The vast majority of these students–who receive financial aid–would also not be able to pay the fee themselves. And a $70,000 would simply be disqualifying for the majority of employers. (As a comparison, refer to the H-1B fee, which was touted as a money generator and has resulted in few payments.)

Given that the majority of undergraduate students–domestic and international–expect hands on practical training as part of their degree or immediately after completion of their degree, creating an insuperable obstacle to pursuing employment related to the degree would effectively remove it as an option for students, despite their eligibility, as already permitted by law. This would undoubtedly lead to a collapse in international student enrollments in the United States, which have already taken a hit, due to a variety of other challenges to the higher education sector.

International students in the United States generate a substantial amount of revenue for U.S. businesses during their stay in the United States. Often, the immigration conversation turns to how much non-citizens “take” (e.g. jobs) without a necessary focus on how their needs generate job and economic growth for communities. In Indiana, for example, international students contribute nearly a BILLION dollars to the state economy across a number of sectors, from accommodation and dining to retail and telecomm, among others. In Washington DC alone, that number is a half a BILLION dollars. These needs in turn create jobs for citizens. In other words, putting roadblocks on legitimate, lawful employment and study by nonimmigrants who are studying in the United States ultimately hurts American citizens. Both supply and demand need to be considered together, not in isolation.

It has frequently been said that the non-U.S. citizen population most tracked and surveilled in the United States is the student population, in particular the F student community. If DHS wants to combat fraud, it need only look to SEVIS to beef up its reporting of individuals and employers. DHS could require that all OPT employers use E-verify, for example. Presumably, this oversight would ensure that all employers would have already been vetted by the U.S. government and would then also already be legitimate. Alternatively, DHS could institute checks of employers, require job offer letters on letterhead, and require that universities make contact with employers to verify their legitimacy. These are much more reasonable (as far as implementation) and could potentially create well-paying job opportunities in DHS or at universities (depending on the structure) for U.S. citizens. What’s more, these updates would require much less burdensome updates to the SEVIS system–and the many university systems that would otherwise be impacted.

In addition, introducing a super high fee without any other meaningful oversight does nothing to deter fraud. In fact, it punishes legitimate universities and colleges who simply do not have cash flow or revenue stream to make such outsize payments but who want to work, contributing their gifts, their talents, and their effort to an employer in the United States who needs their inputs. The middle-class students attending my current university (and even the average student at a very expensive private I used to work at) would simply not be able to come up with the necessary funding. Given that international talent is directly responsible for such a large number of start-ups in the United States and such a high amount of innovation, it would be self-defeating for the United States to make it even more difficult for international students to participate in the workplace and the economy.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee rule and requests that it be withdrawn.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT.

I find these proposed amounts astonishing and deeply unreasonable. How can international students, many of whom have already made enormous financial sacrifices to pursue their education in the United States, possibly be expected to bear such costs?

A policy intended to protect the integrity of the immigration system should not undermine the very students and researchers who have invested their time, resources, and expertise in American education.

I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees and consider more reasonable, evidence-based approaches that protect program integrity without imposing disproportionate financial burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule charging universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to focus on when this fee will actually do its damage — not at graduation, but years earlier, at the moment a family chooses where to send a seventeen-year-old to college.

No family evaluates an American university offer on tuition alone. They ask what the degree leads to: can the student work after graduation, gain experience, and test whether a career in the United States is viable? For decades, OPT has been the honest answer to that question, and it has been a decisive factor in choosing an American school over a competitor's offer. Attach a $70,000 fee to the recommendation, and the answer becomes "maybe, if your university can afford it, and if it still offers the program by the time you graduate." No family plans a four-year, six-figure education around a "maybe."

That is the arithmetic DHS has not confronted. A university that loses an international applicant over this fee does not lose one OPT recommendation; it loses four years of full tuition, four years of rent and spending in a college town, and four years of a student who might have become a research assistant, a teaching assistant, or a founder. Multiply that across a recruiting class, and the $8.4 to $16.5 billion the agency expects to collect looks small beside the enrollment revenue American higher education will quietly forfeit — revenue that pays for American students' scholarships and American faculty salaries.

Meanwhile the competitors' offers have not changed. Canada still offers post-graduation work permits of up to three years, the United Kingdom two years of unrestricted work and three for PhD graduates, and Australia up to four years — all without charging the student's university six figures, and all without the threat of a surprise fee appearing mid-degree. When the American offer carries a contingency and the Canadian offer does not, the rational family picks certainty. Prestige does not beat a guaranteed work permit.

And the damage will outlast the rule itself. Even if DHS withdraws this proposal, the cohorts that chose Toronto, Manchester, or Sydney in the meantime will not transfer back. A lost recruiting class is gone for the length of a degree and beyond, along with the research ties, business relationships, and goodwill those graduates would have carried home as bridges between their countries and ours. The United States is not merely risking this year's OPT numbers; it is spending down decades of trust in American higher education, one family decision at a time. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
RE: Public Comment Opposing Optional Practical Training Fees — Docket ICEB-2026-0100

To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement:

I respectfully oppose the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees (91 FR 64566), requiring SEVP-certified institutions to pay $70,000 for initial and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations. While I recognize the government’s legitimate interest in preventing fraud and protecting domestic labor, this fee structure introduces severe economic distortions and lacks the necessary evidentiary basis under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

1. Adverse Economic Impacts and Market Competitiveness
The United States operates in a highly competitive global market for talent. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported over 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. OPT provides a vital bridge for these graduates to apply their skills locally. Imposing prohibitive financial burdens risks discouraging institutions from participating, reducing the return on educational investments, and restricting access to high-skilled talent. This disproportionately impacts smaller institutions and businesses with less capital, leading to market consolidation rather than broad-based innovation. High-skilled immigrants and domestic workers act as complementary assets; restricting the former directly limits the growth and hiring capacity of American enterprises.

2. Insufficient Legal and Evidentiary Justification under the APA
Under the APA, 5 U.S.C. § 553(c), agencies must examine relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for their actions, including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made. DHS has not provided empirical evidence demonstrating that $70,000 or $30,000 fees are correlated with fraud reduction. An institution's liquidity is an inaccurate proxy for compliance integrity. By failing to model the broader macroeconomic impacts on university enrollment, research capacity, and employer hiring, the proposed rule lacks the reasoned justification required to withstand judicial review. Capital barriers do not deter sophisticated fraudulent actors; instead, they penalize compliant, high-value participants.

3. Proposed Clear and Effective Solution: Risk-Based Compliance
Rather than implementing arbitrary, economically disruptive financial barriers, DHS should adopt a Risk-Based Enforcement and Cost-Recovery Model. This effective framework consists of:
• Targeted Compliance Audits: Allocate enforcement resources based on historical institutional risk profiles rather than a flat fee.
• Proportionate, Cost-Based Fees: Structure administrative fees strictly around the documented, itemized cost of SEVP oversight and verification activities, ensuring compliance with the Independent Offices Appropriation Act (IOAA).
• Enhanced Data Integration: Leverage existing electronic verification databases to flag anomalies automatically without disrupting legitimate participants.

As a professional who entered the U.S. via a lawful academic pathway in cancer research and is expanding expertise in healthcare administration and business analytics, I have directly contributed to the domestic economy through high-skilled labor and tax revenue. I request that federal oversight distinguish compliance risks from lawful, high-value participation. DHS should withdraw the current fee proposal and implement a data-driven, risk-based compliance framework that safeguards system integrity without compromising American competitiveness.

Thank you for your consideration.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they impose severe economic distortions and harm competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Paul Bradley
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Paul Bradley and I am a retired physicist living in Los Alamos,NM

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

Universities do not have the funds to pay up to $100K per student. This effectively eliminates a critical pool of people for subjects that are already don't have enough workers.

We need more qualified people in these areas and there are not enough U.S. born people. Attracting the best and brightest from other countries can fill the gap. They also have different ways of looking at problems.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Paul Bradley

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to impose substantial mandatory fees—specifically $70,000 for initial recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent periods—on Optional Practical Training (OPT). These proposed fees are disproportionately high and create an unreasonable financial barrier for international students pursuing legitimate experiential learning opportunities in the United States.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal or substantially revise it to implement reasonable, cost-proportionate fees if any fee adjustment is deemed necessary. International students already invest significant financial resources in higher education within the United States. OPT is a core component of this educational investment, enabling eligible F-1 students to obtain temporary practical training directly related to their field of study. Imposing excessive fee requirements on the program threatens to make post-graduation training cost-prohibitive, undermining the primary purpose of the nonimmigrant student framework. While the proposed rule includes provisions allowing institutions to request refunds if an Employment Authorization Document (EAD) is denied or not issued, this mechanism fails to mitigate the immediate harm. USCIS adjudication timelines for OPT applications routinely range from three to six months.

Requiring the advance deposit and holding of tens of thousands of dollars per student for extended periods imposes an undue financial burden on institutions and students alike, regardless of whether a refund is eventually granted. Furthermore, because the rule explicitly permits institutions to shift these costs onto individual students or employers, shifting the legal responsibility of payment does not remove the underlying financial burden—it merely redistributes it onto parties ill-equipped to absorb such extreme costs. DHS asserts that these fees are necessary to enhance oversight and curb program misuse. However, an applicant’s or institution's ability to pay high fee amounts bears no rational relationship to program integrity or compliance; financial capacity is not evidence of misconduct, nor does a high price tag ensure compliance. DHS should explain how imposing prohibitive costs improves oversight beyond serving as a blanket financial deterrent. Instead of establishing financial barriers that penalize compliant participants, the agency should evaluate tailored, less burdensome regulatory alternatives, including:Targeted compliance reviews of participating entities;Enhanced verification of degree-related training plans (such as Form I-983);Direct employer accountability and verification mechanisms; andFocused enforcement against identified bad actors.

Enforcement measures targeted specifically at demonstrated misconduct are far more effective and equitable than punitive financial barriers applied broadly across compliant institutions and students.If implemented as proposed, this fee structure will create severe market distortions. Designated School Officials (DSOs) and institutions may feel compelled to decline recommending otherwise fully qualified students due to liability risks. Employers may withdraw legitimate entry-level training opportunities rather than assume prohibitive fee obligations. Consequently, qualified international graduates will be deprived of practical experience despite fulfilling every academic and regulatory requirement.

While protecting the U.S. domestic workforce is a legitimate regulatory goal, discouraging global talent from participating in the U.S. economy directly harms American competitiveness. International students on OPT contribute significantly to campus communities, fuel innovation, and support key economic sectors. Restricting their ability to obtain practical training deprives American employers of vital talent in critical fields.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that DHS rescind the proposed fee structure and consider less restrictive alternatives that uphold program integrity without disrupting the U.S. higher education system and talent pipeline.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, calling them disproportionate and an unreasonable financial barrier.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international graduate student at Yale University, and I write to strongly oppose the proposed rule requiring schools to pay $70,000 for their first OPT recommendation for a student and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation.

Optional Practical Training is not a loophole or a favor. It is the bridge between the education the United States offers the world and the contribution international graduates make to this country. International students pay full tuition, staff labs, advance research, and enrich classrooms for American students. OPT is how that investment is returned to the American economy, in taxes paid, companies built, and problems solved.

A $70,000 fee bears no relationship to the administrative cost of recommending a student for OPT. It is, plainly, a barrier designed to deter. DHS itself concedes that schools may pass these costs on to F-1 students, to all students, or to employers. Every one of those paths is destructive:

- Passed to students, it prices practical training out of reach for all but the wealthiest, turning opportunity in America into a privilege of birth rather than merit.
- Passed to employers, it taxes companies for hiring the very graduates American universities trained, and it will fall hardest on startups and smaller employers that cannot absorb a $70,000 surcharge per hire.
- Absorbed by schools, it forces universities to ration recommendations, deciding which international students deserve a future in this country on the basis of institutional budgets.

I speak from direct experience. I have earned a full-time offer from a U.S. technology company, contingent on my ability to work lawfully after graduation through OPT. Under this rule, my university would have to pay $70,000 simply to recommend me, or my employer would have to pay it to hire me, or I would have to pay it myself on top of years of tuition already paid in full. None of those outcomes reflects my merit, my contribution, or the needs of the American workplace. They reflect only a price tag placed on my right to work.

The damage extends far beyond any one student. Every international graduate pushed out by this rule is talent the United States educated and then surrendered to competitor nations that are actively recruiting precisely the researchers, engineers, and builders this rule would drive away. American classmates lose collaborators, labs lose researchers, employers lose hires, and the country loses the return on its own universities.

If the goal is a fair and functioning immigration system, this rule fails on its own terms. It does not recover costs, it does not protect American workers OPT hires are made on merit for roles employers cannot otherwise fill and it does not strengthen American education. It weakens all three.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in full.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Violet  Xu
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule requiring academic institutions to pay exorbitant fees ($70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations) to recommend students for Optional Practical Training. 
This proposed fee structure represents an arbitrary and destructive barrier to American higher education and the U.S. economy for several critical reasons: 
1. Unbearable Financial Burden on Higher Education and Students:
Most colleges and universities operate on constrained budgets and cannot absorb tens of thousands of dollars per participating student. As DHS explicitly acknowledges, these costs will inevitably be shifted onto students, tuition payers, or employers. Placing a $70,000+ financial hurdle on recent graduates will effectively end OPT access for low- and middle-income international students, reserving post-graduate practical training exclusively for the ultra-wealthy. 
2. Severe Harm to Academic Research and STEM Innovation:
International graduate students and researchers form the backbone of critical university labs, engineering projects, and scientific research nationwide. Threatening their ability to transition into post-completion practical training disincentivizes top global talent from pursuing degrees at U.S. institutions in the first place, severely undermining America’s competitive edge in STEM and technological innovation.
3. Disruption to the U.S. Workforce and Local Economies:
OPT allows U.S. employers to evaluate and retain highly skilled graduates who fill acute talent shortages in technology, healthcare, and engineering. Pricing employers and institutions out of this pipeline harms American businesses, shrinks tax contributions, and causes valuable talent to relocate to competing nations with more welcoming post-study work policies (such as Canada, the UK, or Germany).
4. Lack of Regulatory Justification:
The proposed fee amounts bear no rational relationship to the administrative cost of processing an OPT recommendation in SEVIS. Using punitive fees to de facto restrict a longstanding statutory training benefit circumvents congressional intent regarding the F-1 visa framework.
Conclusion:
Practical training is an essential component of a comprehensive U.S. education. By imposing prohibitive fees that institutions cannot sustain and students cannot afford, this rule would dismantle the OPT program in practice. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule entirely.

I am writing to express my strongest opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial OPT fee and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT periods. I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal in its entirety.

Optional Practical Training (OPT) is far more than a temporary employment opportunity. It is an essential bridge between American higher education and professional life, allowing international students to apply their knowledge, develop practical skills, and contribute to the U.S. economy. For many, OPT represents an important part of the American Dream: the belief that education, hard work, and determination can create opportunities regardless of one's country of origin.

First, the proposed fees are excessive, disproportionate, and fundamentally unfair. Although the fees would formally be imposed on educational institutions, their consequences would inevitably affect international students. Universities may be unable to absorb these enormous costs, potentially limiting or eliminating OPT opportunities. Access to professional development should be based on merit and educational qualifications, not financial privilege.

Second, this proposal unfairly penalizes legitimate students in the name of preventing fraud.I support immigration enforcement and efforts to prevent abuse, but imposing extraordinary fees on all participating institutions is not an effective solution. Paying $70,000 does not prove compliance, and being unable to afford such fees does not indicate fraud. DHS should instead pursue targeted employer audits, stronger verification procedures, and meaningful penalties against those who actually violate immigration regulations.

Third, this policy would undermine America's global competitiveness and economic interests. International students contribute billions of dollars to the U.S. economy through tuition, housing, and daily spending. Many also become valuable employees, researchers, entrepreneurs, and innovators. OPT helps American employers access skilled graduates with specialized knowledge and diverse perspectives. Restricting these opportunities would push talented individuals toward competing countries and weaken America's ability to attract and retain global talent.

Introducing an extraordinary financial barrier after these commitments have been made damages trust in the stability and fairness of the U.S. educational system.

Finally, this proposal contradicts the values that have historically made America a global leader in education and innovation. The United States has benefited tremendously from welcoming ambitious individuals who come to study, work, innovate, and contribute to their communities. International students should be evaluated based on their skills, integrity, and contributions—not their ability to overcome an unreasonable financial obstacle.

I respectfully but unequivocally urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and pursue reasonable, evidence-based measures to strengthen OPT oversight without destroying legitimate opportunities for students, educational institutions, and American employers.

The American Dream should be built on education, hard work, opportunity, and merit，not reserved for those who can afford extraordinary fees.
I strongly oppose this proposal and request its complete withdrawal.

As a graduate student, I am deeply concerned that proposing fees of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent requests creates insurmountable financial barriers.

Because universities will likely pass these costs on to students or employers, this policy will drastically reduce post-graduation employment opportunities, hitting lower-income students hardest. In turn, these barriers directly threaten university research and teaching programs that depend heavily on graduate scholars' contributions.

Furthermore, DHS has provided insufficient justification for such unprecedented fee amounts and has failed to meaningfully consider less burdensome regulatory alternatives to achieve program oversight. I urge DHS to reconsider and withdraw this proposed rule.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule increasing Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees (Docket ICEB-2026-0100), as this policy runs counter to the long-term economic and global interests of the United States.

As someone who has served as a Designated School Official for almost 30 years, it's difficult to describe how devasting this proposal would be not only to the U.S. economy, but to the students who pour hundreds of thousands of dollars into our economy only to be asked for an exorbitant amount more for an opportunity to gain experience in the United States. Too often have I seen students struggle to pay the current fee of $470 let alone $70,000 (more than my annual salary as their advisor). OPT is one of the main benefits of studying in the U.S., and if students know that they have to pay that much to work for one year, they'll simply study elsewhere in the world. Then guess who's out of a job: advisors and other international education professionals like me. Stopping F-1 students from participating in OPT won't help American jobs, it will destroy them! It will destroy us, the advisors who have stood beside INS/Department of Homeland Security to ensure that our students are not only in compliance with the laws, but have taught the students to appreciate, respect, and love the United States and take a positive experience home with them. And for most students, having that one year of work experience in the United States puts them ahead in their job market or get a better salary in their home country. Without OPT, why would students bother coming to the U.S. to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars only to be at par with graduates in their home country?

The absence of international students on university campuses would also contribute to the ignorance of American students. Many American college students have never left their county or state, let alone met someone from another country. Having students from another country sitting with them in their classrooms, living in their dorms, and sharing their culture opens their eyes to the world giving them better understanding and experience to work in a global society.

I'm not going to deny that fraud has taken place, but it can be stopped with the right policies and practices in place. Don't let a few ruin it for everyone. Seventy thousand dollars is absolutely ridiculous and excessive. Instead, the keep the cost as is and create better systems to monitor, track, and hold OPT students and employers more accountable. Neglecting the average international student from OPT is not the solution.

I graduated with a master’s degree in a STEM field earlier this year and now work as a software engineer at a U.S. company on OPT. I am writing to oppose the proposed fees.

1. Students already on OPT should not be charged for their STEM extension. I chose my degree program, paid tuition, and accepted my job knowing that STEM graduates could extend OPT for 24 months. Under this proposal, students like me whose OPT began before the rule would still owe the full $70,000 for a STEM extension recommended afterward. That changes the rules midway through a path we have already committed to. If DHS moves forward with any fee, it should exempt STEM extensions for students whose initial OPT was approved before the effective date.

2. The fee does not target fraud. OPT currently costs around $500, and this proposal raises that cost about 140 times. Every student pays the same amount whether their employer is legitimate or not, so it does nothing to separate fraud from honest participation. Checking employers, auditing schools with unusual OPT patterns, and penalizing those who break the rules would address fraud directly without pricing out students who follow every requirement.

3. It is unlikely to create jobs for U.S. workers. Many tech companies, including mine, have engineering teams outside the U.S. When hiring a graduate on OPT costs an extra $70,000, the easiest choice for these companies is not to hire someone else here. It is to move the role to the team abroad. The proposal does not show that the positions affected would go to U.S. workers instead of leaving the country.

Please withdraw this proposed rule, or at least protect students who are already on OPT.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I strongly oppose the proposed rule, "Optional Practical Training Fees" (91 FR 64566), and respectfully urge DHS to withdraw it.

I am an international PhD student in electrical and computer engineering at a U.S. research university. My research focuses on artificial intelligence and medical imaging, with applications to healthcare. Over several years of doctoral training, I have contributed to research projects, scientific publications, and collaborations with researchers and industry professionals. I hope to apply this expertise in the U.S. workforce after graduation.

The proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT would create extraordinary barriers for students like me and the institutions that educate us. I urge DHS to consider the following concerns.

**1. Disproportionate costs for universities and students**

Although the proposal requires schools to pay the fees, universities may be unable or unwilling to absorb tens of thousands of dollars for each eligible student. Some may stop recommending students for OPT altogether. Others may reduce services or shift costs indirectly onto students. Access to practical training would then depend on institutional finances rather than eligibility, qualifications, or the legitimacy of employment.

**2. Harm to U.S. research, innovation, and employers**

International doctoral students often spend five or more years developing specialized expertise at American universities. During that time, we contribute to laboratories, publications, and research that benefits U.S. science and industry. OPT helps translate that training into productive employment. These fees could discourage future students from choosing the United States and prevent graduates already trained here from contributing to sectors such as AI, engineering, and healthcare. Universities and American employers would also lose access to valuable talent.

**3. Weak connection between the fees and fraud prevention**

I support effective oversight of OPT and enforcement against fraudulent institutions or employment arrangements. However, a university's ability to pay $70,000 does not demonstrate that a position is legitimate, and inability to pay does not indicate fraud. DHS should explain why such high fees are necessary and demonstrate that their benefits outweigh foreseeable harms. More targeted measures—such as risk-based audits, employer verification, and enforcement against proven misconduct—would better address fraudulent activity without penalizing compliant students and schools.

**4. Unfair disruption to students nearing graduation**

Students like me planned years of education and career development under the existing OPT framework. The proposal's 60-day transition after publication of a final rule would not give universities and students sufficient time to adjust. A student who has complied with all immigration rules and obtained a legitimate job offer could lose a practical training opportunity solely because the school cannot pay the new fee. This would be especially damaging for PhD candidates close to graduation, who have already made long-term commitments based on current rules.

**5. Insufficient consideration of economic consequences**

DHS estimates approximately $12.4 billion in annual fee transfers under its primary scenario. This is not simply an administrative adjustment. The proposal could change which students can enter the workforce, reduce research continuity, and impose substantial costs on institutions. DHS should fully assess effects on OPT participation, institutional budgets, hiring, and U.S. competitiveness before pursuing such a policy.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposed rule and instead pursue evidence-based, proportionate measures to address specific instances of OPT fraud. The United States should protect the integrity of its immigration system while allowing qualified international graduates who follow its rules to contribute to American research, industry, and economic growth.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Respectfully,
An International PhD Student in the United States
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it due to high fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anyonymous Anonymos
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to submit formal testimony in strict and total opposition to the suite of interconnected regulatory changes proposed by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) regarding high-skilled immigration pathways. Specifically, this comment addresses and opposes:
1. The elimination of the deference policy for nonimmigrant worker extensions [Docket No. USCIS-2026-0529];
2. The implementation of prohibitive, aggregate $100,000 fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT programs [Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01]; and
3. The removal of the 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers facing sudden job separation [Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364].

Taken individually, each of these rules creates immense friction for American businesses, universities, and international professionals. Taken collectively, they represent a systematic dismantlement of the United States’ ability to attract, train, and retain global scientific, technological, and corporate talent.

I. Opposing the Elimination of Deference for Visa Extensions (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0529)
The proposal to eliminate the long-standing policy of deference to prior approvals for nonimmigrant worker extension petitions (8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)) is an inefficient allocation of agency resources that heavily penalizes American employers. Forcing U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) adjudicators to re-adjudicate previously approved petitions "from scratch"—when the underlying facts, operational duties, employers, and employees remain completely unchanged—defies common-sense administrative logic.

This redundant workflow will severely compound existing USCIS backlogs, increase processing delays, and lead to an arbitrary spike in unnecessary Requests for Evidence (RFEs). For American businesses, the removal of deference injects extreme operational volatility, transforming routine administrative renewals into unpredictable hurdles. This directly harms domestic companies that invest significant financial and legal capital to maintain stable, specialized workforces.

II. Opposing Prohibitive Optional Practical Training (OPT) Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100)
The proposal to levy a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for the STEM OPT extension on participating institutions represents an unprecedented financial barrier that functions as a de facto ban on post-graduate training. American academic institutions do not possess the discretionary budgetary resources to absorb a massive $100,000 cost per international student, and passing these extreme fees down to students will instantly price the United States out of the global higher education market.

International students are foundational to the research ecosystems of American universities. Driving the world's brightest mathematical, scientific, and engineering minds to competing nations like Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia will permanently impair domestic research and development. The financial structure of this rule is short-sighted and threatens the long-term competitive edge of the American tech and scientific sectors.

III. Opposing the Removal of the 60-Day Grace Period (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364)
Eliminating the 60-day grace period currently granted to H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN, and other employment-based nonimmigrant workers following unexpected job termination is an unnecessarily punitive measure. The existing framework, established in 2017, ensures a humane, orderly window for lawful workers to manage sudden personal disruption, safely wrap up their local affairs, or transition to a new sponsoring enterprise.

Stripping away this buffer forces specialized professionals—many of whom are deeply integrated into their local communities with families and school-aged children—to immediately flee the country upon sudden layoff. From an economic standpoint, this rule cuts off American employers from a vital pool of pre-vetted, domestic talent. Instead of allowing growing U.S. enterprises to quickly absorb laid-off specialized professionals, this regulation forces that talent entirely out of the domestic marketplace.

Conclusion
A healthy, competitive American economy relies on regulatory predictability, the retention of top-tier talent trained in our universities, and basic administrative fairness. The combined impact of these three proposals creates a hostile environment for innovation and professional growth. I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw these economically disruptive proposals in their entirety and preserve the established frameworks that support American excellence.

Respectfully submitted,
Anonymous Citizen
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states total opposition to the prohibitive $100,000 OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a Designated School Official (DSO) at a public, two-year community college serving an average enrollment of 25–30 F-1 international students per term.

1. Disproportionate Financial Burden on Small Two-Year Colleges
At my tuition, the international tuition rate is around $480.00/credit hour across 36 required credits per academic year ($17,280.00/year; $34,560.00 total two-year degree), our annual international tuition revenue totals $432,000–$518,400. Processing just one OPT application per year highlights the severe impact on small institutions:
- Fee vs. Total Degree Tuition: A $70,000 fee represents 202.5%—more than double—a student’s total $34,560 two-year Associate degree tuition.
- Impact on Institutional Revenue: For a college to absorb or guarantee one OPT fee ($70,000), it consumes 13.5% to 16.2% of our total annual international student tuition revenue, creating a net deficit over $35,000 per participant. Community colleges operate on strict public budgets. Tuition revenues are restricted by institutional policy to instructional and campus support services; we have no budget line or legal mechanism to pay federal administrative fees for individual students.

2. Extreme Overhead for Low-Volume Programs
DHS wrongly assumes institutions can distribute overhead across large applicant volumes. For an institution averaging one applicant annually, fixed overhead costs become crippling:

- Unrecoverable Merchant Fees: Credit card processing fees for a $70,000 transaction introduce $1,750–$2,100 in unrecoverable merchant costs and financial liability per student.
- Unfunded Operational Burden: Establishing tracking, invoicing, and compliance systems for single-digit application volumes creates an unsustainable administrative cost ratio.

3. Breakdown of the "Cost-Pass-Through" Assumption
DHS’s assumption that institutions can pass this fee to students or employers fails in practice:

- Students Cannot Pay: Budget-conscious Associate graduates who spent $34,560 on two years of tuition specifically to manage costs cannot afford a $70,000 fee upon graduation. Entry-level associate-degree roles typically pay under $45,000 pre-tax annually.
- Employers Will Not Pay: Local small businesses hiring entry-level technical graduates lack corporate budgets to advance $70,000 per entry-level employee.
- Forced Program Exit: Small collages that are unable to absorb $70,000 per student or collect it from applicants will be forced to stop issuing OPT recommendations, severing local employer talent pipelines.

4. The Assessment Functions as an Unauthorized Executive Tax
- General Treasury Rerouting: Directing multi-billion-dollar collections to the General Fund of the U.S. Treasury rather than dedicated cost-recovery accounts converts the charge into a general revenue-raising tax.
- Lack of Proportionality: A $70,000 assessment bears zero rational nexus to the actual agency cost of processing an adjudication, exceeding administrative cost recovery.

5. Unacceptable Financial Risk & Deterrence
USCIS approval is never guaranteed. Forcing applicants or institutions to risk a non-refundable $70,000—more than double a two-year degree’s tuition—on an application subject to denial creates an arbitrary financial penalty. Blanket fees do not curb fraud; proactive DSO pre-OPT advising and SEVIS monitoring already protect program integrity.

Conclusion and Requested Action
The proposed rule imposes an impossible burden on small community colleges and eliminates practical training pathways. I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fee requirements.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee creates a disproportionate financial burden and extreme overhead for small colleges.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing as a staff member at Portland Community College (PCC) to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule published on October 8, 2026, which would mandate a $70,000 fee per student for institutions recommending initial Optional Practical Training (OPT).This proposed fee structure is fiscally impossible for public community colleges like PCC to absorb and would effectively eliminate access to experiential learning for our international students.

1. Disproportionate Impact on Community Colleges and Public Higher Education
At PCC, we serve 270 F-1 visa students who enrich our classrooms, campus life, and local community. Unlike large private research institutions with vast endowments, public community colleges operate on tight public budgets designed to keep education accessible. Requiring an institution to pay $70,000 per student just to issue a recommendation for standard practical training creates an insurmountable barrier. In practice, this serves as a de facto ban on OPT for community college students.

2. Erosion of Educational Value and Practical Application
OPT is an integral component of the American educational model, allowing students to apply classroom concepts directly to workplace environments, gain professional skills, and contribute meaningfully to regional industries before returning home or pursuing further academic pathways. Denying F-1 students the ability to complete practical training undermines the academic value of the programs they enroll in and penalizes students who have complied with all immigration and institutional regulations.

3. Long-Term Damage to U.S. Higher Education and Local Economies
Prospective international students choose destinations where they can gain both high-quality academic instruction and hands-on professional growth. If practical training becomes financially inaccessible in the United States, talented students will simply choose to study in competing countries—such as Canada, the UK, or Australia—that encourage practical skill development. The loss of international talent harms not only campus diversity and global exchange, but also local small businesses, healthcare systems, and tech sectors that benefit from student intern contributions and community engagement.International students contribute immensely to our academic community and local economy. Imposing an arbitrary $70,000 fee on institutions to recommend students for OPT is punitive, economically unviable, and damaging to the mission of American higher education.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by shitian li
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT, including STEM OPT extensions. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

I am an F-1 PhD candidate in cancer biology at the University of California, San Diego, conducting research at the Salk Institute. My research examines how chromatin regulation affects the immune system's ability to recognize cancer, and I have contributed to work published in Cell. Under sections IV.C and V.A, schools must pay before recommending OPT, but DHS explicitly permits them to pass the expense to students or employers. Universities may simply decline to issue recommendations, and for initial OPT, the fee would be due even before a student necessarily has an employer. Second, the proposal would damage biomedical research without distinguishing it from the abuses DHS seeks to prevent. Doctoral scientists spend years acquiring specialized expertise in experimental methods and research projects. OPT can allow them to continue as postdoctoral researchers or move into U.S. companies developing therapies. A laboratory or small biotechnology company might have a legitimate need for a scientist yet be unable to absorb a $70,000 charge. Losing trained researchers can delay experiments, undermine collaborations, and disrupt knowledge transfer. The consequences affect U.S. colleagues, patients, and research institutions—not just international graduates.

Third, the fee is not adequately connected to its anti-fraud purpose. I recognize DHS's interests in preventing fraud, ensuring genuine training, and protecting U.S. workers. But a uniform six-figure financial burden for OPT plus STEM OPT does not establish whether a particular training position is legitimate. The proposal does not itself create employer verification, site visits, or independent training-quality assessments. DHS states in section IV.C that fee revenue will go to the U.S. Treasury, not be earmarked for ICE or SEVP enforcement. DHS should demonstrate why these fee amounts would prevent violations more effectively than targeted oversight, and why compliant university researchers should bear the same burden as high-risk arrangements.

Fourth, the regulatory impact analysis understates important long-term risks. DHS estimates roughly $4.1 billion in annualized costs in its primary scenario, but acknowledges it cannot precisely quantify the opportunity cost of lost OPT participation and uses unpaid fees as a proxy (section VII.A). That is not a direct assessment of lost scientific output, reduced innovation, disrupted research teams, or diminished retention of U.S.-trained talent. The National Science Board's The State of U.S. Science and Engineering 2026 (https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsbsep20261/stem-talent-education-training-and-workforce-2) reports that approximately 73% of temporary-visa holders earning U.S. science and engineering doctorates in 2017–2019 were still in the United States about five years later. Their contributions can extend far beyond an initial OPT period.

Finally, the proposed 60-day implementation period is unfair to students who began multiyear programs under the existing framework. Graduate students cannot readily replan years of training, research, and career development in two months. DHS should assess these reliance interests and, at minimum, protect currently enrolled students from abrupt new fees.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposal and instead consider risk-based audits of schools and employers, verification of genuine training, stronger enforcement of existing STEM OPT training-plan and wage protections, and administrative fees tied to demonstrated program costs. These measures could combat abuse without closing legitimate pathways for biomedical scientists. The United States should assess scientists by the legitimacy and quality of their work—not by whether someone can pay $100,000 to apply their training here.
