comments.commentText:
Comment on Optional Practical Training Fees: Collection Authority and Fee Design
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01
91 Fed. Reg. 64566-64600 (October 8, 2026)
Sections III.A, IV.C, V.A and VII.A.5.d(3); proposed 8 C.F.R. 214.13(i)

I oppose the proposed assessment and request its withdrawal. Fraud prevention, lawful practical training and protection of U.S. workers are legitimate objectives. The unresolved questions are whether Congress authorized this particular collection from schools and whether its amounts and triggers reasonably fit those objectives.

1. Identify the power to collect, including its limits.

Section III.A relies principally on broad immigration-management powers and 8 U.S.C. 1184(a)(1), which permits regulation of nonimmigrants' time and conditions of admission and stay. That provision also expressly authorizes bonds to secure departure. DHS should explain why the general conditions language authorizes this materially different assessment on educational institutions, including the limits on the payer, amount and refund design.

Washtech, 50 F.4th 164, 177-81 (D.C. Cir. 2022), upheld OPT and substantial conditions authority. It did not decide the validity of this monetary assessment. Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (February 20, 2026), Part II.B, slip opinion 14-15, rejected tariff authority inferred from general regulatory wording in IEEPA. That decision concerns another statute and does not determine this proposal's legality. Its distinction between regulatory power and revenue-raising power nevertheless warrants an explanation here. This objection does not demand that Congress use a particular word or deny that Congress can delegate fee-setting power.

2. Reconcile this collection with Congress's specific fee framework.

Congress addressed student-information fees in 8 U.S.C. 1372(e) and (g), including cost-related adjustments, and adjudication-service fees in 1356(m), including cross-subsidization and an identified account. These provisions do not necessarily prohibit every separately authorized charge. DHS should explain how its asserted general authority fits that statutory structure.

Section IV.C states that the receipts would enter Treasury and could not be retained by ICE. 31 U.S.C. 3302 governs deposit of money received; it does not independently create authority to demand payment. Treasury deposit is not itself unlawful or inconsistent with deterrence. It does mean the receipts should not be represented as funding additional ICE oversight under this proposal. This comment does not assert that every immigration fee must equal the cost of processing one application.

3. Explain the dollar amounts and recommendation-based trigger.

Sections IV.C and V.A should explain why $70,000 initially and $30,000 subsequently are appropriate, and compare plausible alternatives. A comparison with another visa program must address different durations, payers, eligibility requirements and legal foundations. A reference to tuition does not establish the reasonable price of a separate training recommendation.

Section VII.A.5.d(3), 91 Fed. Reg. 64590-64591, recognizes that splitting the same twelve months between pre-completion and post-completion OPT produces $100,000 in charges, while post-completion OPT alone produces $70,000. DHS anticipates movement away from pre-completion training. Please explain the additional $30,000 by reference to a relevant risk or policy benefit, and evaluate the resulting educational cost.

DHS may reasonably contend that OPT confers a special benefit, that this is a regulatory participation charge rather than a tax, and that uniform conditions simplify administration and encourage institutional scrutiny. They do not by themselves establish the delegation or select these amounts from plausible alternatives. Administrative convenience also needs to be considered alongside lawful training discouraged by the payment schedule.

Please identify the collection authority and limiting principle; reconcile the specific fee statutes; and compare lower amounts and triggers linked to training duration or documented risk. Explain the effects on legitimate participation and institutional screening. If adequate authority or a reasoned basis for the selected design is unavailable, withdraw the assessment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Comment on OPT Fees: Fraud Evidence and Targeted Controls
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01

DHS should withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT charges unless it explains their effectiveness and compares concrete alternatives. This comment addresses IV.A and IV.C, 91 FR 64570-64576, and VII.B.6, 64596. Fraud prevention is legitimate; the question is whether these charges improve program integrity.

Under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A) and Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), an agency must examine important aspects of the problem and explain its choice. Reasonable predictions are permissible; neither a randomized trial nor elimination of all fraud is required.

Question 1: What residual risk remains after existing controls, and how representative is the cited evidence?

Distinguish suspected misconduct, investigations, established violations and convictions. Reliable investigative evidence need not await conviction. Targeted investigations alone do not establish a program-wide prevalence rate. Please identify relevant periods, populations, denominators, selection methods and overlapping cases, using aggregated or redacted disclosures where necessary. Program growth alone cannot establish a rising violation rate.

The subsequent status entries for GAO-14-356 report implementation of OPT risk indicators, employer-information requirements and guidance on the relationship between employment and study. Implementation does not prove fraud disappeared. But older deficiencies cannot be assumed to remain unchanged. Explain what newer evidence shows about remaining failures.

Question 2: Why should payment identify more compliant or educationally valuable participation?

A decline in participation, fewer total violations, a lower violation rate among remaining participants, and retention of legitimate training are different outcomes. A uniform charge may reduce workload even without improving the remaining population's compliance. DHS should state which outcome it predicts and the evidence supporting each additional inference.

Section IV.C permits schools to shift costs to students, all students or employers. If a school passes through the charge, explain the additional financial incentive it retains to perform better screening. A well-funded violator might pay while a compliant participant cannot. This is a mechanism to evaluate, not a claim that adverse selection has already occurred. Compare legitimate opportunities lost with misconduct deterred.

Question 3: Why is this charge preferable to completing and strengthening identified controls?

GAO-19-297 reports implementation of recommendations concerning a fraud risk profile, network analysis and other SEVP controls. Recommendations 6 and 7, however, remained Open - Partially Addressed in the July 2026 status updates: mandatory DSO training and mandatory fraud-specific DSO training were not fully implemented. These concern SEVP generally, not every OPT participant.

DHS should compare a funded completion plan for those recommendations with the proposed charge, alongside employer verification and risk-based inspections. Section IV.C discusses site visits, additional reporting and student training plans. An I-983 student training plan is different from training a DSO to detect fraud; discussion of the former does not establish evaluation of the latter.

The government's strongest response is that fees offer immediate deterrence, reduce the population requiring oversight and avoid the staffing demands of broader enforcement. Those are relevant considerations. Existing safeguards may fail, and training alone may be insufficient. But administrative convenience does not explain the amount selected or establish superior screening. The request is a meaningful comparison of feasible measures, not a claim that the cheapest alternative is legally required.

Please publish the residual-risk assessment and an incremental comparison of effectiveness, government resources and private burdens. Evaluate lower charges, targeted verification and completion of DSO training. If DHS relies on previously undisclosed evidence that changes the proposal's critical basis, provide a meaningful opportunity to address it. Absent an adequate explanation, withdraw the charges and pursue controls tied to identified misconduct.

GAO-14-356, recommendation status:
https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-14-356

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-297

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Reliance and a Workable Transition for Enrolled F-1 Students
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01
Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)

I oppose the proposed assessment and request withdrawal. In particular, Sections V.C and VI, 91 Fed. Reg. 64577-64579, and proposed 8 C.F.R. 214.13(i)(3), at 64600, do not adequately explain why the selected transition accommodates students who already enrolled under the existing rules. DHS has discussed reliance and proposed a 60-day delay after publication of a final rule, with protection for earlier recommendations. The objection is to the adequacy of those choices.

The relevant distinction is between a prospective applicant who can reconsider where to study and a student who has already committed tuition, time, and educational opportunities to a U.S. degree. Section VI, footnote 124, acknowledges this distinction. A student need not regard OPT as the sole reason for attending a U.S. institution for related practical training to have materially influenced the decision. Educational quality, cost, and the opportunity to apply acquired skills can jointly determine a course of study.

DHS v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1, 30-33 (2020), requires an agency changing policy to identify and assess relevant reliance interests and weigh them against competing concerns. Temporary or discretionary benefits do not automatically exclude reliance. DHS may conclude that enforcement objectives outweigh particular interests. That conclusion still needs an explanation addressing the actual commitments and realistic transition options, rather than treating the absence of guaranteed approval as a sufficient answer.

Section VI relies in part on the annual share of OPT participants in the F-1 higher-education population. That ratio cannot establish a graduating cohort's eventual participation or the influence of OPT availability on enrollment decisions. Its denominator includes people at different educational stages, including students who have not yet reached graduation. A low annual share is compatible with substantial reliance among particular graduating groups. AIP reports that 82 percent of international physics and astronomy PhD recipients from the 2022-23 and 2023-24 cohorts who remained in the United States to work used OPT. That conditional, field-specific result supports disaggregation; it does not describe all international students.

The transition also deserves closer analysis for existing OPT participants. Under proposed 214.13(i)(3), a later STEM recommendation can trigger the new $70,000 initial assessment if that assessment has never been paid. Prior participation in OPT does not itself establish eligibility for the $30,000 subsequent rate. An existing authorization and a future recommendation are distinct. The latter can nevertheless be part of an educational and training sequence around which institutions, students, and employers have already organized commitments.

A recommendation-date cutoff is administratively clear. It does not necessarily give an enrolled student a practical opportunity to adjust. Someone years away from a timely OPT application cannot recover completed semesters or reconstruct an earlier enrollment decision during a 60-day interval. Schools likewise may have recruitment commitments and annual budgets that cannot be revised immediately. These are concrete questions for evidence and comparison, not a demand that immigration policy remain permanently unchanged.

Please separately evaluate prospective students, enrolled students approaching graduation, enrolled students earlier in their degrees, and current OPT participants approaching a STEM recommendation. Use graduating-cohort data, relevant degree and field differences, and evidence of actual commitments. Explain how much adjustment the proposed cutoff permits each group.

Please compare protection through an already enrolled student's current degree and related OPT/STEM sequence, phased implementation, and a longer budget transition. Identify the enforcement consequences and administrative costs of each alternative and explain any rejection. If DHS retains the present cutoff, explain why its benefits justify the particular disruption remaining for those unable to make practical use of the transition. A categorical claim of policy flexibility does not complete that analysis.

https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/19pdf/18-587_5ifl.pdf

comments.commentText:
Comment on OPT Fees: Economic Assumptions and U.S. Workers
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01

DHS should withdraw the proposed OPT charges or revise the analysis before finalizing them. This comment addresses IV.B, 91 FR 64572-64574, and VII.A.3, 5 and 6, 64582-64591. Protecting U.S. workers does not by itself justify these amounts and this collection method.

Question 1: Why does the participation range adequately cover the possible response of STEM students, schools and employers?

The high scenario assumes unchanged participation; the low scenario retains a STEM-oriented pipeline without non-STEM participation. The primary estimate averages them. A lower annualized STEM price does not prove affordability. The midpoint is not automatically the likeliest outcome.

Test scenarios where STEM participation also falls, distinguish transition from later cohorts, and explain the assumptions. Separate observed estimates from sensitivity tests. Identify who ultimately bears the charge; school payment does not determine economic incidence.

Clemens, IZA Discussion Paper 18933 (2026), section 3.2 and Table 5(b), printed pages 22-23, supplies a relevant alternative scenario. With full university incidence and withdrawal where the whole-degree margin falls below the charge, its $70,000 case implies a 63.5 percent decline in combined bachelor's and master's OPT starts. This conditional simulation is not an observed response, a STEM-specific forecast or a doctoral-program estimate. Cost error, cross-subsidies, cost shifting and sunk tuition can change it. It warrants broader tests, not certainty about that percentage.

Question 2: What validates unpaid fees as the proxy for lost opportunities?

Section VII.A.5.b uses unpaid charges as a proxy for opportunity costs and reasons that parties can share costs when benefits exceed the charge. That reasoning needs scrutiny. Private willingness to pay, current cash, benefits a school or employer can recover, and benefits to other U.S. residents are distinct. A future employer may not yet be identified when payment is due. Borrowing constraints and coordination failures can prevent a valuable placement even if its eventual benefits exceed the price. Research spillovers may not finance an individual recommendation.

Conversely, substitute workers or other lawful employment options may reduce losses. The analysis should evaluate both directions rather than assume all unmeasured effects increase harm. Fee payments themselves are transfers, not automatically an equal amount of consumed social resources. Real financing, implementation and behavioral costs should be identified separately without double counting.

Please provide evidence for the proxy, test alternative values for lost opportunities and identify the conditions under which relevant benefits outweigh costs. Uncertainty can justify a range; it does not make the range's endpoints self-validating.

Question 3: Which U.S. workers benefit, and what costs fall on other U.S. residents?

Demirci, Canadian Journal of Economics 53(4), 1495-1522 (2020), studies an OPT-related increase in STEM labor supply. Its published abstract reports lower employment for recently graduated native-born master's holders and higher earnings for experienced native-born master's holders in the same field. This evidence should be acknowledged rather than claiming that OPT cannot harm any U.S. worker. It also illustrates why effects cannot be reduced to a uniform replacement of one worker by another.

Distinguish fields, experience, regions and time horizons. Explain how historical expansions inform this price increase. Compare measures directed at actual substitution or inadequate training. Expansion studies do not directly estimate these charges' effects.

The government's strongest response is that a new price has no exact historical analogue, transparent scenarios are reasonable, benefits may resist monetization, and protecting directly competing U.S. graduates can be an independent policy goal. Not every group must gain. But distributional choices and material assumptions need a reasoned explanation under 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A) and State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983).

Please publish a reproducible analysis of incidence, STEM responses, financing barriers and heterogeneous worker effects. Compare lower charges and targeted measures, and allow comment on material new foundations. Withdraw the proposal if its central assumptions cannot be adequately supported.

Sources:
NPRM:
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-08/pdf/2026-20660.pdf
Clemens, IZA DP 18933:
https://docs.iza.org/dp18933.pdf
Demirci:
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/caje.12478

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Small Institutions, Financial Exposure, and Refund Safeguards
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01
Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (Oct. 8, 2026)

I oppose the proposed assessment and request withdrawal. Section VII.B, 91 Fed. Reg. 64591-64596, and proposed 8 C.F.R. 214.13(i)(1)-(2), at 64600, should be evaluated together: amount, timing, financial incidence, and refund uncertainty jointly determine whether a school can continue recommending lawful training.

DHS has prepared an initial regulatory flexibility analysis, recognized substantial effects on some small institutions, and considered alternatives including a small-institution exemption and additional oversight. The issue is whether the analysis adequately compares realistic institutional circumstances and explains the rejection of significant ways to reduce burdens while meeting statutory objectives.

Section VII.B rejects a small-institution exemption in part because small entities constitute a majority of regulated institutions and fraud could continue. A count of institutions does not establish the distribution of misconduct, the effectiveness of their controls, or the relative efficacy of charging and targeted oversight. Small size does not establish either innocence or high risk. Compare actual risk indicators and compliance performance before treating the number of small schools as an effectiveness measure.

The financial analysis also needs to distinguish annual revenue from usable liquidity and costs that a school can actually recover. An institution may have restricted funds, fixed commitments, or an academic-year budget. A large payment before the DSO recommendation may require financing even when the institution's annual revenue appears sufficient. Conversely, pass-through, subsidies, and other resources may reduce the school's ultimate burden. Please test these possibilities rather than assuming either that every school absorbs the full charge or that it can routinely shift it elsewhere.

DHS acknowledges that schools may pass costs to students, other students, or employers. That possibility is not itself evidence that reimbursement will be available before payment is due. An initial OPT recommendation may precede identification of an employer willing to contribute. A school that advances payment can face collection risk; a school that refuses to advance it may exclude an otherwise eligible student. Identify these pathways and their implications for participation, administration, and the proposed institutional screening incentive.

The refund provisions create financial uncertainty. SEVP may grant refunds case by case only before the relevant EAD is issued; for subsequent fees, the text also requires that the associated OPT extension has not been granted. The DSO must first remove the recommendation. Refunds after EAD issuance and administrative appeals are barred. Beyond these threshold conditions, substantive refund standards and decision deadlines remain unspecified. Schools need both to assess an advance.

Section VII.A.5.d(2) acknowledges that refund volume and associated costs cannot be estimated and invites data. That uncertainty does not itself establish illegality. It strengthens the need to evaluate financing exposure and adopt clear administration.

Please publish objective refund criteria, required documentation, decision deadlines, written reasons, and a correction or reconsideration process for clerical errors. Address duplicate payments, incorrect student identifiers, and an authorization not issued through no fault of the school or student. Explain how removal of the recommendation interacts with an otherwise pending application. Evaluate whether payment credits or correction mechanisms can resolve administrative mistakes without a second full advance.

Under 5 U.S.C. 603(c), compare lower or staged assessments, risk-based verification, DSO and fraud-specific training, and arrangements reducing financing exposure. Evaluate effectiveness against statutory objectives; small institutions are not automatically entitled to exemption.

In the final regulatory flexibility analysis, respond to significant comments and provide factual, policy, and legal reasons for the selected approach and rejection of significant alternatives, as required by 5 U.S.C. 604(a)(2) and (6). Evaluate the combined fee and refund design using realistic risk, liquidity, and cost-recovery scenarios. If DHS cannot support this institutional burden as proposed, withdraw the assessment.

Sources:

https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/5/603
https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/5/604

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ian Billinge
comments.commentText:
To whom it may concern,

My name is Ian Billinge. I am a postdoctoral researcher at Yale University, where I study how to purify water using ultraviolet light. My work has clear benefits to the United States -- in disinfection, so that our drinking water is clean, in treating industrial waste, so that industry can operate on our shores and in our cities in a socially-acceptable manner. The proposed rule, docket ICEB-2026-0100, which increases the fee for OPT extension of following a student visa from $500 to $70,000, is a bad idea. I urge lawmakers to oppose this rule.

Increasing the fee in this manner will make it prohibitively expensive for talented students in the US to stay in the US. The people who use OPT are some of the most valuable workers in the American economy. They came to our shores to study, and having graduated, want to work in the US. These folks are ready to contribute to the American economy, driving growth and innovation that makes America so great. ICEB-2026-0100 means that almost none would be able to stay. No employer would be willing to pay such a fee, and very few students could afford to pay it. The proposed rule change will make it impossible for talented scientists and engineers to contribute to our country. It represents a brain drain that will have profound and long-lasting effects on our economy.

In my own workplace, I know of several postdoctoral researchers here on OPT. Their work helps raise the indoor air quality in American homes, recover fuels from wastewater, and makes water drinkable. If the rule passes, this research will stop entirely, and American science and engineering will be set back tremendously.

I urge DHS -- with draw this proposed rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Max Greenwald
comments.commentText:
My name is Max Greenwald, and I am a 6th year MD/PhD student at Yale in Al Powers's computational psychiatry lab studying the origins of psychotic symptoms like hallucinations and delusions like seen in conditions such as Schizophrenia. I am writing to ask DHS to please withdraw the proposed rule, Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

I believe that the negative effects of this rule will significantly outweigh its intended benefit by discouraging the world's most talented scientists from:
1) Choosing to do their research and reside in the US, keeping the US as a world leader in scientific innovation and the place where new, potentially disruptive discoveries (like AI) first occur.
2) Being able to do groundbreaking research in the first place.

Over the years, Dr. Powers has had visiting graduate students from Turkey, Hungary, Germany, the UK, Brazil, and more. Speaking as a grad student who has worked with them daily during their rotations, these individuals are consistently the brightest and hardest working! I know for a fact that this OPT rule is actively discouraging these scientists from continuing their work in the United States. It was a massive loss to the lab when Orsolya Lanyi, a graduate researcher from Hungary, told us that she would not pursue a postdoc in the united states because she and her partner are looking to get stable jobs and have a child, and she could not afford to risk the disruption of having this OPT rule in place (which would guarantee that she would be forced to leave the country). Not only will she be conducting her research outside the US, it is likely that whatever work she produces will be of less value to the world because she does not have the world-class resources of an institution at Yale. She talked constantly about the massive gulf in resources between Yale and her home institution in Budapest. I think this is an incredible shame, since she is a researcher trying to identify brain targets that could help us prevent devastating conditions like Schizophrenia from occurring in the first place (she studies people at clinical high risk for psychosis).

This has also actively left her project orphaned. The project will require far more time and resources for someone else to pick up part-way through or -- even worse, given the stress on scientists at this time -- may be dropped entirely.

This is only the specific, concrete example I know of. Considering how much Orsi (her Hungarian nickname) wanted to stay and do science in the US, I feel very confident that there are thousands of talented scientists like herself who will choose to study elsewhere if this rule is adopted.

I respectfully ask that you please withdraw this rule for the good of the country and humanity.

I would welcome an opportunity to discuss further --
maximillian.greenwald@yale.edu
-Max

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Zach Riley
comments.commentText: As an international graduate student at Northwestern University, I support this administration's goals of protecting American workers, strengthening immigration enforcement, preventing fraud, and ensuring that immigration programs serve the national interest. However, I respectfully disagree with the proposed $100,000 OPT fee because I believe it could undermine these same objectives by discouraging American employers from hiring qualified international graduates. I have a background in civil engineering and am pursuing a STEM-designated Master of Science in Organizational Dynamics, combining technical problem-solving with project management, leadership, and organizational change. I want to use my education to contribute to American businesses and the U.S. economy. A fee of this magnitude could make employers reluctant to consider international graduates regardless of their qualifications, the legitimacy of their employment, or the value they could bring to American companies. I believe it is possible to support strong immigration enforcement while recognizing the value of legitimate international students who have invested in American universities and want to contribute their skills after graduation. Rather than imposing a substantial financial barrier on OPT, I encourage DHS to pursue targeted fraud prevention, employer accountability, and effective enforcement against actual violations. I support the administration's broader objectives, but I believe this particular proposal risks harming American businesses, universities, and the country's ability to attract talented graduates.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. These excessive fees would effectively deprive many international students of meaningful practical training opportunities and undermine the educational mission of American universities.

Optional Practical Training is not merely an employment benefit. It is an important extension of academic education, allowing students to apply their knowledge, develop professional skills, and gain practical experience in their fields of study.

As an international student studying art and design in the United States, I am particularly concerned about the disproportionate impact on students in creative disciplines. In fields such as fine arts, design, and crafts, professional development often depends on hands-on experience, studio practice, apprenticeships, exhibitions, and collaboration with artists and institutions. These opportunities are essential to artistic and educational development, yet they frequently offer limited financial compensation.

The educational value of such experiences cannot be measured solely through salaries or immediate economic returns. Imposing extraordinarily high fees would make practical training inaccessible to students pursuing careers in fields where professional opportunities are already financially limited. It would effectively favor students in higher-paying industries while excluding those whose educational contributions are equally valuable.

Furthermore, requiring universities to pay tens of thousands of dollars for OPT recommendations would impose an unreasonable financial burden. Whether universities absorb these costs or transfer them to students, access to practical training would become dependent on financial resources rather than educational merit.

A training opportunity that is technically available but financially inaccessible is not a meaningful opportunity.

I urge DHS to obtain and carefully evaluate empirical evidence from U.S. universities before finalizing this rule. Universities should provide data on OPT participation, their capacity to absorb the proposed fees, the anticipated reduction in training opportunities, and the potential consequences for international enrollment, academic programs, and educational outcomes.

DHS should also specifically examine the disproportionate impact on students in art, design, humanities, and other fields where professional training may not generate substantial immediate income.

International students invest years of study and significant financial resources in American higher education. Restricting their access to practical training after they have made these commitments would fundamentally undermine the educational opportunities associated with their academic programs.

While preventing fraud is a legitimate government objective, imposing prohibitively expensive fees on legitimate students is neither a proportionate nor an appropriately targeted solution.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee requirements and pursue evidence-based alternatives that protect program integrity without depriving international students of essential educational opportunities.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessive and would harm international students, especially in creative fields.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: More than half of international students in the U.S. rely on substantial home-country loans when scholarships or assistantships are unavailable. Upon graduation, most enter entry-level positions. Imposing an additional $100,000 fee benefits neither party: it exceeds the graduate's net annual salary, while employers cannot find local talent, should face an unsustainable penalty if forced to bear it to hire required talent. Beyond individual employers, this policy creates severe structural losses for the U.S. economy. Firstly, a direct loss to local economies. International students inject over $42–$50 billion annually into the U.S. economy and support upwards of 350,000 American jobs through university tuition, housing, taxes, and local business spending. Pricing them out diverts this massive capital flow to competing host nations like Canada, the UK, Germany, France, Italy and Australia. Secondly, loss of top innovation and high-tech talent. Highly skilled graduates are taxpayers who fill critical workforce gaps. A staggering 25% of all U.S. billion-dollar startup founders entered the country as international students—including tech visionaries like Elon Musk (SpaceX/Tesla/Neuralink/X Corp.), Sundar Pichai (Google), and Jensen Huang (NVIDIA). Restricting this pipeline forfeits the next generation of industry builders. Finally, the brain drain in critical research. Over 40–50% of U.S. STEM graduate degrees are earned by international students. Ditching or penalizing these researchers directly weakens American leadership in AI, biotechnology, clean energy, and defense technology.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the $100,000 fee exceeds salaries and harms the U.S. economy, innovation, and talent retention.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing in opposition to the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) for F-1 international students. Based on my four years of experience working as a Designated School Official (DSO) at Portland Community College (PCC), I have seen firsthand how important practical training opportunities are for students pursuing career and technical education.

During my time at PCC, I supported international students seeking practical training opportunities connected to their programs of study. These students invested significant time, effort, and financial resources into developing the skills necessary to enter their chosen professions. Practical training allowed them to apply their classroom learning in real-world settings, gain relevant experience, and strengthen their preparation for the workforce.

Career and technical education programs are designed to help students develop practical, industry-relevant skills. For students in these programs, the opportunity to gain experience related to their field of study can be an important part of translating their education into professional skills and career readiness. Restricting access to practical training would undermine these educational and professional development opportunities.

I am particularly concerned that the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT could create significant barriers for educational institutions and the students they serve. These costs could discourage institutions from supporting eligible students' participation in OPT, regardless of a student's qualifications, educational achievement, or the relevance of their training to their field of study.

I recognize the importance of maintaining program integrity, preventing fraud, and protecting U.S. workers. However, I encourage DHS to consider approaches that address these concerns without imposing fees that could make practical training inaccessible. Oversight and compliance measures should be proportionate and should preserve legitimate opportunities for students who have followed the rules and completed their academic programs.

Based on my experience supporting F-1 students at a public community college, I believe practical training serves an important educational purpose by helping students connect their academic preparation with real-world professional experience. These opportunities are particularly meaningful for students in career and technical education programs, where applied learning and field-specific skills are central to their preparation.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees or consider a substantially less burdensome alternative that preserves access to legitimate practical training while maintaining appropriate oversight and protections for U.S. workers.

Thank you for considering my comments and for the opportunity to share my professional perspective.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create significant barriers and harms students and educational institutions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Greg Bryan
comments.commentText:
I am a Professor of Astronomy at Columbia University, where for many years I have taught, supervised, and worked alongside graduate students and postdoctoral researchers from the United States and around the world. I am writing to respectfully but firmly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an F-1 student’s initial period of Optional Practical Training and a $30,000 fee for subsequent periods, including STEM OPT extensions. A fee of this size bears no relationship to the cost of administering the program. In practice it would end OPT for nearly all students at universities like mine. This would harm American students, American research, and the American economy.

The students who use OPT are among the most talented and best-trained young scientists and engineers anywhere. In my experience, their presence makes the training of domestic students better, not worse. American students in my group and my classes learn from these peers every day. They share techniques, debug code together, co-author papers, and build the collaborative habits that modern science depends on. OPT is often the bridge that lets an international student finish a project they began in graduate school, or move into a postdoctoral or industry position here rather than abroad. One former member of my group used OPT to make exactly that transition. Today that person is a faculty member at the University of Massachusetts, training the next generation of American-born scientists. That is what OPT does: it keeps exceptional talent in this country, where it multiplies. That continuity is a large part of why the best students in the world choose the United States in the first place. Our competitors in Canada, Europe, the UK, and Asia are actively recruiting the same people, and a fee like this sends them an unmistakable signal to go elsewhere. The cost would not stop with the students. Research groups would lose skilled people midway through federally funded projects, universities would lose the international enrollment that helps support their broader educational mission, and the country would lose the startups, patents, and technical leadership that these graduates disproportionately create when they stay.

I also want to address the stated justifications directly. In decades of working with international students and their university sponsors, I have not encountered OPT fraud. University OPT participation is already closely monitored through designated school officials, SEVIS reporting, and, for STEM OPT, formal training plans with employer attestations. Where specific abuses exist, the appropriate response is targeted enforcement against bad actors, not a blanket charge that falls on every legitimate student and institution. Nor are these students a source of cheap labor. In my field, OPT positions are paid exactly the same as positions held by American workers, on the same salary scales and under the same terms. OPT students do not displace Americans. Demand for people with advanced quantitative and computational training far exceeds the domestic supply, and OPT graduates fill roles that would otherwise go unfilled or move offshore, paying taxes and spending in their communities while doing so. Placing this fee on universities would also force institutions to divert funds from teaching and research, including funds that support American students, or else deny opportunities based on a student’s ability to pay rather than their merit. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and to work with universities on measures that address real problems without dismantling a program that has served the nation so well.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the massive fee would effectively end OPT and harm research, students, and the economy.

I write to express strong opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 extension fee on Optional Practical Training (OPT). This punitive policy harms both international students and the strategic interests of the United States.

1. International Student Perspective: Destroying Equity and Career Pathways

Unbearable Financial Burden: Although levied on universities, the proposal concedes that institutions will likely pass these costs onto students via tuition hikes or administrative fees. Adding $100,000 for temporary work authorization—which guarantees neither a job nor a visa—prices out middle- and working-class global talent.

Erosion of Meritocracy: Employers will not absorb tens of thousands of dollars in fees for entry-level graduates. Conditioning practical training on extreme wealth rather than academic merit undermines the core purpose of F-1 educational exchange.

2. U.S. Government Perspective: Economic Self-Sabotage and Talent Drain

Crippling Higher Education: International students contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy, subsidizing domestic tuition and university research. Eliminating practical training access will drive prospective students to competing nations like the UK, Canada, and Australia, triggering severe financial crises across American campuses.

Weakening U.S. Innovation: OPT is the primary pipeline for global STEM talent. Blocking this pipeline will not create domestic jobs; instead, it will force U.S. corporations to offshore R&D centers and high-paying roles abroad, directly reducing U.S. tax revenue and technological leadership.

Legal Vulnerability: Following the federal court’s invalidation of the similar $100,000 H-1B fee, imposing an unauthorized, punitive tax via executive rulemaking exceeds statutory authority and will inevitably waste public resources in prolonged litigation.

For the sake of American economic competitiveness and educational integrity, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule immediately.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
After reading through this proposed rule, I am appalled by its lack of consistency and basic logic. The administration claims that the purpose of this fee is to combat fraudulent abuse of the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, citing examples of fraudulent sponsors collecting illegal fees from international students. But how exactly would charging educational institutions such an extraordinary fee reduce fraud? If the goal is genuinely to combat abuses of the OPT program, the federal government already has substantial investigative resources and legal enforcement mechanisms at its disposal, including the FBI, DHS and ICE. Why not use these existing authorities to investigate and prosecute fraudulent activities rather than impose an enormous financial burden on educational institutions?

Universities collect tuition from students, including international students, in exchange for providing education. In higher education, they also provide the intellectual and institutional environment in which graduate students and PhD researchers conduct critical scientific research. Asking universities to pay an astonishing $70,000 fee to the federal government would establish an extraordinary precedent: that academic and educational institutions must pay the government simply so that individuals who have earned degrees from those institutions can pursue internships, employment, or other opportunities to apply the knowledge and skills they acquired through their education and research. What is the logical justification for such a financial requirement?

I would particularly like to hear the administration explain the actual intent and purpose of requiring universities to pay this OPT fee. No university in its right mind would willingly pay such an exorbitant amount. Is the intended outcome, therefore, to effectively eliminate OPT opportunities for international students, preventing them from pursuing internships or short-term employment, including postdoctoral research positions? If that is the goal, the administration should state it explicitly rather than disguise it as an effort to combat fraud.

And if the financial burden is ultimately shifted from universities to employers, wouldn’t that simply reinforce the very mechanisms that have enabled fraudulent practices in the first place? The administration cites the exploitation of international students by fraudulent sponsors as a justification for this proposal, yet its proposed solution risks creating even greater financial incentives for exploitation. How does that make any sense?

OPT is a temporary program, generally allowing eligible international graduates to work in the United States for up to one year, with a possible two-year extension for qualifying STEM graduates. Why should these individuals be treated as liabilities rather than welcomed as guests and contributors? They are legally present in the United States, have received their education from American institutions, and have invested years of their lives in developing skills, conducting research, and contributing to American society. Many international graduates have gone on to establish successful businesses, advance scientific research, and make lasting contributions to the American economy and technological leadership.

I fear that the ultimate consequence of this proposal will be to drive talented individuals away from the United States. After investing years in obtaining an American education, many will simply choose to pursue their careers elsewhere. And frankly, who would want to build a future in a country that makes it so abundantly clear that their contributions are not welcome?

If the administration genuinely wishes to prevent fraud, it should target those who commit fraud, rather than punish the educational institutions and international graduates who have followed the laws . The proposed rule appears fundamentally disconnected from its stated purpose, and I urge the administration to reconsider both its justification and its potentially devastating consequences for American higher education, scientific research, and international competitiveness.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed fee is illogical and imposes an extraordinary financial burden on educational institutions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Optional Practical Training Fees, Docket ICEB-2026-0100 (RIN 1653-AB01)

To the Department of Homeland Security:

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees, particularly for graduates of accredited Doctor of Medicine (MD), Juris Doctor (JD), Doctor of Dental Surgery/Medicine (DDS/DMD), and Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) programs. DHS has legitimate interests in preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers, but uniform fees of this magnitude disregard these professions' oversight and public-service roles.

1. The cited fraud evidence does not establish comparable risk in these fields.

DHS describes shell companies, fictitious employment letters, and questionable worksites, including IT-related arrangements. These are serious concerns. But the rule does not identify widespread substantiated OPT fraud involving MD, JD, DDS/DMD, or DPT graduates, nor provide fraud rates by degree. Absence of cited cases does not mean fraud is impossible; it means DHS has not shown comparable risks.

DHS should disclose substantiated fraud cases and OPT participation totals by degree, distinguish suspected from proven misconduct, and separate employer fraud from student misconduct. It should explain why a fee imposed regardless of risk is preferable to enforcement against fraudulent employers.

2. These are highly regulated professions.

State licensing boards oversee medicine, law, dentistry, and physical therapy. Lawyers face bar examinations and character-and-fitness investigations addressing honesty and suitability. Physicians undergo credential verification, examinations, training requirements, and medical-board scrutiny. Dentists and physical therapists face state-specific education, testing, licensing, and disciplinary requirements; background checks may apply. Practicing without required licensure can carry serious consequences.

Professional regulation is not a substitute for immigration screening, and some graduates pursue supervised OPT before full licensure. Nevertheless, accredited education, credential checks, state oversight, and disciplinary systems provide additional accountability. DHS should evaluate these protections rather than assume all degree pathways pose identical fraud risks.

3. The fees risk harming essential public services.

America needs doctors, dentists, and physical therapists to provide healthcare, including in underserved communities. It also needs lawyers to protect constitutional rights, help businesses operate lawfully, represent vulnerable people, and support government services. These graduates may work in hospitals, community clinics, public-interest law offices, and government institutions unable to absorb a $70,000 cost. Although schools would owe the fee, they may pass on costs or decline OPT recommendations.

DHS should revisit its statement that it anticipates no health or safety impacts. It should assess effects on healthcare access, access to justice, public services, and employers with limited budgets. Many professional graduates, including most JD graduates, cannot rely on a STEM OPT extension, making a $70,000 barrier to a limited training period especially severe.

4. Exempt professional graduates and use targeted safeguards.

I request an exemption from the proposed additional OPT fees for graduates of accredited MD, JD, DDS/DMD, and DPT programs pursuing lawful, degree-related practical training. Alternatively, DHS should establish reduced fees and meaningful waivers, particularly for nonprofit and public-service roles. It should prioritize employer verification, institutional audits, credential checks, and evidence-based investigations, and explain how the proposed fees deter the fraud schemes it cites.

5. Create a lawful green-card pathway.

Beyond this rulemaking, I urge the Administration and Congress to establish a direct, appropriately vetted permanent-residency pathway for qualified graduates of these programs. During his June 20, 2024 All-In Podcast appearance, then-candidate Donald Trump proposed giving international graduates of U.S. colleges green cards upon graduation; his campaign later described vetting conditions. This proposal deserves consideration for graduates who can serve American patients, clients, businesses, and communities. I recognize that a new green-card category may require legislation and cannot simply be created through this OPT fee rule.

DHS should not impose extraordinary uniform fees without degree-specific evidence and analysis of existing professional safeguards and public-service consequences. I urge the Department to exempt these graduates, adopt risk-based enforcement, and support lawful avenues for retaining qualified professionals educated in the United States.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they unfairly target highly regulated professional degrees.

comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 graduate student in the United States, expected to graduate in 2028, and I plan to apply for Optional Practical Training (OPT) in my field of study. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees.

The proposal would require a school to pay $70,000 before its designated school official recommends a student for initial OPT, and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including a STEM OPT extension. For a student who uses initial OPT and a STEM extension, that is $100,000 in total. That amount bears no apparent relationship to the actual cost of entering a recommendation in SEVIS or adjudicating an employment authorization application. DHS should reconsider the proposed fee amounts and provide clear evidence showing how they relate to the actual costs of administering and overseeing OPT.

Although the fee would formally be paid by the school, the proposal expressly contemplates that schools may pass the cost on to F-1 students, to students generally, or to employers. In practice, many schools and employers will not absorb $70,000 to $100,000 per student. The predictable result is fewer OPT recommendations, especially at institutions with fewer resources, and fewer training opportunities for students who have completed their degrees in good faith.

A blanket fee of this size does not target fraud. It penalizes legitimate students and programs along with any bad actors. Fraud and misuse should be addressed through targeted oversight, enforcement against specific schools or employers, and SEVIS controls, not by pricing OPT out of reach.

OPT is practical training directly related to a student's field of study. Making it unaffordable would discourage international students from studying in the United States, reduce the research and STEM workforce available to US universities and employers, and push talented graduates toward other countries. For students like me, who are already enrolled and planning their careers around OPT, the change would be deeply disruptive.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal. At a minimum, DHS should not finalize any fee until it publishes a detailed, cost-based justification and considers a fee set at actual administrative cost.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule imposing new OPT fees. While it targets international students, they are an economic asset of the country and is currently losing under those new policies. NAFSA estimates they contributed $42.9 billion and supported more than 355,000 jobs in 2024–25, a 2 percent decline from the prior year’s record, with contributions dropping a further $1.1 billion this fall and costing nearly 23,000 jobs. A six-figure barrier to post-study work would deepen that slide, especially since surveys show 66 percent of students would study elsewhere without post-study work options, draining the tuition that helps fund universities and subsidize domestic programs along with it.
Pushing these students out would not create jobs for Americans. A 2019 National Foundation for American Policy study found no evidence that OPT reduces opportunities for U.S. workers, a 2023 Niskanen Center analysis reached the same conclusion for STEM, and DHS itself offered no research showing that practical training harms U.S. workers. When firms cannot hire the graduates they train here, the roles tend to move abroad rather than convert into openings for U.S. workers, so the likely result is lost economic activity, not gained jobs. This also threatens innovation: more than half of international students are in STEM fields, former international students have founded a quarter of U.S. start-ups worth $1 billion or more, and many pursue OPT in medical and scientific research that sustains U.S. leadership. Cutting off both the talent and the tuition that supports research would weaken universities’ capacity to compete.
Finally, the fee does not even go to the program it claims to protect. DHS frames it as an anti-fraud measure, yet by its own account the revenue would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302 and would not be retained by ICE or used for OPT oversight or enforcement. A charge that is untethered from the government’s actual cost of administering the program and diverted into the general Treasury cannot be justified as protecting that program’s integrity, and observers note these are the very features that led a court to treat a comparable $100,000 H-1B fee as an unlawful tax. For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed OPT fees will harm the economy, drive away students, and fail to create U.S. jobs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations.

I am an F-1 master's student in a STEM field at a U.S. university. Through authorized practical training, I have applied my education to actual supply chain forecasting, inventory planning, and operations. This work has strengthened my professional skills and helped me contribute to a U.S. business. OPT is a temporary, regulated opportunity to build on an American education, not an automatic right to employment or a substitute for other visa classifications.

First, the proposed fees are grossly disproportionate and would restrict access based on ability to pay rather than lawful eligibility. Under Section V.A, schools must pay before recommending a student, but DHS acknowledges in Section VI that they may shift this expense to international students, other students, or employers. Most students could not afford $70,000, and many schools cannot reasonably absorb that amount for every eligible graduate. A qualifying student would be denied an educational opportunity not because of fraud or ineligibility, but because their school cannot finance the recommendation. The rule would also create inequities between wealthy and less-resourced institutions and between STEM and non-STEM students.

Second, the proposal does not establish that these extraordinarily high fees will prevent fraud. I recognize that fraudulent employers and sham employment arrangements require serious enforcement. However, financial capacity is not proof of compliance. Legitimate students may be excluded while dishonest actors able to pay remain. DHS estimates only an additional 0.5 hour of DSO review and 0.5 hour of administrative payment processing per application (Section VII.A.5.a), without demonstrating why fees of $70,000 or $30,000 are necessary to fund these activities. A more direct response would be risk-based employer verification, targeted site visits, stronger action against fraudulent entities, and DSO fraud training. The Government Accountability Office has specifically recommended stronger SEVP fraud-risk assessment and oversight (GAO-19-297).

Third, DHS has not sufficiently justified the economic and educational losses. The proposal's own analysis estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs under its primary scenario (Section VII.A.1), and its low-participation scenario assumes that institutions may stop paying for non-STEM OPT entirely. This is a foreseeable loss of lawful training opportunities, not merely a reduction in fraud. International education also contributes to American jobs and communities: NAFSA reports that international students supported $42.9 billion in economic activity and more than 355,000 U.S. jobs in the 2024–25 academic year. DHS should evaluate the damage that reduced enrollment, lost talent, and disrupted employer hiring may cause rather than assume these costs can be transferred without consequences.

Fourth, the transition provisions are inadequate. Under Sections V.C and VI, a student who already received an OPT recommendation may be protected for that period, but a later STEM OPT extension may still trigger a $70,000 initial payment if no fee was paid under the new system. Students already enrolled, or already planning their lawful post-graduation training, cannot realistically redesign their finances or careers within 60 days. Future extensions of previously authorized OPT should not be subjected to new prohibitive fees.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed fees as disproportionate and harmful to students and institutions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an F-1 international student currently in my first year of post-completion Optional Practical Training. I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees and respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal. My comments address Section V.A on the proposed fees, Section V.C on the transition period, and Section VI on reliance interests.

For me, OPT is an opportunity to connect my education with practical experience in my field. Having reached my first year of OPT, I am concerned that this proposal would make access to legitimate training depend on financial resources rather than educational purpose, eligibility, and compliance.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would create an extraordinary financial barrier. Requiring educational institutions to make the payment does not shield students from its consequences. A school could pass the cost to students or employers, or decide that it cannot afford to recommend otherwise eligible students. Students could therefore lose access to training because of a school's budget or an employer's willingness to pay, even when their training is legitimate.

I am particularly concerned about the treatment of students already studying or participating in OPT. These students have already committed time and resources to their U.S. education. In addressing reliance interests, DHS should not require OPT to have been the sole reason for choosing a U.S. education before recognizing that access to practical training can meaningfully influence a student's plans. Education and the opportunity to apply that education are closely connected.

I recognize that the proposal does not impose a new fee simply because someone is already participating in an authorized OPT period. However, protecting an existing authorization alone does not resolve concerns about future training opportunities. DHS should explicitly protect current students and OPT participants from new fees throughout their remaining eligibility, including a STEM OPT extension where the student qualifies. A short transition period cannot meaningfully address commitments made over years of study.

I support preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. However, the ability to pay a substantial fee does not establish that a training opportunity is legitimate, and an inability to pay does not indicate fraud. DHS should explain, with evidence, why these particular amounts would distinguish abusive arrangements from legitimate participation. It should also evaluate targeted investigations, employer verification, and enforcement against documented misconduct as alternatives.

DHS should further assess whether these fees could discourage smaller employers, research organizations, and other institutions with limited budgets from offering legitimate training. Reducing participation through financial exclusion should not itself be treated as proof of improved program integrity or a benefit to U.S. workers.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees, preserve affordable access to legitimate practical training, and pursue proportionate measures directed at actual misconduct. If DHS proceeds with any new fee, it should provide a transparent justification for the amount and explicitly exempt current students and OPT participants, including their otherwise eligible future extensions.

Thank you for considering the perspective of an international student currently in the first year of OPT.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they create an extraordinary financial barrier for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100)

I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation, including STEM OPT extensions.

As an international graduate of a U.S. university, I believe this proposal fundamentally misunderstands the economic value international students bring to the United States. International students invest significant financial resources in American higher education, contribute to local economies, and develop skills that American businesses need. OPT provides an essential bridge between education and professional experience, allowing the United States to benefit from the talent its universities have helped develop.

First, this proposal would undermine American economic competitiveness. The United States competes globally for highly educated professionals, entrepreneurs, researchers, and innovators. Imposing fees of up to $100,000 would discourage talented graduates from remaining in the country and encourage them to pursue opportunities in competing economies. America would risk losing skilled workers after investing years in educating them.

Second, the proposed fees would disproportionately harm smaller institutions, startups, and growing businesses. While the proposal places the payment obligation on educational institutions, its economic consequences would extend to students and employers. Universities may become unwilling or unable to recommend otherwise qualified students for OPT. Smaller employers, which often depend on specialized talent but lack extensive recruitment resources, would lose access to qualified candidates.

Third, the proposal does not adequately distinguish legitimate participants from those who abuse the system. Preventing fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate policy objectives. However, imposing extraordinary fees on all participants is not a targeted solution. Stronger verification, employer accountability, and enforcement against fraudulent employment arrangements would address misconduct more directly without penalizing legitimate students and employers.

Finally, the proposal threatens America’s long-term reputation as a destination for education and innovation. International students make educational and career decisions years in advance. Introducing such substantial financial barriers would weaken confidence in the stability of the American education-to-employment pathway and could discourage future generations of talented students from choosing U.S. institutions.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and pursue proportionate, evidence-based alternatives that strengthen program integrity without compromising America’s ability to attract and retain global talent.

Protecting American workers and maintaining America’s global competitiveness should be complementary objectives, not competing ones. This proposal risks undermining both.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they undermine economic competitiveness and harm businesses.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Parva Patel
comments.commentText:
Subject: Public Comment on Proposed OPT Fees — Docket ICEB-2026-0100

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am an international graduate student pursuing a Master of Science in Industrial Engineering at Texas Tech university Lubbock

I am deeply concerned about the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees of $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for subsequent OPT.

International students invest significant time, effort, and financial resources in pursuing higher education in the United States. Many of us hope to gain practical experience in our fields after graduation and contribute our knowledge and skills to American industries.

I understand the importance of maintaining immigration program integrity and protecting American workers. However, I am concerned that these substantial fees could create serious financial barriers for educational institutions and international students, particularly those from middle-income families.

As an engineering graduate student, I hope to contribute to the U.S. manufacturing and industrial engineering sectors. I respectfully ask DHS to carefully evaluate the economic and educational consequences of this proposal and consider less financially burdensome alternatives.

Thank you for considering my perspective as an international student.

Sincerely,

An International Graduate Student at Texas Tech University Lubbock
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create serious financial barriers for students and asks DHS to consider alternatives.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Alexander Starushchenko
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT). This is an unreasonable and potentially devastating financial burden on international students who have already invested significantly in their education in the United States. Such a fee would discourage talented graduates from remaining in the country, undermine American universities and research institutions, and weaken U.S. competitiveness in science, technology, and innovation. International graduates make valuable contributions to our economy, research, and workforce. The OPT program should remain unchanged, without imposing additional financial barriers.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed OPT fee is an unreasonable burden that harms students and U.S. competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees. I believe this policy could significantly harm American economic interests in three important ways.

First, the United States risks losing highly skilled talent. American universities attract talented students from around the world, many of whom contribute to American innovation, research, and technological development. Making post-graduation employment prohibitively expensive could push these graduates toward countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia.

Second, American universities could suffer substantial financial losses. International students often pay higher tuition than domestic students, providing an important source of revenue for American universities. If the opportunity to gain practical work experience after graduation becomes financially inaccessible, prospective students may choose to study elsewhere. Declining international enrollment could reduce tuition revenue, threaten university employment, and weaken funding for educational programs and research.

Third, international students and graduates make meaningful contributions to the American economy. Many international graduates pay federal, state, and local taxes while working in the United States. They also spend money on housing, groceries, restaurants, transportation, and other services. This spending supports American landlords, small businesses, service workers, and local communities. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 American jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. These figures demonstrate the substantial economic value of international education to American communities.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees, arguing they harm the economy, universities, and international students.
