comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100) that would charge SEVP-certified schools $70,000 before a student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation, including STEM OPT extensions.

1. It defunds American universities and the research they produce.
International students overwhelmingly pay full tuition, and that revenue is not profit — it funds research labs, faculty lines, and facilities that American students and American science depend on. Graduate research in this country runs substantially on international students, paid for substantially by international tuition. If a $100,000-per-student toll makes the US the most expensive and least welcoming place to study, enrollment will fall — and university research budgets will fall with it. The schools DHS itself estimates would owe $8.4–16.5 billion a year under this rule are American institutions, and the research they would have to cut is American research.

2. It raises costs for American students.
Full-pay international enrollment is one of the main things keeping tuition lower and programs viable for domestic students, especially at public and regional universities. Lose that revenue and American families make up the difference — through higher tuition, fewer course offerings, or closed programs. A master's program in engineering that loses its international enrollment often doesn't shrink; it closes, and the American students in it lose their program too.

3. It costs American jobs, including far from any campus.
International students contribute on the order of $40+ billion a year to the US economy and support several hundred thousand American jobs — in housing, retail, transportation, health care, and the local businesses of college towns across the Midwest and South, not just in big coastal cities. Every student this rule deters is spending that never happens in an American community.

4. It hands the technology race to our competitors.
The United States is in a direct competition with China for leadership in AI, semiconductors, and advanced engineering. The single greatest structural advantage America has in that race is that the world's best students want to come here, train here, and stay here. This rule taxes exactly that advantage. Students deterred from the US do not vanish — they go to Canada, the UK, and Australia, which are actively recruiting them, or they stay home and build for our competitors. We would be paying to train talent and then charging a toll that pushes it into rival economies.

5. It cuts off a proven pipeline of American founders and employers.
A large share of America's most valuable startups were founded by immigrants, and many of those founders first entered the country as students and stayed through OPT. That pipeline produces American companies, American jobs, and American tax revenue. A $100,000 gate at the exact moment a graduate tries to start working is a filter for wealth, not talent — and the companies never founded because of it are a loss no one will ever be able to count.

6. The fee is not a fee.
A legitimate fee recovers the cost of a service. Processing a SEVIS recommendation does not cost $70,000, and this charge — payable to the general Treasury — is a tax on American educational institutions, imposed on a population with no vote and no voice in the process, to fund general government. If SEVP needs operating funds, Congress can appropriate them, or DHS can set a fee at the documented cost of the service.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule because it imposes high fees that defund American universities and raise costs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by NAGENDRA VENU
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern in the DHS office,
I am writing to express my strong, unequivocal support for the proposed 70,000 dollar Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee. As a United States citizen and a professional in the information technology sector, I have experienced firsthand how the current structure of the OPT program inadvertently disadvantages qualified domestic workers and distorts the entry-level tech job market.
The financial incentives currently tied to hiring through the OPT program create an uneven playing field. Because employers are exempt from paying FICA taxes for OPT workers, foreign graduates are often artificially favored over equally or more qualified American citizens. This dynamic drastically reduces the job opportunities available to domestic tech professionals who are trying to build their careers within their own country.
My personal experience directly illustrates this systemic issue. Approximately five months ago, I applied for an open position within the IT services department at CVS. Despite holding the necessary qualifications and a strong background, my resume was not even shortlisted for an initial interview (I can provide the evidence if needed). I later discovered that the position was filled by an OPT candidate, recruited under the explicit promise of future visa and Green Card sponsorship.
When major corporations like CVS pass over qualified U.S. citizens to recruit OPT candidates with the intent of immediately entering them into the visa sponsorship pipeline, it proves that the program is no longer functioning merely as temporary "practical training." Instead, it is being utilized as a low-cost recruitment channel that bypasses the domestic workforce.
Implementing a substantial 70,000 dollar fee for the OPT program is a necessary and balanced corrective measure. This fee would effectively offset the tax loopholes that make foreign student labor cheaper than domestic labor. It would compel companies to prioritize American citizens and permanent residents first, ensuring that foreign labor programs are only utilized when a genuine domestic labor shortage exists.
I urge the government to move forward with this fee to protect U.S. citizens from unfair hiring practices and restore balance to the American tech job market.

Sincerely,
Nagendra Venugopal
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly expresses strong support for the proposed OPT fee to level the playing field for domestic workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Gay Stewart
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Gay Stewart. I am a professor of physics and of STEM education at West Virginia University. My day-to-day efforts focus on how to build the STEM talent pipeline our country needs to stay a world leader.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

I am not an international student, but there are several excellent international students helping the faculty in our department (and many others on our campus and throughout the country) contribute to keeping the United States a leader in science. There are so many workers needed in science, technology and engineering...these students are not taking jobs away from US citizens, but helping us all keep our country competitive. The United States is built on attracting the best talent from around the world and making it part of us.

If excellent international students decide to go to other countries for their graduate studies, we miss out on the opportunity to have that talent help keep the U.S. a world leader.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Dr. Gay Stewart
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are excessive and would harm the U.S. STEM talent pipeline.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a currently enrolled F-1 doctoral student in the United States, and I expect to complete my degree and apply for post-completion OPT in 2027. I respectfully ask DHS to consider a clear grandfathering or transition provision for students who are already enrolled before any final rule takes effect.

For international students, studying in the United States requires years of financial planning. Before coming here, I calculated tuition, housing, insurance, transportation, and living expenses very carefully. I also had to account for exchange-rate differences, which can make U.S. expenses even more difficult for students whose families or savings are in another currency.

My doctoral education alone is expected to cost more than $90,000. I have worked very hard to complete my PhD in less than three years partly because every additional semester means more tuition and more living expenses.

I am now less than a year away from graduation and have already started preparing for the U.S. job market. My academic, financial, and career plans were made under the OPT framework that existed when I decided to pursue my degree in the United States.

That is why the proposed $70,000 OPT-related fee is so concerning for students like me.

Even if the educational institution is technically responsible for making the payment, students do not know whether schools would absorb that cost or eventually pass some or all of it on to students. For someone who has already invested years of work and tens of thousands of dollars into a U.S. education, an additional cost of this magnitude near graduation would be extremely difficult to plan for.

Future students can look at new rules and costs before deciding whether studying in the United States is financially realistic for them. Students who are already here, especially those who are close to graduation, do not have that same opportunity.

For this reason, I respectfully ask DHS to grandfather students who were already enrolled in U.S. academic programs before the effective date of any final rule. At minimum, students who are already within a defined period of graduation should be protected from a major new financial requirement that did not exist when they began their degree.

I also ask DHS to provide clear advance guidance about how any new OPT-related fees would be paid, whether schools may pass those costs to students, and when those requirements would begin.

International students understand that immigration policies can change. However, when a major new financial obligation is introduced near the end of a degree program, students who have already relied on the existing framework have very limited ability to adjust.

I respectfully ask DHS to consider the financial planning, reliance, and significant investment of currently enrolled F-1 students and provide reasonable transition protections.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed $70,000 OPT fee is concerning and asks for grandfathering due to financial hardship.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Applying academic knowledge in a supervised professional setting can be an important part of education, particularly in STEM fields. Completing classroom coursework does not eliminate the educational value of practical experience.

DHS’s authority to authorize this training is not simply an assumption. In Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS (2022), the D.C. Circuit upheld the agency’s statutory authority to authorize OPT, including the STEM extension.

As a prospective graduate, I consider the opportunity to apply my education an important part of the value of studying in the United States. Considering career development does not make an international student’s educational purpose less legitimate. Making practical training financially inaccessible would weaken that value and could encourage students to choose countries where they can both study and gain relevant experience.
comments.reason: Argues that making practical training financially inaccessible weakens educational value and harms students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Fei Hsu
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees. Imposing exceptionally high fees would create financial barriers for students and institutions without directly addressing unfair employment practices.

International students already face significant obstacles when entering the job market, including limited employment authorization, application costs, strict deadlines, and uncertainty about their ability to remain employed after OPT expires. Additional financial burdens could discourage employers from considering qualified international graduates and prevent students from gaining practical experience related to their education.

I am particularly concerned about preserving access to STEM OPT. STEM OPT already requires a formal training plan, compensation and working conditions comparable to those of similarly situated U.S. workers, and an employer attestation that the student will not replace a U.S. worker.

Most recent graduates, regardless of citizenship, are still developing their professional skills. Practical training exists precisely because students need opportunities to apply their education and gain experience. Requiring them to demonstrate exceptional uniqueness before receiving that experience would undermine the educational purpose of OPT.

Employers should be able to evaluate applicants based on their qualifications, relevant skills, and suitability for the position. They should be accountable for fair compensation, meaningful training, and compliance with worker protections. They should not have to establish that no American could possibly perform the work before offering an international graduate a training opportunity.

The proposal also risks weakening the appeal of U.S. higher education. Students invest substantial time and money in their degrees, and access to relevant practical training can influence where they choose to study. Making OPT financially inaccessible could encourage future students to choose other countries and lead U.S.-educated graduates to contribute their skills elsewhere. The agency should fully evaluate these consequences rather than assume that reducing international graduate employment will automatically benefit American workers.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees, preserve accessible OPT and STEM OPT opportunities, and address documented abuses through targeted oversight and enforcement. Protecting U.S. workers should be compatible with providing lawful international students a fair opportunity to apply their education.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the proposed OPT fees create financial barriers and harm international students and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Coral Chen
comments.commentText:
I am a U.S. citizen and Ph.D. student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Yale, and I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule changes under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 requiring exorbitant fees for F-1 visa holders to participate in the Optional Practice Training program. Many of my colleagues in the Geophysics subgroup are international graduate and postdoctoral workers—we benefit by drawing talent from the strong university Geophysics programs in countries such as Germany, India, China, Switzerland, and Japan. Placing a $70,000 price tag on their ability to continue working in the U.S. is guaranteed to divert that talent and experience to other countries.

My parents both studied electrical engineering in China, and came to the U.S. for graduate school. While on OPT, my mother researched flexible displays at Arizona State University for U.S. military use, and my father used OPT to work at Bell Laboratories, the research company that famously made American telecommunications what it is today. Neither of them came from money. If they had been required to pay $70-100k to stay in the U.S., they would have been forced to return to China, and would not have further contributed (and continued to contribute) to the U.S.'s development as the world leader in tech.

The proposed rule changes in Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 are counterproductive to our country's national interests. I strongly urge the DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Andrew Couperus

Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Andrew Couperus, and I'm a PhD astrophysicist and STEM educator.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

Dr. Andrew Couperus

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Howard Stone
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Howard Stone. I am the Neil A. Omenn '68 University Professor of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering at Princeton University.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

For generations, the United States has been the world's leading destination for talented students and researchers. A key reason for that success is that America has welcomed outstanding individuals from around the world and given them opportunities to contribute to our universities, industries, and society. In particular, international students and immigrants have played pivotal roles in advancing American science, engineering, medicine, and technology. Many of the nation's most influential researchers, entrepreneurs, inventors, and innovators first came to the United States as students. Their contributions have strengthened our universities, fueled economic growth, created jobs, and enhanced American leadership in emerging technologies. OPT has long served as an important bridge between academic training and productive participation in the U.S. workforce.

The United States became the global leader in science and technology not by erecting barriers to talented individuals, but by welcoming them. Our research universities have been engines of discovery precisely because they bring together the most gifted students and scholars regardless of national origin. Policies that make it more difficult for international graduates to remain in the United States and contribute their talents threaten this longstanding source of national strength.

The proposed fees would create a substantial new barrier for international students and for the universities that educate them. Universities, departments, and research laboratories generally do not have the resources to absorb costs that may reach tens of thousands of dollars, let alone approach $100,000 per student. As a practical matter, such fees would discourage participation in OPT and weaken the ability of the United States to retain highly trained talent. Moreover, temporary visa holders earn a substantial share of U.S. doctoral degrees in engineering, computer science, and other STEM fields.

The proposal also runs contrary to America's long-standing scientific and technological interests. As noted above, the United States has benefited enormously from students and immigrants who came here for education and then helped drive innovation. According to a 2026 analysis by the National Foundation for American Policy, immigrants founded or co-founded ≈60% of America's privately held billion-dollar startup companies, and nearly one-quarter of those companies had founders who first came to the United States as international students.

The scientific impact is equally striking. Immigrants have won approximately 40% of the Nobel Prizes awarded to Americans in chemistry, medicine, and physics since 2000. These achievements are not accidents. They reflect a system that attracts exceptional talent and allows that talent to flourish.

At a time of intense global competition in science, engineering, and technology, the United States should be strengthening pathways that enable highly trained graduates to contribute to our economy and research enterprise. Other nations are actively competing for this talent. Policies that make America less welcoming will ultimately make America less competitive.

I respectfully urge the Department to withdraw this proposal and preserve an OPT system that supports U.S. innovation, economic growth, and scientific leadership.

Sincerely,
Dr. Howard Stone

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Aman Kar
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

My name is Aman Kar and I'm a graduate student at Georgia State University.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

The OPT program is a fundamental part of obtaining an education experience in the United States. Without it, the US loses the talent that it itself trained. Universities are a long-term investment from the past where student can received an education, to 'apply' their skills and contribute to the economy. International students are no different to domestic students except with additional barriers for employment, like what this fee would create. Education should be a human right, regardless of their national origin. International students pay their tuition fees (sometimes more) just like domestic students, to receive the same education. When students apply their skills and join the US workforce, the US economy at large benefits (regardless of the citizenship). Companies hire students because of their merit, not because of where they are from. If meritocracy is the goal here, providing opportunities to discriminate students by adding financial barriers, does everyone a disservice. Additionally, if american students should be prioritized over foreign students, the question then becomes should a less qualified candidate be hired simply because they are American? If the answer is yes, then this line of argument can be taken further to ask the question, should a less qualified American be hired over another well-qualified American simply because of their race/gender? Furthermore, if these fees are meant to prevent employers offering lower wages to foreign students instead of american students, then that is an argument to increase the minimum wage or to impose federal wage structures. The well-qualified student should not be denied employment simply because the federal government refuses to increase the minimum wage or tell employers what salary tiers they should be hiring at. Either an employer is free to choose "who to hire" and "at what wages" or the government steps in and provide constraints. But imposing arbitrarily defined fees, to solve a problem that does not exist, only enables opportunity for discrimination; a feature that is the antithesis of what the US stands for. Finally, the OPT is by definition, a limited term opportunity (3 years maximum), for a foreign student to apply their skills, just like a domestic student would, but with an added barrier of requiring to obtain additional work permits/visas past the 3-year mark, which a domestic student would not have to do. So the real question here remains: Is this arbitrarily designed-fee imposed to prevent fraud/wage abuse OR prevent international students from joining the US workforce? Because if it is the latter, then why not require universities to only accept students who are American? And if that is possible, then also why not require universities to accept Americans of specific race/gender? The end goal must either be employment that is merit-based or identity-based, but cannot be both. Because if it is both, then that is the definition of employment based on discriminatory practices, where employers can choose who to hire based on race, gender, or in this case national origin.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.

Sincerely,
Aman Kar

I am writing as an F-1 international undergraduate student at a U.S. university to strongly oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees under Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100.

Students could consequently lose access to practical training regardless of their academic qualifications, employment opportunities, or compliance with immigration regulations.
I am particularly concerned about the impact on undergraduate students pursuing careers in science, technology, mathematics, and other specialized fields. Internships, research positions, and practical work experience are essential for applying classroom knowledge and developing professional skills. Making these opportunities dependent on whether a university can afford tens of thousands of dollars would undermine the educational purpose of OPT.
I understand the importance of preventing fraud and protecting the integrity of the immigration system. However, imposing extremely high fees on all participants is not a targeted or proportionate solution. Legitimate students and institutions should not bear such substantial costs because of misconduct by others. More effective alternatives could include stronger verification procedures, targeted audits, and enforcement against institutions or employers that violate existing regulations.
This proposal could also discourage talented students from choosing American universities, reducing the contributions international students make to academic research, innovation, and the broader U.S. economy. The United States benefits from attracting students who want to study, conduct research, and contribute their skills. Restricting access to practical training through excessive fees would weaken that advantage.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and pursue more targeted, evidence-based approaches to preventing fraud without penalizing legitimate international students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed "Optional Practical Training Fees" rule. This comment raises one question the NPRM never asks: which regions, states and communities would carry the cost. A flat national fee lands very differently in different labor markets. DHS has the data to measure that and did not use it.

1. DHS skipped the regional analysis
UMRA section 202(a)(3) asks for estimates of "any disproportionate budgetary effects" on "particular regions of the Nation," on particular state or local governments, and on "urban or rural or other types of communities." DHS answers with two sentences. It says it "has provided compliance costs for the main provisions" and that state and private entities "make the cost-benefit decisions" about OPT. There is no state table, no metro and non-metro split, and no list of the most exposed communities. Circular A-4, which DHS cites in footnote 126, asks agencies to describe distributional effects, including by geography. DHS built its regulated population of 2,478 schools from OPT authorizations with start dates in 2022 to 2024. It knows which schools these are, where they are, and how many students each recommends. The regional analysis was feasible.

2. A flat fee is not a flat burden
The fee is $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for each later recommendation, everywhere. Entry pay and tuition are not the same everywhere. Where starting salaries are lower, the fee is a larger share of what the training job pays. DHS names H-1B fees as its benchmark. But the H-1B program sets wage rules by the area of intended employment (20 CFR 655.731). The OPT fee has no locality adjustment at all.

DHS assumes that if OPT is worth more than the fee, the parties "could collectively cost share to preserve OPT." That assumption fits best where employers pay high salaries and hire graduates in volume. It fits worst for a regional manufacturer, a county engineering office or a small-city firm that hires one graduate every few years.

3. The screen sorts by geography, not fraud
DHS says the rule would end OPT "as a pathway for low-paid employment." It asks schools to weigh "the value each F-1 nonimmigrant student's OPT participation brings to the institution." Under that test, a school paying $70,000 will favor students with offers in high-wage metros. A normal regional salary will look like "low-paid employment" next to the fee, even when it matches local pay for the job.

DHS's own fraud evidence shows no regional pattern that would justify this. It cites site visits at IT services companies in Northern Virginia, a high-cost metro. It describes the 10,000-student investigation as "nationwide fraud, with problematic worksites across multiple states." A fee that shifts OPT toward a few large metros moves training away from some places. It does not move it away from fraud.

4. The low scenario was never mapped
In DHS's low scenario, schools pay only for students eligible for the 24-month STEM extension, and non-STEM OPT ends. DHS did not check which schools, states or regions place more non-STEM OPT participants. It cannot say whether those losses are spread evenly or concentrated in particular states and kinds of institutions.

5. Labor-market effects are local
DHS says the rule would "alleviate the job market from depressed wages." That is a national claim. The effect of removing a worker depends on the local market. In a tight local market, a lost OPT hire may mean an unfilled job, not a job for a U.S. worker. DHS itself concedes employers "may face productivity losses if they are unable to replace" OPT participants. DHS already uses BLS wage data in this RIA (footnote 131). It should use local data to estimate where replacement is likely and where it is not.

6. State budgets carry part of it
Of the 2,478 schools, DHS counts 1,044 as public. A public university that pays the fee pays from state-supported budgets or from tuition. How much each state's institutions would pay depends on their OPT counts. DHS did not estimate it by state.

7. Request
I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. Before proposing any OPT fee again, DHS should:
(a) publish a state-by-state and metro and non-metro table of expected fee exposure and lost OPT placements, built from the SEVIS data it already used;
(b) complete the UMRA section 202(a)(3) estimate of disproportionate regional and community effects;
(c) explain why a fee with no locality adjustment fits a program whose H-1B benchmark adjusts wages by area; and
(d) allow at least 60 days for comment on that analysis.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and criticizes DHS for failing to conduct regional economic analyses.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Mihai Pop
comments.commentText:
I am writing this to express my strong opposition to the proposed institution of fees for Optional Practical Training applicants. I will detail below two major points:

1. The American industry and scientific enterprise critically depend on international talent.
2. Attracting and retaining top international talent in the United States is critical for our national security.

The proposed fees will, thus, undermine both our security and the welfare of our industrial and scientific enterprises. The new fees will lead to more talented individuals leaving our country, and will also discourage foreign students for coming to the US since they will no longer see a promising path towards a career in our country.

Before I provide more justification for my points, I want to comment on my own credentials. I have worked in biomedical research for over 25 years both at a private research institute and in a large public research university. In these roles, I have been involved in mentoring scientists, both American and foreign, and have been an active member of recruitment efforts aimed at helping to grow our nation's scientific workforce, and at advancing American leadership in science and technology. These roles give me a unique perspective of the national and international talent landscape, directly relevant to the proposed regulation.

Regarding my first point, that the US needs foreign talent to retain its leadership, I want to make the point that groundbreaking discoveries are rare - much like home runs in baseball. The more "at bats" one gets, the more likely one is to eventually "hit it out of the park. In other words, the more talented, well-trained, and motivated individuals we engage in scientific discovery, the more likely it is that breakthrough discoveries will be made. The United States has become the uncontested scientific and technological leader of the world because our country has been able to attract top talent from around the world, and to retain this talent here. Google, for example, a company that has had an outsized impact on the US economy, was co-founded by the son of Russian scientists who chose the US as their new home.

Importantly, this is not a "US talent" versus "international talent" debate - it's not "either/or" - to remain competitive, we need both.

My second point, that our national security is critically dependent on foreign talent is related to the first. Threats to our nation, whether military, cyber, or biological, require innovative defenses. The same conditions that promote scientific and industrial innovation, also allow us to rapidly respond to attacks and to develop creative solutions to emerging threats. In the biodefense space, for example, our ability to control, in a record time, the COVID-19 pandemic, was in large part due to the contribution of a Hungarian scientist who had moved to the US - Katalin Karikó. Our nation's advanced military capabilities (such as the Patriot missile interceptors) are also the result, in part, of basic and applied scientific contributions by talented immigrants.

And to close, I want to focus briefly on the risks of pushing talented individuals out of the US. A great example is the great scientific exodus of scientists from Germany during WW2 and from from Soviet Russia and the Eastern bloc during the Cold War, exodus that greatly benefited the United States. This brain drain weakened Nazi Germany and communist Eastern Europe while strengthening the US, eventually leading to the collapse of these regimes. Pushing international talent out of the US will weaken our country, and strengthen our enemies - this is yet another significant risk of the proposed OPT fees.

In light of all of the above, I strongly urge you to rescind the plan to institute such fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule charging universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. DHS suggests the fee is manageable because schools can pass it along — to students, to employers, or across the student body. That suggestion fails on a point the proposal never addresses: timing. The fee comes due before anyone who could pay it has anything to pay with.

The fee attaches when the Designated School Official enters the recommendation in SEVIS. For a student seeking pre-completion OPT — say, a summer internship between academic years — that moment arrives before the internship begins, before any paycheck, and often before the employer has even finalized the offer. A $70,000 charge for the privilege of a three-month internship is not a cost to be shared; it is a wall. No internship pays enough to justify it, and no student can borrow against wages they have not yet earned.

Post-completion OPT is no better. The recommendation is entered before graduation, before the graduate has a job, and frequently before the graduate has an employer at all. Asking the student to pay presumes savings they do not have; asking the employer to pay presumes a relationship that does not yet exist. And even where an employer is identified, shifting a federal immigration cost onto a worker as a condition of employment raises pay-to-work problems that employers will sensibly refuse to touch — the rational response is to hire someone who does not carry a $70,000 surcharge.

Spreading the fee across all students is the last refuge, and it fails too: public universities operate under state tuition rules, and private schools face a market in which a surcharge on every student's bill is a competitive disadvantage against schools that simply stop recommending OPT instead.

A cost that no one can pay, at a moment when no one has the money, is not a pass-through. It is a shutdown with extra steps, and I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Goucher College
comments.commentText: Goucher College respectfully urges the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw the proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee rule. The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would create prohibitive barriers to educational opportunities for our international students. Goucher would not be able to pay these fees on behalf of our students. Even if funding were available from students or third parties, the logistics of collecting, administering, and facilitating payments would impose an undue burden on the college. We support meaningful oversight of the F-1 program and efforts to prevent fraud and protect American workers. However, conditioning access to practical training on payments of this magnitude would exclude otherwise eligible students based on financial resources rather than educational merit or compliance. We have detailed all our objections to the proposed new rules in the attached letter.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Adam Powell
comments.commentText:
I oppose DHS's proposed Optional Practical Training fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100). The rule would require schools to pay $70,000 for each student's first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each one after that, so three years of STEM OPT would cost $130,000. OPT is the main bridge from U.S. training to U.S. employment: 82% of international STEM graduates who stay to work use OPT before getting an H-1B. Most international PhDs were trained on assistantships funded by U.S. universities and federal grants. DHS projects $8.416.5 billion in fees a year, and its own analysis shows 60% of affected small schools facing first-year costs above 1% of revenue. Economist Michael Clemens estimates OPT participation would fall 2399%, depending on who bears the cost. Lower international enrollment would mean about 46,000 fewer American students enrolling each year, by the Institute for Progress's estimate. It would also push talent toward competitor countries, whose post-study work visas cost a small fraction of this amount. DHS's own cited investigation found only about 3% of participants at suspect employers. Barring those employers and extending STEM OPT's E-Verify and training-plan safeguards to all OPT would address fraud without these costs. I urge DHS to withdraw the fee and pursue those alternatives.

Several of my former students have used this mechanism to gain employment in companies, and even founded companies, which are doing critical work for US materials supply security. As a former startup company founder in rare earth and magnesium metals, we could not have found sufficient talent to develop production technologies for these materials without the OPT. And these fees would be prohibitive, effectively shutting down this essential pipeline for essential science and engineering talent.

It would be hard to imagine a more dangerous and damaging change to the US talent pipeline, right when administration policies are cutting off supplies of materials from even friendly nations like Canada.

Please consider our manufacturers' needs over ideology, and cancel this dangerous plan.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw them due to negative economic and educational impacts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I urge that the proposed rule (8 CFR Part 214 [DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100] RIN 1653-AB01 Optional Practical Training Fees) be withdrawn in its entirety, and that the current regulations remain in effect. I’d like to outline the following reasons for the withdrawal of this proposed rule:

1.SEVIS already provides sufficient oversight to accomplish DHS's goals, so the rule is duplicative and unnecessary.
-As a PDSO, I work with SEVIS on a daily basis, so I have first-hand knowledge that SEVIS gives DHS immediate access to detailed information related to every student’s F-1 OPT/STEM OPT information that could impact a student’s compliance with the regulations. Students and schools report each student’s practical training place of employment, dates, position information, etc.
-For information not directly submitted in SEVIS, DHS also has the authority to request all information and documents from schools, students and their employers, if they have a concern about a particular student or OPT/STEM OPT employer.
-Students in the period of STEM OPT extension are also required to submit Form I-983 Training Plan, completed and signed by them and their employers. These plans are retained by the school, and the government can request them at any time.
-DHS has not made a strong case of widespread systematic fraud in OPT; they have only anecdotal evidence, very few cases compared to overall OPT numbers.

DHS already has all the tools to effectively enforce the current immigration laws by focusing on risk factors, rather than subject entire F category to an extremely expensive fee. SEVIS reporting obligations are already heavy and extensive. The combating fraud excuse that DHS is using to implement the proposed OPT fees seem to be an excuse and not a real reason for the fees.

2.DHS doesn’t have the legal authority to impose the fee as it is proposed.
-Even if there is fraud that needs to be addressed, the revenue from the fee will be going to the Treasury, not DHS, so it is clear that the fee will not be used for OPT fraud prevention, as the proposal claims.
-Per the Administrative Procedures Act, the agency must find the least burdensome way to address the issue (e.g., fraud), and leveling this gigantic fee is certainly not the least burdensome way.
-Fees are supposed to be payments to just offset an agency’s cost of providing a service. The fee amounts are way higher than DHS’s cost for OPT/STEM OPT processing and law enforcement.
According to the above, the OPT fee is not a fee but a tax: it is going to the Treasury, not DHS, and it is certainly way higher than the cost of DHS’s services. DHS doesn’t have the authority to institute a new tax but calling it a fee doesn’t change the nature of this payment (it is really a tax).

3.This rule makes US higher education less competitive internationally and will result in the loss of a significant number of international students.
-Many international student who come to study in the U.S. are also looking for gaining practical experience in their field, outside of the classroom. The unreasonably high OPT fee that the proposed rule will create will discourage international students from applying to higher education institutions in the U.S.
-All the talented international students who have been enriching our education and research and contributing billions of dollars to the U.S. economy may decide to study in another country as a consequence. The U.S. will then lose a critical pipeline of advanced STEM knowledge and talent, potentially to competitor nations.
-Other countries see the value of international students and have policies to attract and retain them. It is a mistake to create yet another hurdle to study in the U.S.
This is a very short-sighted approach: discouraging international students to study in the U.S. It will harm U.S. education and research and will negatively impact domestic students in the long run.

DHS should withdraw this proposal; it is illegal, misguided, and harmful to the U.S.
comments.reason: The commenter urges that the proposed rule be withdrawn in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Eric Anderson
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule. I do not believe charging an expensive fee for OPT is a reasonable or effective solution.

The main problem is that these fees do not directly address fraud. DHS has identified fake employers, false job offers, and shell companies. These problems should be handled through better investigations and stronger enforcement. Charging every university a large fee does not prove that a student or employer is legitimate. It simply makes it harder for honest students to participate.

I am also concerned about the financial impact on American universities. International students contribute tuition revenue and help support academic programs, research, and university jobs. If OPT becomes too expensive, fewer international students may choose to study in the United States. Universities could lose revenue while facing additional costs, potentially leading to higher tuition or reduced services for American students.

This could also hurt local economies, especially in smaller towns where universities are major employers. International students rent apartments, buy groceries, eat at restaurants, and support local businesses. Losing these students means losing customers and revenue for American businesses and workers.

Another concern is America's ability to attract talented people. International graduates contribute to medical research, science, engineering, and technology. Making it harder for them to gain practical experience in the United States may encourage them to take their skills to other countries. This would weaken American innovation and competitiveness.

DHS's own analysis estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs under its primary scenario, while the monetized benefits have not been estimated. I believe the government should provide stronger evidence that these fees would actually prevent enough fraud to justify such substantial economic costs.

Fraud prevention is important, but it should not come at the expense of universities, American students, local communities, and scientific progress. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and focus on targeted enforcement against those who actually violate immigration laws.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees harm honest students, universities, local economies, and U.S. competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to impose a $70,000 fee for an F-1 student’s first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for every subsequent OPT period, including STEM extensions. If the goal is to “protect American workers” and root out fraud, this policy is a factually unsupported, economically destructive sledgehammer that will harm U.S. competitiveness, universities, and the very talent pipeline that fuels American innovation.

First, the numbers themselves reveal the policy’s true aim. The current OPT application fee is a few hundred dollars; this proposal represents an increase of roughly 140 times. DHS’s own language concedes that the fees are intended to “reduce the pool of participants,” and the agency has even suggested that without the fees, it might shut down OPT entirely. That is not “program integrity” — it is a deliberate attempt to price most international graduates out of the workforce.

Second, the claim that a $70,000 fee will deter fraud collapses under scrutiny. Fraud should be investigated and punished, but the rule does not tie the fee to any specific employer or violation; it is triggered simply because a school recommends a student for OPT. Two students can meet identical eligibility requirements, yet only the one whose school, family, or employer can afford the fee would be allowed to work. That is a “pay-to-play” system, not a merit-based one. It will not distinguish legitimate participants from bad actors; it will only distinguish the wealthy from the qualified.

Third, the economic damage would be immediate and widespread. Universities are already under severe financial pressure; many cannot absorb a $70,000 charge per student and would be forced to scale back or eliminate OPT participation altogether. The fee would be especially devastating for STEM graduates, who rely on the 24-month extension to bridge to H-1B sponsorship. Cutting off that bridge does not protect American jobs — it pushes highly skilled talent to Canada, the U.K., and Australia, where post-study work routes remain open and far more affordable. The result is a net loss of innovation, tax revenue, and global competitiveness for the United States.

Finally, the timing is indefensible. The U.S. is already facing a tightening labor market in critical fields. Layering a six-figure fee on top of an already complex immigration system will not make American workers more competitive; it will simply make American employers less able to hire the talent they need. DHS’s own regulatory impact analysis should quantify exactly how many students, universities, and employers would be affected — and the public deserves that data before any final rule is issued.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and instead pursue targeted, evidence-based enforcement against actual fraud.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees are economically destructive and harm U.S. competitiveness and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee structure because of its potential impact on regional universities, smaller institutions, and specialized graduate programs.

International students contribute significantly to the academic and financial sustainability of many American universities. These institutions often operate with limited budgets and depend on their ability to attract students from diverse international backgrounds.

Requiring educational institutions to pay $70,000 for initial OPT recommendations could create substantial financial and administrative challenges. Universities may respond by restricting access to practical training or reconsidering international student enrollment.

The proposal could particularly disadvantage smaller universities that lack the financial resources available to larger institutions.

I respectfully request that DHS conduct a comprehensive assessment of the effects on regional universities, graduate enrollment, institutional budgets, and local economies.

A fee structure that places extraordinary financial pressure on educational institutions risks weakening the accessibility and international competitiveness of American higher education.

I urge DHS to withdraw or substantially revise this proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the fees due to their negative impact on regional universities and requests withdrawal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fee requirements because they risk undermining America's long-term national interests, technological leadership, and global competitiveness. The United States has maintained its leadership in artificial intelligence, semiconductor technology, biotechnology, and advanced engineering partly through its ability to attract and retain highly skilled talent from around the world. According to the National Science Foundation's Science and Engineering Indicators 2026, international students holding temporary visas earned 38% of U.S. science and engineering doctoral degrees in 2024, including 61% in computer and information sciences and 54% in engineering. These figures demonstrate the importance of international talent to America's scientific and technological ecosystem. Imposing a $70,000 initial OPT fee and an additional $30,000 for subsequent OPT could discourage highly qualified graduates from contributing their expertise to American universities, research institutions, and businesses. Instead, these individuals may pursue opportunities in competing economies, allowing other nations to benefit from talent educated and trained in the United States. At a time when technological innovation is closely connected to economic strength and national security, creating unnecessary barriers to retaining skilled talent could weaken America's strategic advantages. While preventing immigration fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives, imposing exceptionally high fees on legitimate participants does not directly address misconduct. Targeted enforcement, stronger verification, and risk-based oversight would address program integrity without creating the same barriers to lawful participation. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and pursue alternatives that safeguard both immigration integrity and America's long-term national interests.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the OPT fee requirements because they undermine U.S. technological leadership.

comments.title: MM15 Comment Submitted by Inchul Cho
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,By submitting this comment, I am expressing my opposition to this proposed rule. America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. I ask you to rescind this proposed rule. Inchul Choinchul.cho@masm.eduNew York, New York 10029

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a physician practicing in Texas, and I am writing to express my concerns about the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2).

Working in healthcare has taught me that the quality of patient care depends on far more than physicians alone. Hospitals and clinics rely on laboratory scientists, medical researchers, biomedical engineers, health data analysts, and many other trained professionals. Their work is often less visible to patients, but it is essential to keeping healthcare systems functioning safely and efficiently.

Many of these professionals receive their education at American universities, including international students pursuing degrees in biomedical sciences, public health, biotechnology, and related fields.

OPT provides an important opportunity for these graduates to apply their academic knowledge in real healthcare and research environments. A student who has spent years studying laboratory techniques or medical data analysis still needs supervised professional experience to understand how that knowledge translates into actual clinical workflows, quality control procedures, and patient safety requirements.

I am particularly concerned about how the proposed fees could affect smaller hospitals, medical laboratories, and research institutions in Texas.

Not every healthcare organization has the resources of a major academic medical center. Smaller institutions already face challenges recruiting specialized personnel, particularly in communities where the available workforce is limited.

Although the proposed fees would be imposed on educational institutions, the consequences could extend well beyond university campuses. If schools become unable or unwilling to support OPT applications because of these costs, healthcare employers may lose access to qualified graduates who have already received their education in the United States.

This does not necessarily mean those positions would be filled by American workers. Some specialized positions may remain vacant, increasing workloads for existing employees or delaying important laboratory and research activities.

I also question whether such substantial fees are an effective way to prevent immigration fraud.

A $70,000 payment does not demonstrate that a graduate is properly trained, that an employer is legitimate, or that an individual is complying with immigration requirements. These matters should be evaluated through appropriate verification and oversight.

I support protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, those objectives should be pursued through measures that directly address documented violations rather than financial barriers that may affect legitimate educational and professional training.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), and consider targeted compliance measures instead.

Healthcare depends on a reliable pipeline of qualified professionals. Policies affecting that pipeline should be evaluated carefully, including their potential consequences for medical research, workforce availability, and the communities that depend on these services.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses concerns that the proposed OPT fees will harm healthcare and research institutions.

I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees. As an international graduate currently working in the United States, I find this proposal deeply concerning. Like many international students, I have invested significant time, money, and effort into pursuing an education and building a professional future here. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Troy Anderson
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,As an American citizen and a biomedical scientist, this policy would be disastrous to not only domestic research, but also to American-born researchers. Our research programs are the best in the world, allowing us to attract the most talented scientists from across the globe. Foreign scientists enter the pipeline and most commonly stay to start their own labs, which in turn train American citizens in science from undergraduate to postdoctoral training. Among these scientists, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make American science great across fields, from energy to medicine. This proposed increase in OPT fees for both initial and renewed F-1s will not only make American science less competitive with other countries, but also prevent our future American scientists from being trained by the best and brightest across the globe. We stand to fall behind other countries, whose collaboration and ability to poach other countries’ scholars allows them to do impactful work. Proposed Increased fees will only mean that more funding for research will be put towards administrative fees than funding life-saving research, wasting taxpayer dollars and slowing medical breakthroughs. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I serve as a Director of a STEM university Career Center.  Our university has historically had, over the past couple of decades, some of the highest numbers of international students as a percentage of the overall student population.  I want to make a couple of points as it pertains to this proposed rule.

1) I've worked with hundreds of employers who are seeking talented engineers and scientists of all stripes.  I can count on one hand the number of employers who prefer to hire international/f-1 talent.  Almost all recognize the red tape that already exists to limit opportunities for F-1 students in this country, so they ask to connect with domestic students first.  Companies have by and large only interviewed/hired our F-1 student talent when they have failed to find the talent they need in our domestic student pool.  This is a supply-side problem (ie not enough domestic talent to meet employer needs), and not one that is going to be fixed by just closing the door to international talent.  

2) Our international students pay, on average, significantly more in tuition than our domestic students, who receive a lot of discounts on the posted tuition rates through scholarships, aid, etc.  We are able to subsidize our domestic students, many of whom are first generation college students, through the tuition fees we charge to international students.  Less international student tuition, less opportunities for domestic students to get degrees at a reasonable price.  I get that the narrative around international students is that they take spots that should be reserved for domestic students, but that is only the case at ivy league and flagship schools which make up less than 1% of the 4,000+ 4-year institutions in this country.  But effectively shutting the door to employment training in this country to anyone who isn't a citizen/permanent resident, the loss in international student tuition revenue will hurt domestic student access to affordable higher education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by University of Toledo
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I oppose the proposed OPT fees described in Section V.A and urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee.

OPT allows students to apply their academic knowledge through practical experience directly related to their field of study. Fees of this magnitude could make that opportunity financially inaccessible to otherwise eligible students. Access to legitimate practical training should not depend on whether a student, university, or employer can provide tens of thousands of dollars.

Although schools would be responsible for submitting payment, this does not eliminate the financial burden. Schools may lack the resources to cover these amounts, and employer funding cannot be assumed. If costs are passed to students, those without substantial personal or family wealth could lose access. If schools cannot fund the fees, students could be excluded despite meeting the academic and immigration requirements.

I support preventing fraud and protecting workers. However, the ability to pay a large fee does not establish that a training opportunity is legitimate. DHS should explain, with evidence, why these particular amounts are necessary and why targeted audits, verification, and enforcement against documented violations would not adequately address its concerns.

Regarding Section V.C, I also urge DHS to protect currently enrolled students from any new fee requirements. A 60-day transition would provide little opportunity to adjust educational plans and financial commitments made years earlier.

Please withdraw these proposed fees and pursue proportionate measures that address misconduct while preserving access to legitimate practical training. Any alternative should include a transparent justification for its costs and a meaningful assessment of its effects on students, educational institutions, and employers.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fees because they create prohibitive financial barriers for students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I'm writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees. As an American professional working in corporate finance, I believe this proposal is a big mistake that will severely damage our offices, our companies, and our national economy.

The justification for this rule is that it protects American jobs and fights fraud, but the math does not add up. Charging a $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and another $30,000 for a STEM extension is a functional shutdown of the program. Universities cannot absorb a $100,000 cost per student, and neither can the vast majority of businesses.

In my day-to-day work life, I see how critical international graduates are to keeping our teams running smoothly. They do not take away our jobs. Instead, they help fill talent gaps that allow our companies to scale, which actually creates more management and operational roles for American workers like me. According to data from the National Association of Foreign Student Advisers, international students contributed over $40 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 370,000 jobs in a single academic year. Stripping our workplaces of this talent pool will shrink corporate growth and lead to less opportunity for domestic workers.

Furthermore, a survey of over 800 higher education institutions showed that 92 percent of college leaders believe international students would simply choose to study in other countries if OPT were gutted. If we drive these bright minds away, we lose the tuition revenue that keeps our local universities funded, and we lose the next generation of innovators to competitors in Europe and Canada.

DHS suggests that schools can just pass these astronomical fees onto employers. In reality, a $70,000 price tag just to get a graduate through the door will cause small and mid-sized companies to stop hiring international talent altogether. Only the massive tech giants will be able to afford it, further consolidating wealth and hurting regular mid-market businesses.

We can protect American jobs and fight fraud through smarter enforcement, not by pricing talented graduates out of our economy. I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule entirely.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they act as a functional shutdown of the program.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Poorya Khajouie
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. These excessive fees would create significant barriers for international graduates, employers, and American universities.

1. The $70,000 Fee Makes Employment Financially Unrealistic

How can a recent graduate realistically find an employer willing to absorb an additional $70,000 just to hire them? Although universities would formally pay the fee, they may pass the cost to students or employers. This financial burden would discourage hiring, especially among small businesses, startups, and research institutions.

2. The Fees Punish Legitimate Students Rather Than Targeting Fraud

Preventing immigration fraud is important, but imposing enormous fees on all international students unfairly penalizes those who follow the rules. DHS should focus on targeted investigations and stronger compliance measures instead.

3. The Rule Would Harm American Businesses and Discourage International Talent

International students contribute significantly to American universities, research, and economic growth. Making OPT financially inaccessible would discourage talented students from studying and working in the United States, potentially pushing skilled graduates toward other countries.

4. The Fees Disproportionately Harm Recent Graduates

Many international students already face financial challenges after paying substantial tuition and living expenses. A $70,000 fee for potentially just 12 months of work authorization is unreasonable and would make professional opportunities dependent on financial resources rather than qualifications and skills.

5. DHS Should Reconsider the Economic Impact

The proposal does not adequately demonstrate that students, universities, or employers can realistically afford these fees. DHS should carefully evaluate the consequences for employment opportunities, university enrollment, and American economic competitiveness.

Conclusion and Request

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and consider more reasonable, evidence-based alternatives to prevent fraud while preserving legitimate OPT opportunities.

International graduates who have invested in American education should have a fair opportunity to contribute their knowledge and skills to the U.S. economy without facing unreasonable financial barriers.

Thank you for considering my comments and the concerns of students, graduates, universities, and employers affected by this proposal.

comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

First, regarding evidence (Sec. IV.A), DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

Second, to claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

Third (Sec. IV.C), DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. This does not support the principles of academic honesty and fair competition but rather whoever can afford the price tag will be able to apply. Additionally, DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

Fourth, the money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

Fifth, benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

Sixth, DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

Seventh regarding reliance and perverse incentives, DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

Eighth, regarding small entities and states. In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

Lastly, regarding process and baseline. DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it. I am a student current pursuing my Master in the United States. 

Supporters of the rule, and the preamble itself (Sections IV.B and VI), rely on two claims: that F-1 is a study visa and should carry no work rights, and that restricting OPT will return jobs to American workers. Both are mistaken.

1. Practical training is part of studying, not a departure from it.

Practical training has been part of the F-1 framework since 1947, and Congress has revised immigration law many times since without eliminating it. OPT must be directly related to the student’s major area of study (8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)). In engineering, architecture, accounting, public health and many other fields, applied training is how an education is completed, and many professional licenses require supervised experience. The D.C. Circuit upheld OPT and the STEM extension as lawful conditions of F-1 status in Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. DHS (2022), and the Supreme Court declined review in 2023.

The rule is also internally inconsistent. If work were truly incompatible with study, a fee would not cure the problem. A $70,000 charge does not make OPT more educational; it only makes it available to students whose schools or families can pay. That rewards wealth, not merit or educational purpose.

Our competitors understand this. Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and Germany all offer post-study work options as part of international education. Pricing out OPT sends the strongest students to those countries.

2. Restricting OPT will not bring manufacturing or other jobs back to Americans.

OPT is available only to students who have completed at least a full academic year at a U.S. college or university, and the job must relate to their degree. Participants are mostly graduates in STEM and business fields, and most come from India and China. They are not the workforce in factories, construction, agriculture or service industries. The rule’s own labor analysis (Section IV.B) focuses on computer occupations, not manufacturing. Workers from Mexico and other countries in those sectors are in entirely different visa categories, which this rule does not touch.

Manufacturing jobs left largely because of automation, global supply chains and trade, not because of international graduates. Rebuilding domestic manufacturing in semiconductors, batteries and advanced materials requires engineers and scientists, and U.S. universities train many of them on F-1 visas. Driving them out deepens the talent shortage that slows new factories.

When companies cannot hire talent here, they hire it abroad. Work moves to offices in Toronto, Bangalore or London, along with the American support jobs around it. Many major American companies were founded by immigrants who first came as students.

The rule also harms American students directly. DHS admits schools may pass the fee on to “all students” (Section IV.C), meaning higher tuition for Americans. Lost international enrollment also cuts revenue that supports programs, faculty and local jobs.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to withdraw it, defending practical training as part of study.
