The proposed rule to charge schools for students seeking employment does nothing to address the root of the issue which is occurring at the workplace. Even still, the evidence presented in the proposal is based on scant evidence of the effectiveness of the fee ad relies on cherry-picked anecdotes that support the position rather than assessing the facts. 
The fee also creates a financial barrier that would perpetuate inequality and discriminate against universities who could not afford the fee. It is unlikely schools would even be willing to pay, meaning the responsibility would fall on students, which would deter them from seeking education in the US. Not only would we lose their dollars at business, in housing, or local economies, but we would also lose their knowledge, talent, and skills. 

The proposed rule has potential for long-term consequences for individuals, institutions, and the nation. OPT is important because there is only so much a person can learn in the classroom. It provides students with important skills of knowing how their knowledge can be applied in the real world. F1 visas help US institutions to attract students from other nations, and in my experience, international students have contributed large amounts of labor, time, and knowledge for the betterment of our social, political, and economic institutions. Without international collaboration, I am confident the US would not be where it is today. 
The United States was built upon the work of immigrants, and we would not be as “advanced” without their perspectives and knowledge. We also need to consider that this rule is rooted in discrimination, racism, and xenophobia, which are not valid reasons to impose this rule.
For these reasons, I urge the DHS to withdraw this rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB)
comments.submitterName: Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB)
comments.commentText:
The Honorable Markwayne Mullin
Secretary, U.S. Department of Homeland Security
Washington, DC 20528

Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01 
Comments of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB) on Optional Practical Training Fees, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

Dear Secretary Mullin: 

The Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology (FASEB) respectfully urges the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw its proposed rule on Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees (91 FR 64566, October 8, 2026). 

FASEB represents 21 scientific societies and more than 100,000 researchers in the biological and biomedical sciences. For more than a century, we have advanced biomedical research and education in the United States. American labs compete for the best scientists in the world. Many scientists who now lead those labs, train American students, and serve in our societies first came here as international students. OPT was often their bridge from a U.S. degree to a U.S. research career. It let the nation keep the return on its investment in their training. Today, our members train, mentor, and work alongside the next generation of international scientists. This rule would decide whether those scientists stay to advance American research. 

FASEB supports DHS's goal of preventing fraud in OPT. The proposed rule does not show that a fee would advance that goal. It would require schools to pay $70,000 to $100,000 or more for each international student who uses OPT, whether or not any fraud is involved. DHS estimates that schools would pay $12.4 billion a year. Under the proposed rule, that money would go to the general Treasury, not to fraud prevention or oversight. The rule reports no fraud rate, and it cites no OPT fraud case involving a research institution.

DHS states that it cannot confidently predict how much OPT participation would decline. However, the available evidence indicates it would fall sharply. If schools pay the fee, independent estimates project that OPT participation among bachelor's and master's graduates would fall by nearly two-thirds at $70,000 and by about four-fifths at $100,000. Doctoral graduates have even more at stake. Two-thirds of international doctoral graduates on F-1 visas are approved for OPT. Temporary visa holders make up 58% of postdoctoral researchers in U.S. science, engineering, and health. This rule would narrow the path that brings these highly skilled, U.S.-trained scientists into our research workforce. More broadly, researchers estimate that a sustained one-third decline in international STEM graduates entering the U.S. workforce could reduce annual U.S. economic output by $240 billion to $481 billion after a decade (Clemens, Neufeld, and Nice, 2026).
 
FASEB's recommendations: 
1.	Withdraw the proposed fees. DHS has not shown that fraud is common or that a fee would reduce it. The fees would go to the Treasury, not to oversight. DHS should pursue targeted oversight of the employers and schools it has already identified. 

2.	Exempt universities and nonprofit research organizations. Congress exempts these employers from the H-1B training fee and the H-1B cap. DHS's concern about avoiding the cap does not apply to them, and none of the OPT fraud cases DHS cites involves a research university or nonprofit research organization. To implement this exemption, schools should not be charged the OPT fee for students employed by universities or nonprofit research organizations. 

3.	Exempt the STEM OPT extension. It already requires E-Verify, a signed training plan (Form I-983), and DHS site visits. DHS's own STEM OPT site visits uncovered some of the fraud it cites. 

4.	Do not extend the $70,000 fee to each new degree level. The rule sets no maximum fee per student. This option would multiply fees for students who pursue advanced degrees. 


Please see the attached letter from FASEB President Michael N. Lehman, PhD, for our complete comments.

CC: Darla P. Henderson, PhD 
Executive Director & Chief Executive Officer 
Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology 




See attached file(s)

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees for the following reasons:
 
1. These positions can be scientifically valuable without generating enough direct revenue to justify an additional $100,000 cost per person. A principal investigator with a limited grant budget may be unable to retain a talented researcher even if that researcher is essential to the project.

2. DHS says the proposal is intended to combat fraud, strengthen program integrity, protect U.S. workers, and prevent employers from using OPT to circumvent other employment-based visa requirements. However,  the fee is triggered by an institution's OPT recommendation—not by a finding of fraud, underpayment, or displacement of an American worker. Consequently, a legitimate university hiring an exceptionally qualified graduate could face the same fee as an institution whose practices raise serious concerns. A more proportionate approach would target documented violations, improve compliance audits, enforce existing labor protections, and impose penalties where misconduct is established.

3. It treats educational and employment circumstances as interchangeable: OPT is associated with education; it allows students to gain practical experience related to their field of study. The proposed fee, however, is partly designed to prevent OPT from being used to bypass the H-1B system. That rationale risks treating legitimate educational training as an alternative route to ordinary employment-based immigration. Yet a graduate undertaking a research fellowship, for example, may be gaining experience directly connected to their degree rather than exploiting a visa category. The distinction matters because a policy designed around suspected misuse can discourage legitimate educational and scientific activity.


4. It creates a particularly harsh barrier for STEM graduates: For eligible STEM graduates, the proposed $30,000 subsequent fee would apply to the STEM OPT extension. Combined with the initial $70,000 fee, that produces the $100,000 total. The extension is especially important for graduates whose work involves long experiments, complex software, specialized laboratory methods, or other activities requiring sustained training. The financial barrier could make these graduates much less attractive to employers and universities. The harm would not necessarily be limited to international students: U.S. research groups and employers could lose access to trained personnel and the knowledge those individuals contribute.

5. It could shift the costs onto people who had no role in the alleged abuse: If a university spreads these expenses across its general budget, domestic students and other research programs could also bear some of the cost. If it passes them to individual students or employers, those parties bear the burden instead.

In other words, the proposal creates a large financial penalty without ensuring that the people who ultimately pay are responsible for any misconduct.


6. It could undermine U.S. competitiveness

International graduates trained in the United States are already familiar with U.S. institutions, research practices, and professional networks. OPT offers a way to retain some of that expertise after graduation. If universities and employers cannot afford to retain these graduates, some may pursue opportunities in other countries. That could weaken the return on U.S. educational investment and make it harder for American institutions to recruit international students in the first place. The magnitude of these effects remains uncertain, but they are legitimate concerns in evaluating the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, stating they impose undue financial costs and burden legitimate researchers.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT).

As an international graduate student pursuing higher education in the United States, I believe this proposal would create significant financial barriers, undermine the competitiveness of American universities, and discourage highly skilled international graduates from contributing to the U.S. economy.

First, the proposed fees are disproportionately high and would restrict access to practical training opportunities. Although the fees would formally be paid by educational institutions, universities may be unable or unwilling to absorb such substantial costs. This could effectively eliminate OPT opportunities for many qualified students, regardless of their academic achievements, professional skills, or potential contributions. Access to practical training should not depend primarily on an institution's financial resources.

Second, this proposal could weaken America's ability to attract and retain global talent. International students invest significant financial resources and years of effort in obtaining American degrees. Many pursue specialized training in fields such as healthcare, engineering, data science, and quantitative analysis. OPT provides an important bridge between academic education and practical professional experience. Creating additional barriers to this transition could encourage talented graduates to pursue opportunities in countries with more accessible post-graduation employment pathways.

Third, the proposed fee structure does not appear sufficiently targeted toward its stated objectives of preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. I recognize the importance of maintaining the integrity of the immigration system. However, imposing the same substantial fee regardless of an individual student's compliance history, educational qualifications, or employment circumstances risks penalizing legitimate participants without directly addressing misconduct. More targeted enforcement, stronger employer verification, and improved reporting mechanisms may offer more proportionate alternatives.

Finally, the proposal could damage the long-term relationship between American higher education and the U.S. labor market. International students contribute to university communities, support local economies, and develop specialized skills through American educational institutions. Making practical training substantially less accessible could reduce the attractiveness of U.S. higher education and diminish the potential economic returns from educating these students.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee structure and consider more proportionate, evidence-based alternatives that address compliance concerns without imposing excessive barriers on legitimate students and educational institutions.

The United States has long benefited from attracting talented individuals from around the world. Preserving reasonable opportunities for international graduates to apply their education in practice is important not only for students, but also for American universities, employers, and the broader economy.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the high OPT fees, arguing they create financial barriers and undermine U.S. talent retention.

I strongly support the DHS proposal to introduce significant fees for OPT and STEM OPT programs. I hope this proposal is implemented because American graduates and workers deserve a fair opportunity to find employment, build their careers, and achieve financial independence.

From startups to medium-sized companies and major technology corporations, layoffs and hiring reductions have created significant competition for limited job opportunities. The transition from F-1 student status to OPT, STEM OPT, and potentially H-1B creates an extended pathway for foreign graduates to participate in the American workforce. At a time when many qualified American graduates are struggling to find entry-level employment, the government should carefully examine how these programs affect domestic hiring opportunities.

Unemployment and underemployment among young American graduates have consequences far beyond the job market. When young people cannot find stable employment, they struggle to repay student loans, pay rent, purchase homes, start families, and become financially independent. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**Public Comment Opposing the Proposed OPT Fees**

I strongly oppose the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for an initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendation and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations for F-1 international students. I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal.

**1. Financial Burden on International Students**

OPT allows eligible international students to gain practical experience related to their academic programs. Students and their families invest substantial resources in tuition, housing, insurance, and other educational expenses. Although the proposed fees would be charged to educational institutions rather than directly to students, institutions could pass on costs through higher tuition, reduced financial assistance, or fewer OPT opportunities. This could disproportionately affect students from modest-income families.

**2. Harm to Universities and the Economy**

International students contribute to American universities through tuition, research, and academic participation. The proposed fees could discourage institutions, especially smaller colleges, from recommending eligible students for OPT. Reduced enrollment and participation could affect university finances, research programs, employment, and local businesses. DHS should consider these consequences before adopting the proposal.

**3. Loss of Skilled Talent and Innovation**

The United States attracts international students through its educational excellence, research opportunities, and career development pathways. These graduates contribute to technology, healthcare, scientific research, and entrepreneurship. Excessive OPT fees could encourage talented graduates to pursue opportunities in other countries, weakening America's ability to attract skilled workers and remain globally competitive.

**4. Impact on Employers and Workforce Development**

OPT helps eligible graduates apply their academic knowledge in professional settings. Employers benefit from their specialized skills and experience. If universities reduce OPT recommendations because of the proposed fees, employers could face recruitment challenges and lose access to qualified graduates. Protecting American workers is important, but this goal should be pursued without unnecessarily restricting legitimate educational and workforce opportunities.

**5. Disproportionate Fees and Better Alternatives**

DHS has a responsibility to prevent fraud, maintain immigration compliance, and protect American workers. However, these objectives do not automatically justify fees of $70,000 and $30,000. DHS should explain how these amounts were determined and provide evidence that they are necessary and proportionate.

Less burdensome alternatives include stronger verification procedures, targeted compliance reviews, improved reporting systems, and appropriate penalties for proven violations. These measures could address legitimate concerns without creating excessive financial barriers for educational institutions and eligible students.

**6. Wider Economic and Family Consequences**

Many international students rely on family savings, scholarships, and loans to complete their education. The proposed fees could increase financial pressure on institutions, resulting in reduced student support and fewer practical training opportunities. International students also contribute to local economies through housing, transportation, food, and other spending. Reduced enrollment or OPT participation could harm universities, employers, and local communities.

DHS should conduct a comprehensive assessment of the proposal's educational, financial, economic, and workforce consequences before proceeding.

**Conclusion and Request**

For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee.

I support reasonable measures to prevent fraud, maintain immigration compliance, and protect American workers. However, regulations should be evidence-based, proportionate, transparent, and fair to educational institutions and eligible international students.

At a minimum, DHS should reconsider the proposed fees, explain their justification, evaluate their likely consequences, and consider less burdensome alternatives.

The United States should continue promoting educational excellence, research, innovation, and responsible workforce development while protecting the integrity of its immigration system. Excessively high OPT fees could undermine these goals and encourage talented international graduates to contribute their skills to other countries instead.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal and adopt a balanced approach that protects American workers without imposing unreasonable financial burdens on universities or restricting legitimate opportunities for eligible international students.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal due to financial burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Dhananji  Karunarathna
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket ID ICEB-2026-0100 - Optional Practical Training Fees

Dear Department of Homeland Security:

I am an international student from Sri Lanka, currently in my fourth year of graduate study in the United States. I respectfully oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and the $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions.

As a graduate student, I cannot afford these amounts. Using an approximate exchange rate of 330 Sri Lankan rupees per U.S. dollar, the proposed initial fee of $70,000 would equal 23.1 million Sri Lankan rupees. An additional $30,000 fee would equal 9.9 million rupees. If both applied to my training, the combined cost would be $100,000, or approximately 33 million Sri Lankan rupees. For me, these amounts represent an insurmountable financial barrier, not simply an additional application expense.

I understand that the proposal would require schools to submit payment before recommending OPT. However, allowing schools to obtain funding from students, employers, or other sources does not ensure that such funding will be available. If my university could not cover the fee, I could not afford to pay it myself. I also cannot assume that a prospective employer would be willing or able to pay tens of thousands of dollars to support my practical training.

I have already devoted years of effort to my graduate education and professional development. OPT would allow me to apply the knowledge and skills gained through my degree in a practical setting directly related to my field. These proposed fees could prevent me from pursuing that opportunity because of my financial circumstances, regardless of my qualifications or the educational value of the training.

As a fourth-year graduate student, I am particularly concerned about the impact on students who are already well into their degree programs. We have invested substantial time and effort in our education. Introducing such a large financial barrier at this stage would create serious uncertainty as we prepare to complete our studies and plan our careers.

I support appropriate oversight to ensure that OPT serves its intended educational purpose. However, I respectfully urge DHS to pursue targeted measures rather than impose fees that make practical training financially inaccessible to students like me. Access to degree-related training should not depend on personal wealth or the ability to find a university or employer willing to pay such large amounts.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 fees. If DHS proceeds with a new fee structure, I ask that it consider substantially lower, clearly justified fees, meaningful financial-hardship protections, and protections for students already enrolled in U.S. degree programs.

Please consider the real financial impact on international students from Sri Lanka and other countries where these dollar amounts translate into enormous local-currency costs. For me, the proposed fees would make OPT financially inaccessible.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees due to insurmountable financial barriers.

I am writing from the perspective of an American small business and startup employer to oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 extension fee. Simply put, this rule is a massive handout to Wall Street banks and tech monopolies at the direct expense of Main Street businesses and early-stage American startups.

When a small manufacturing firm, a local engineering shop, or a seed-stage startup hires a recent college graduate, $70,000 to $100,000 isn't "regulatory pocket change"—that is an entire annual salary. Whether this fee is billed to the university and passed down, or shifted onto the student and their prospective employer, the result is the same: small and mid-sized American businesses will be completely priced out of hiring top STEM graduates from our own local universities.

People who don't run businesses often assume that if you block an international graduate from working on OPT, that job automatically goes to a U.S. citizen the next day. In the real world, that is not how hiring works. We always look for qualified local candidates first because it is simpler and faster. When we hire an engineer, data analyst, or specialist on OPT, it is because we spent months trying to fill a critical technical role and found a graduate from an American university who had the exact skills we needed to launch a product or fulfill a contract.

And here is what economists and business owners actually see on the ground: every time we bring on a specialized engineer or product developer, that person enables us to grow and hire three or four more American citizens in sales, marketing, customer support, and operations. If you slap a $100,000 tax on that pipeline, small companies won't magically find missing specialists—we will simply lose contracts, cancel expansion plans, or be forced to hire offshore contractors overseas instead of employing people who live, rent, and pay taxes right here in our community.

Only the wealthiest trillion-dollar corporations can shrug off a $100,000 fee. If DHS wants American startups and small businesses to compete and create domestic jobs, please withdraw this rule immediately.

OPT is not simply an opportunity to work in the United States. It is an important extension of students' education, allowing them to apply their academic knowledge, develop professional competencies, and gain meaningful experience in their respective fields. As a graduate student preparing for a career that requires specialized professional training and practical experience, I understand how essential these opportunities are for connecting academic learning with professional practice. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Lauren Perry
comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,Dear Secretary Mullin,I oppose the proposed rule. It is likely to be both contrary to the Administrative Procedures Act and to undermine moral and economic goals. First, imposing the fee likely exceeds DHS' statutory authority. There is no clear statutory authority for DHS to impose such a fee. It has major economic implications because it will essentially eliminate a class of potential high-skill workers. It also fails to consider the reliance interests of F-1 students and employers who considered this a bridge program or relied on their ability to be able to gain valuable work experience before returning to their home countries. Moreover, the proposed rule appears to require the student's school --- not the student-worker or the employer --- to pay the proposed fee. It is the government's job to screen prospective students effectively for admission to the United States and this is an abdication of that responsibility. It places an extraordinary financial burden on schools, and a large burden on DHS itself and banking institutions because of proposed refunds. Moreover, the proposal is likely to undermine its own economic goals. The program is used to recruit and employ workers with skills American workers lack. Preventing them from working does not suddenly give American workers those skills. Companies may be forced to relocate or slash jobs if there are insufficient skilled workers and no means to recruit them. The program may also incentivize fraud by encouraging workers to perform under-the-table work or have schools alter the program descriptions to make them eligible for different forms of OPT. This will drive up enforcement costs without addressing the underlying problem. Finally, America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who use Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an international doctoral student in bioengineering at a U.S. research university. I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees on OPT and STEM OPT recommendations. Doctoral students are in a different position from other OPT participants, and the proposal does not account for that.

1. The fee exceeds what a doctoral graduate would earn in a year.
Most international PhD students are on F-1 visas, and after graduating, most of us go directly into postdoctoral research positions. A first-year postdoc earns roughly $60,000 to $65,000, in line with NIH’s own postdoctoral stipend scale. A $70,000 fee for one recommendation is more than the salary of the position OPT is meant to make possible. No lab or department can reasonably absorb that, and federal research grants are unlikely to cover it. Schools will either decline to recommend doctoral graduates, or pass the cost to students, labs, or employers. I ask DHS to state who is expected to bear this cost for research trainees.

2. OPT is how doctoral graduates enter the U.S. research workforce.
OPT and the STEM extension give up to three years of work authorization, which is the bridge from graduation to a postdoc and then to a permanent position. This pipeline depends on international scientists trained in U.S. labs with public funding. Pricing these graduates out of OPT would send them to Canada, Europe, or Asia, and the U.S. would lose the return on its own investment in their training.

3. The fraud rationale does not fit doctoral students.
DHS cites fraud involving shell companies and suspect employers. Doctoral graduates work at universities, hospitals, and research institutes, under named mentors, with documented STEM OPT training plans. A flat fee on every student penalizes legitimate participants far more than it deters bad actors. Targeted tools such as employer verification, site visits, and SEVP audits address fraud without cutting off research trainees. At minimum, DHS should consider exempting doctoral students, or students employed by accredited institutions of higher education and nonprofit research institutions.

4. The fee amount has no stated relationship to administrative cost.
I ask DHS to explain how $70,000 and $30,000 relate to the actual cost of processing an OPT recommendation, and what statutory authority supports fees of this size.

5. Enrolled students relied on existing rules.
Doctoral students commit five to six years to a program, often after moving countries, on the understanding that OPT would be available afterward. DHS should clarify how grandfathering applies to students already enrolled when a final rule takes effect, and whether a student whose OPT was authorized before the effective date would owe $70,000 for a later STEM extension. I also urge DHS not to adopt the alternative that would charge the $70,000 fee again at each degree level. That would double-penalize students who earn a master’s and then a PhD, which is common in my field.

6. Many international graduate students are in dual-student households.
Many of us are married to other international students whose own timelines depend on OPT. Compounding costs and uncertainty make it much harder to plan a career, and to stay, in the United States.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal or, at minimum, to exempt doctoral students and accredited research institutions and to give enrolled students a transition period.
comments.reason: The doctoral student opposes the fees, pointing out that the proposed cost exceeds a first-year postdoc salary.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This public comment is submitted in formal opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding the imposition of unprecedented fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations. The proposed financial barriers—specifically $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent STEM extensions or pre-completion OPT—would effectively dismantle the OPT program, inflict severe unintended consequences on U.S. higher education, exacerbate domestic economic vulnerabilities, and weaken overall national competitiveness.

DHS should fully withdraw this proposed rule based on the following policy and economic considerations:

1. Arbitrary Disruption to Current Students and Lawful Visa Holders
The proposed fee structure abruptly alters the foundational rules under which current international students and existing OPT participants made their academic and financial investments. International students enter the United States lawfully, adhering strictly to federal regulations and contributing substantial tuition. Imposing prohibitive financial costs at the practical training stage retroactively devalues their education and undermines the reasonable expectations established upon enrollment.

2. Disregard for Lawful Contributions and Fiscal Impact
Participants in the OPT program operate entirely within the legal frameworks established by federal immigration law. During their post-graduation training, OPT employees pay federal, state, and local income taxes while drawing minimally from public benefits. Imposing punitive administrative fees overlooks the fiscal contributions made by these high-skilled, lawful taxpayers.

3. Financial Instability for U.S. Higher Education and Increased Costs for Domestic Students
The steep fee increases will make American universities cost-prohibitive for global talent, leading to a sharp decline in international student enrollment. Because international students frequently pay full tuition, institutions rely heavily on this revenue to maintain academic programs, research infrastructure, and institutional stability. A sudden drop in international enrollment will destabilize university budgets, potentially forcing campus downscaling, program closures, and tuition increases for domestic U.S. students to offset operational shortfalls.

4. Disruption of the High-Skilled Talent Pipeline for U.S. Businesses
The OPT program serves as a critical bridge connecting American industry with top talent educated within the U.S. higher education system. Restricting access to OPT through cost-prohibitive regulations will sever this pipeline, restricting access to specialized skills essential for research, development, and market competition.

5. Mismatch with Domestic Labor Market Needs in Critical STEM Disciplines
The overwhelming majority of OPT participants are concentrated in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) fields—sectors characterized by chronic domestic labor shortages. OPT graduates fill technical roles that exceed the current supply of domestic graduates. Restricting OPT participation will result in unfilled critical technical positions across sectors vital to economic growth, including information technology, advanced engineering, and healthcare.

6. Offshoring of U.S. High-Tech Jobs and Corporate Capital Flight
If domestic regulations hinder U.S. enterprises from retaining qualified foreign graduates, businesses will not simply absorb the labor deficit locally. Instead, multinational firms will be incentivized to relocate research centers, software operations, and engineering jobs abroad to jurisdictions with predictable, competitive talent acquisition framework (e.g., Canada, Europe, and Asia). This outcome results in a net loss of domestic employment and capital investment.

7. Erosion of Long-Term National Competitiveness and Innovation Leadership
For decades, the accessibility of practical training has made the United States the primary destination for world-class talent. Enacting prohibitive administrative fees sends a signal that damages the global reputation of the U.S. innovation ecosystem. Over time, reducing the inflow of global talent will diminish technological innovation, weaken economic capacity, and permanently erode American leadership in global markets.

Conclusion

The proposed OPT fee increases represent an economically counterproductive approach that burdens U.S. academic institutions, disadvantages domestic businesses, and threatens broader national interest. The Department of Homeland Security should withdraw the proposed rule and preserve the standard operation of the OPT program.
comments.reason: The commenter submits formal opposition to the rule, citing arbitrary disruption and severe consequences for higher education.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Public Comment Opposing the Proposed Optional Practical Training Fees (Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01)

Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am an international PhD student currently studying in the United States on an F-1 visa. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and an additional $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation, including STEM OPT extensions.

As a PhD student in a STEM field, I have dedicated years of my life to scientific research and advanced training in the United States. International doctoral students contribute substantially to American universities through research, scientific publications, technological development, and the training of future scientists. Many of us work on projects supported by federal research funding, contributing directly to the advancement of American science and innovation.

First, the proposed fees would create an unreasonable financial barrier for international PhD graduates. Doctoral students typically spend five to six years or longer completing their degrees while receiving modest stipends. A $70,000 initial fee, potentially followed by another $30,000 for STEM OPT, is far beyond what most students could reasonably afford. Although the proposal places the payment obligation on educational institutions, it explicitly allows universities to pass these costs on to students or employers. This would effectively make access to practical training dependent on financial resources rather than academic achievement, scientific expertise, or professional qualifications.

Second, the proposed fees would particularly harm academic research and the postdoctoral workforce. Many PhD graduates pursue postdoctoral positions at universities, medical schools, and research institutions. These positions are essential to scientific progress but generally offer salaries that cannot justify a $70,000 or $100,000 employment-related fee. Universities and academic laboratories also operate under limited research budgets. Requiring institutions to absorb these costs could prevent them from retaining talented researchers whom they have already spent years training.

Third, the proposal could undermine America’s ability to attract and retain highly skilled scientific talent. International students choose American universities because of their research excellence and opportunities for professional development. OPT provides an important bridge between academic training and professional research. Making this pathway financially inaccessible could encourage talented students to pursue doctoral education and scientific careers in other countries. The United States would risk losing researchers whose education, expertise, and discoveries could otherwise benefit American institutions, industries, and society.

Fourth, the proposed fee structure does not adequately distinguish legitimate academic training from the fraud and misuse it seeks to address. I recognize the importance of maintaining program integrity and protecting American workers. However, imposing exceptionally high fees on all OPT participants would also penalize students who have complied with immigration requirements and completed rigorous academic programs. More targeted oversight and enforcement measures would better address potential abuse without disproportionately burdening legitimate students and research institutions.

Finally, I am particularly concerned about the impact on students who are already pursuing their degrees in the United States. Many international PhD students made long-term educational and career decisions based on the existing OPT framework. Introducing such substantial financial barriers after students have invested years in their education would create significant uncertainty and could fundamentally alter their ability to complete their planned professional training.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee. Any future changes to OPT should carefully consider the financial realities of graduate education, the essential role of international researchers, and the long-term consequences for American scientific competitiveness.

As an international PhD student, I hope to continue contributing to scientific discovery and innovation in the United States. I believe that access to practical training should be based on educational qualifications and compliance with program requirements, not the ability to pay an extraordinary financial fee.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,

An International PhD Student in the United States
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create an unreasonable financial barrier for international PhD students.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Karen Ferguson
comments.commentText:
I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. Fighting fraud is legitimate, but this fee cannot reach the fraud DHS describes, rests on misread data and an untenable legal theory, and would impose billions in costs on American employers, universities, and workers.

The fee does not target fraud (III.D, IV.A, V.A). DHS documents fraud at shell employers and phantom worksites, yet the fee is paid by the school, “would not be tied to a specific employer,” and comes due before a first OPT recommendation, when no employer need exist. DHS calls DSOs “overwhelmed” and “not fully trained” (IV.B), then makes them the fraud filter. Schools may pass the cost to students, employers, or “all students” (IV.C); visa mills can price it in. The 10,000-student figure is roughly 3.5% of the 289,938 OPT and STEM OPT starts in 2024 (Table 2), rests on an ICE YouTube video (nn.55-56, 67), and conflicts with n.56 (10,000 employers). Where HSI has identified bad actors, investigation, SEVIS termination, and decertification can reach them directly. Taxing everyone else is not tailored.

The data are misread (IV.A-B). DHS says OPT growth “exponentially outpaced” its review capacity, but Table 2 shows 2024 OPT starts only 27% above 2017 (194,554 vs. 152,681), after a 2021 trough. DHS says STEM OPT “far surpassed” its 2016 projection by citing 165,524 participants, yet Table 2 shows 95,384 STEM OPT starts in 2024, near the 92,000 projected for 2026. The 165,524 figure appears to count overlapping 24-month cohorts (2023 and 2024 starts alone total 157,420), so comparing it to the annual H-1B cap is apples to oranges. The wage study quoted at n.111 matches Bound, Khanna & Morales (NBER 23153), which modeled 1994-2001 H-1B inflows, not OPT, and found immigration raised U.S. natives’ overall welfare. Table 1 lists the rule’s “Effects on wages” as “N/A.” 
nber

DHS shows costs, not benefits (VII.A). DHS’s primary estimate is $4.1 billion in annualized costs, $12.8 billion in annual transfers, and no monetized benefits (“Not Estimated”). Opportunity cost is proxied by unpaid fees, which DHS concedes may be too high or too low. The fee is flat: $70,000 whether OPT lasts three months or twelve, and $100,000 if split before and after graduation, which DHS expects to deter pre-completion training (VII.A.5.d), undercutting its “educational value” rationale. In year one, 841 of 1,389 small institutions would bear costs above 1% of revenue and 116 above 20% (Table 17), yet Table 1 lists effects on State governments as “N/A” despite 1,044 state-run universities (n.137).

DHS lacks authority for this charge (III.A, IV.C). INA §214(a)’s “time and conditions” language does not authorize a $12.4 billion-a-year levy. DHS concedes the statute gives ICE no authority to keep the money, which goes to the Treasury’s general fund. A charge untethered to agency cost (more than 130 times the $470-$520 OPT work-permit filing fee), pegged to the H-1B payment, and earmarked for no program is a tax, and taxing belongs to Congress. In Learning Resources v. Trump (Feb. 20, 2026), the Supreme Court held that a grant of power to regulate does not silently include the power to tax. DHS models the fee on the H-1B payment without disclosing that a federal court vacated that payment policy in June 2026, finding it an unauthorized tax (appeal pending). 
form i 765
 +5

The rule harms U.S. interests. International students contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 U.S. jobs in 2024-25, yet new enrollment already fell 17% in fall 2025 (NAFSA). Immigrants founded or co-founded 59% of U.S. unicorns; 183 were founded by people who first came as international students (NFAP, 2026). A $70,000-$100,000 toll will steer this talent to competitor nations and select on ability to pay: Big Tech can pay, while startups, nonprofits, labs, and small employers cannot. DHS even anticipates foreign adversaries subsidizing the fee (IV.C), favoring sponsored students over independent ones. Its low scenario assumes schools pay only for STEM-eligible students, effectively ending OPT for non-STEM graduates, a result never justified. 
www.nafsa.org

The process was rushed, and alternatives exist. DHS blames limited enforcement resources (IV.A), yet ICE keeps none of the fee (IV.C). About 30 days to comment on an economically significant rule, versus 60 for the information collection, departs from the 60-day norm in E.O. 12866 §6(a)(1) and E.O. 13563 §2(b). DHS should withdraw the rule. If it proceeds, it should place HSI’s data in the docket, extend comment to 60+ days, target identified bad actors, consider a modest cost-recovery fee retained by SEVP, and reject the alternative (V.A) of re-imposing $70,000 at each degree level. “Shut down the program entirely” (IV.A) is a false choice.

Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Optional Practical Training Fees

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation.

I am an international student currently pursuing a master’s degree in Environmental Studies at a U.S. university, having previously completed my bachelor’s degree in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology in the United States. Throughout my education, I have participated in scientific research and gained valuable hands-on experience that has strengthened my academic and professional development.

My concerns primarily relate to Section V.A of the proposed rule and its potential consequences for international students, educational institutions, and the U.S. scientific workforce.

First, the proposed fees would create an unreasonable financial barrier to practical training. Although the rule would initially require educational institutions to pay these fees, DHS acknowledges that institutions may transfer the financial burden to students or employers. For many international graduates, particularly those entering scientific research, environmental conservation, and nonprofit sectors, these amounts would be prohibitively expensive.

Second, the proposed rule could significantly undermine opportunities for international students to contribute to American research and innovation. Many positions in environmental science and conservation are offered by university laboratories, nonprofit organizations, and research institutions operating with limited funding. Requiring tens of thousands of dollars for OPT participation could discourage these organizations from hiring international graduates, regardless of their qualifications or potential contributions.

Third, I question whether imposing such substantial financial barriers is an appropriate or effective method of preventing immigration fraud. The ability to pay a large fee does not demonstrate an individual’s compliance with immigration regulations or the legitimacy of their employment. More targeted oversight, verification procedures, and enforcement measures would better address fraudulent activity without imposing disproportionate burdens on students pursuing legitimate educational and professional opportunities.

Finally, international students make significant financial, academic, and personal commitments when choosing to pursue higher education in the United States. Many plan their education and early careers around the opportunity to gain practical experience through OPT. Introducing such extraordinary fees would substantially disrupt these expectations and could discourage talented students and researchers from choosing American institutions in the future.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee requirements and consider more proportionate, evidence-based alternatives that protect the integrity of the immigration system while preserving legitimate opportunities for international students.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Daniel Smith
comments.commentText:
The proposed rule to impose a $70,000 initial fee and a $30,000 subsequent fee on Optional Practical Training is completely unworkable, legally vulnerable, and effectively acts as a backdoor ban on practical training. Labeling this astronomical fee structure as a measure to combat fraud or protect American workers completely misses the reality on the ground. The underlying logic of the rule collapses entirely when examining how the funds are actually handled. DHS openly admits that these collected fees will not be retained by ICE or SEVP for administrative oversight or enforcement; instead, they are dumped directly into the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302. Slapping a $70,000 price tag on an initial OPT recommendation has zero rational connection to actual administrative costs and functions purely as a punitive deterrent and disguised tax. Furthermore, penalizing hundreds of thousands of law-abiding students, legitimate employers, and accredited universities because of isolated criminal incidents involving a handful of bad actors and shell companies is entirely disproportionate and violates basic administrative law principles against arbitrary and capricious rulemaking.

The broader economic and innovation impacts would be disastrous for the country's competitive standing. In recent years, approximately 200,000 students participated in post-completion or pre-completion OPT, while nearly 100,000 participated in STEM OPT extensions. These graduates fill critical talent shortages across engineering, software development, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced research. Choking off this pipeline does not magically create jobs for American workers; it simply forces global tech and research companies to shift talent acquisition, capital, and innovation overseas to countries like Canada, the UK, and Singapore that are actively courting this expertise. Moreover, the administration's reliance on arguments surrounding FICA tax exemptions ignores that these programs are foundational for bringing top-tier global talent into our ecosystem. Forcing employers and institutions to shoulder an insurmountable $70,000 upfront barrier completely destroys the entry-level hiring market for high-skilled graduates and handicaps American firms against international competitors.

The proposal is equally devastating for educational institutions, especially smaller schools, regional colleges, and non-profit universities. DHS's own Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis reveals that 56 percent of regulated SEVP-certified institutions are small entities, and over 60 percent of small institutions will face severe financial burdens ranging from 1 percent to over 20 percent of their annual revenue. For regional universities and colleges operating on tight margins, absorbing or passing on a $70,000 liability per student is an absolute impossibility. This rule will gut institutional budgets, force massive administrative overhead regarding compliance tracking, and destroy practical training options for students who rely on them to bridge the gap between classroom theory and professional experience.

Furthermore, graduate education—particularly Master's and PhD programs in STEM fields—will suffer catastrophic enrollment declines. International graduate students who fund their education and contribute significantly to university research labs and academic publications will simply look elsewhere if U.S. post-graduate training is placed behind an insurmountable paywall. Even designated school officials are set up to fail under this rigid framework. DSOs will be forced to act as tax collectors and financial auditors, confirming wire transfers, validating institutional funds, and verifying complex ledger entries before entering recommendations into SEVIS. The administrative chaos this introduces—coupled with rigid and unfair refund policies where fees are entirely non-refundable once an Employment Authorization Document is issued—creates an untenable operational nightmare. Docket Number ICEB-2026-0100 fundamentally misdiagnoses the challenges facing the U.S. labor market and immigration system. Rather than enhancing integrity or protecting workers, these punitive fees will drive top-tier global talent away from American shores, cripple institutional budgets, and erode U.S. technological preeminence. DHS must withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: Argues the fees act as a backdoor ban and punitive deterrent that harms innovation and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Richard Williams
comments.commentText:
I oppose DHS’s proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for each subsequent OPT recommendation. Fraud involving sham employers and false records is a serious concern, but DHS has not shown that charges this large, imposed on legitimate students and schools, are necessary or effective. DHS should withdraw it and pursue targeted enforcement.

The fees are not tied to an applicant’s risk, employer, training period, or government processing costs. They apply across pre-completion, post-completion, and STEM OPT, regardless of risk. DHS estimates $12.4 billion in annual fee transfers, compared with $15.7 million in annual OPT review and payment-processing costs. The money would go to the U.S. Treasury, not directly fund ICE or SEVP oversight, and would not be reserved for OPT enforcement. DHS has not explained why a fee so far removed from administrative costs is proportionate.

DHS’s economic analysis raises further concerns. It estimates primary 10-year costs of $35.1 billion at a 3% discount rate ($29.0 billion at 7%) and government fee transfers of $109.4 billion ($90.6 billion at 7%), while leaving monetized benefits unestimated. DHS does not quantify how much fraud the rule would prevent, how many jobs it would create for U.S. workers, or what wage gains would result. Without comparable estimates, the public cannot assess whether benefits justify the costs. DHS acknowledges it cannot fully measure the value of lost OPT opportunities. Using fees collected as a proxy for the value of opportunities that disappear risks circular reasoning. Its projections depend on unverified assumptions about how schools will respond.

The fraud cases cited do not establish that lawful OPT participants are responsible for wider labor-market problems. Cases involving sham companies, false documents, and fraudulent job offers justify investigating and penalizing those involved, not imposing a six-figure barrier on every participant. Increasing STEM OPT participation alone does not prove that OPT caused unemployment or wage depression; broader outcomes are also affected by economic cycles, layoffs, and employer demand. Using a lawful training period while pursuing another immigration status is not, by itself, proof of fraud. DHS should demonstrate a measurable connection between lawful OPT participation and the harms it alleges before restricting the program nationwide.

The fee would select for ability to pay, not legitimacy. DHS says schools may seek funding from students, employers, or other sources, but many cannot absorb a $70,000 charge per student. They may pass the cost on, stop recommending qualified students, or experience reduced enrollment. The burden is especially disproportionate for non-STEM graduates eligible for only 12 months of OPT. The proposal can also trigger $100,000 in fees when a student uses pre-completion OPT and later post-completion OPT, encouraging schools to discourage legitimate training simply to avoid the extra payment.

DHS estimates that 841 of 1,389 affected small institutions would face transition-year fee impacts exceeding 1% of revenue, including 116 facing impacts above 20%. These burdens could harm enrollment, tuition revenue, research capacity, and employers’ access to qualified graduates. It does not adequately assess effects on innovation or U.S. competitiveness. A policy that disproportionately excludes students whose schools lack resources does not reliably identify fraudulent applicants; it risks driving talented people to study and work elsewhere.

The problems DHS describes call for targeted enforcement, not a blanket financial penalty. Its examples involve fake worksites, shell companies, false records, and networks facilitating fraudulent documentation. A flat fee verifies none of these facts. Better measures include risk-based employer site visits, verification of employer identities and payroll records, analysis of suspicious networks and addresses, fraud training for designated school officials, timely school recertification, and meaningful penalties for employers and intermediaries that facilitate fraud. GAO-19-297 identified opportunities to strengthen SEVP oversight and risk management. These measures target warning signs and permit evaluation. Administrative convenience is not enough to justify a fee that could effectively eliminate lawful opportunities.

DHS should withdraw this proposal. Before considering any new fee, it should explain how the amount was calculated, quantify expected fraud-prevention and labor-market benefits, assess effects on students, schools, employers, and U.S. innovation, and compare less burdensome alternatives. Protecting U.S. workers and immigration integrity are legitimate goals. A near-prohibitive fee imposed indiscriminately on legitimate participants, without demonstrated proportionality or dedicated enforcement funding, is not a justified way to achieve them.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees as disproportionate, unjustified by administrative costs, and harmful to legitimate participants.

comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule imposing substantial fees on OPT and STEM OPT. I believe this proposal would disproportionately harm legitimate international students, undermine the value of U.S. higher education, negatively affect American universities and businesses, and create significant economic consequences without effectively addressing the underlying problem of student visa fraud.
Students & University impacts: For many international students, the opportunity to gain practical, industry-relevant experience is an essential part of pursuing a degree that allows them to apply that knowledge to real-world challenges, develop professional skills, and understand industry practices. They choose United States because of the quality of its universities, its research environment, its innovation ecosystem, and its opportunities to gain professional experience. International students are not merely consumers of education. Many contribute to research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and the development of technologies and services that benefit American society.
Without a reasonable opportunity to gain practical experience , an American degree may lose a significant part of its distinguishing value for international students. Students can pursue academic qualifications in their home countries, often at a lower cost. Imposing extraordinarily high fees on these programs could make this opportunity inaccessible and diminish the educational value that students expect when investing in an American degree.  If studying in the US becomes substantially more expensive while access to the practical training becomes uncertain, students may increasingly choose other countries that offer more accessible and predictable pathways. 
This could weaken the competitiveness of American universities, reduce international enrollment, and affect the United States' ability to attract talented students from around the world.
Economic Impact: The potential consequences of reduced international enrollment should be evaluated across the broader economy.International students face substantial financial commitments, including high tuition fees & other educational expenses. They pay significantly more tuition fees than domestic students.They also support local economies through spending on housing, health insurance, transportation, and everyday living expenses like groceries, transportation, restaurants, retail, and other services.
Preventing fraud and protecting the integrity of the student visa system are legitimate government objectives. However, a policy should be designed to address the actual sources of fraud rather than impose broad financial barriers on students who have complied with the rules. The proposed fees appear to risk burdening legitimate students and institutions without clearly demonstrating how the fees would identify or prevent fraudulent conduct. The goal should be to identify and deter fraud at its source, not to make legitimate education and post-graduation training unaffordable. 
I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed fee and preserve access to OPT and STEM OPT under the existing framework, without these additional fees.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees because they would harm legitimate students, universities, and businesses without fixing fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Emma Derrick
comments.commentText:
Dear Secretary Mullin,

I am a US citizen and a PhD student at a university in the United States.

I'm writing to express my opposition to the excessive OPT fees proposed in DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, "Optional Practical Training Fees". As explained in the American Physical Society's public comment (ICEB-2026-0100-2924), the proposed $70,000 initial recommendation fee and subsequent $30,000 extension fee to be levied on universities would likely put OPT out of reach for essentially all international students. Such fees would shatter the U.S. STEM talent pipeline, forcing international, high-skilled students and graduates trained at U.S. institutions to leave the U.S. for competing nations.

Many of my colleagues are international students. They contribute greatly to our lab and research. With these increased fees, my international colleagues will find it increasingly difficult to find postgraduate work in the US. As scientists, we rely on collaboration to form and test new ideas. Excluding international students will be a disadvantage to the entire scientific community in the US.

Once again, I ask you to withdraw this proposed rule. Our economy, national security, and international influence depend on it.



Sincerely,
Emma Derrick
comments.reason: Opposes the excessive OPT fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule to protect the U.S. talent pipeline.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jessie Li
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed rule in its entirety and ask DHS to withdraw it. A full comment with citations is attached.
No statutory authority (Sections III.A, IV.C). INA 214(a) lets DHS set the "time and conditions" of admission. It does not authorize a $70,000 charge on schools deposited in the Treasury as a miscellaneous receipt. DHS concedes ICE cannot retain the funds and does not claim the amount reflects any cost of service. A charge that raises general revenue beyond the cost of service is a tax. National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States (1974). Congress enacts immigration fees expressly (8 U.S.C. 1356(m), 1372(e), 1184(c)(9), (12)). After Loper Bright (2024), DHS gets no deference, and a rule with $74.6–144.3 billion in ten-year transfers requires clear authorization. West Virginia v. EPA (2022).
The fee does not target fraud (Section IV.A). Every fraud example DHS cites involves employers: shell companies, staged worksites, phantom employees. The fee is charged to schools, is not tied to any employer, and is due before initial OPT requires a job offer. DHS's latest probe flagged about 10,000 students, under 3% of the roughly 360,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. The rule charges all of them.
The enforcement rationale defeats itself (Section IV.C). DHS says compliance resources have not scaled with the program and rejects site visits as too resource-intensive. The fee proceeds, a primary estimate of $12.8 billion a year, fund no enforcement.
The fee selects for wealth (Section IV.C). DHS allows schools to pass the fee to students. The practical selection criterion becomes ability to pay $70,000 to $130,000, which excludes qualified students and leaves well-funded bad actors untouched.
The labor rationale does not fit the amount (Section IV.B). The FICA exemption DHS cites is worth about $6,900 a year on a $90,000 salary. The fees for OPT plus STEM OPT total $100,000. DHS's own low scenario eliminates about 106,000 of 194,554 initial OPT placements. That is abolition of most non-STEM OPT by price, without acknowledgment or justification.
Irrational structure (Section V.A). Part-time pre-completion OPT triggers the full $70,000. Pre-completion, post-completion, and STEM OPT total $130,000. Fees are non-refundable once an EAD issues, even if an offer is rescinded; earlier refunds are discretionary and unappealable.
Change in position unexplained. The 2016 STEM OPT rule rested on findings of benefit to institutions, the economy, and U.S. workers. DHS does not quantify the benefits it would forgo. FCC v. Fox (2009). The repeated statement that DHS "may shut down the program entirely" is not a reason for this rule.
Reliance interests (Section VI). About 280,000 students used OPT in 2024. Students chose STEM programs and borrowed tuition in reliance on OPT. DHS grandfathers only students with a DSO recommendation before the effective date and never considers grandfathering all currently enrolled students. DHS v. Regents (2020) requires that analysis.
Procedure. The rule is economically significant, yet DHS allowed 30 days instead of the 60 days EO 12866 and EO 13563 call for. DHS rejected a small-entity exemption in one sentence although 56% of affected schools are small entities.
Requested action: withdraw the rule. Otherwise: extend the comment period 60 days; limit any fee to administrative cost; target employers through I-983 plans, E-Verify, and site visits; grandfather all enrolled students; exempt pre-completion OPT; reject re-charging $70,000 per degree level; make refunds appealable.
comments.reason: Argues the rule lacks statutory authority, does not target fraud, and asks DHS to withdraw it entirely.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for any subsequent OPT. I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal and reconsider its approach to preventing fraud in the OPT program.

1. The proposed fees would create an unreasonable financial barrier to employment.

International students already make substantial financial investments in their education in the United States, including tuition, housing, health insurance, and other living expenses. Many students rely on their personal savings and family support to complete their degrees. An additional fee of $70,000 would make OPT financially inaccessible to an overwhelming number of qualified graduates, regardless of their academic performance, professional skills, or compliance with immigration requirements.

The proposed fee is particularly concerning because OPT is intended to provide eligible international students with an opportunity to gain practical experience directly related to their fields of study. A fee of this magnitude would effectively prevent many students from accessing this opportunity, undermining the educational and professional value of their U.S. degrees.

2. The proposal would undermine the competitiveness of American higher education.

International students choose the United States because of its educational institutions, research opportunities, and professional development pathways. The opportunity to apply their education in a professional setting is an important consideration when deciding where to study.

If graduates face a $70,000 fee before they can pursue initial OPT, prospective students may increasingly choose universities in other countries that offer more accessible post-study employment pathways. This would weaken the United States’ ability to attract talented students, reduce the international competitiveness of American universities, and potentially diminish the long-term contributions of U.S.-educated graduates to the American economy.

3. The proposal would disproportionately harm small businesses and entry-level employers.

Many industries depend on early-career professionals who bring specialized knowledge, technical skills, and new perspectives. In fields such as architecture and design, graduates often begin their careers at small and mid-sized firms, where entry-level compensation is constrained by business size and project-based revenue.

A $70,000 OPT fee would create a substantial obstacle for graduates seeking entry-level employment and could discourage smaller employers from hiring otherwise qualified candidates. Even if the fee were formally imposed on students, employers would face a narrower talent pool, increased recruitment uncertainty, and greater difficulty filling positions. The resulting burden could be especially severe in industries where professional experience and technical training are essential to career development.

4. Fraud prevention should be proportionate, evidence-based, and targeted.

I recognize the government’s responsibility to maintain the integrity of the immigration system, prevent fraud, and ensure compliance with employment authorization requirements. However, the existence of these legitimate objectives does not establish that an exceptionally high fee is a necessary or effective solution.

A fee of $70,000 risks treating eligible students who comply with immigration rules as though they were responsible for the misconduct of others. The Department should demonstrate, with transparent evidence, why this specific amount is necessary, how it would reduce fraud, and whether less burdensome alternatives could achieve the same objectives.

Potential alternatives include enhanced verification of employment and employer information, targeted investigations of suspected fraud, improved oversight of noncompliant employers, and stronger coordination between educational institutions and the relevant government agencies. These measures would more directly address misconduct without imposing a prohibitive financial burden on the broader population of eligible students.
comments.reason: Opposes the proposal because the fees create an unreasonable financial barrier and hurt U.S. competitiveness.
