comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Opposition to Optional Practical Training Fees
DHS/ICE Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01
91 FR 64566 (October 8, 2026)

I am an F-1 graduate student studying computer science at a U.S. public university, commenting in my individual capacity. I support preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fees because the analysis does not adequately establish that these charges would distinguish legitimate training from abuse or justify the burdens on current students.

1. Demonstrate the anti-fraud mechanism (Section IV.C).

Payment establishes access to money; it does not verify an employer, the educational value of a placement, or labor compliance. DHS permits schools to shift the charge to students, employers, or other students. If a school can pass on the entire cost, what evidence shows that the fee will improve its scrutiny? DHS should distinguish fewer participants from less fraud and explain why these amounts are more effective than lower, targeted measures. Because the proceeds are not retained by ICE for OPT oversight, increased fee collections should not be treated as increased enforcement capacity.

2. Protect existing educational commitments (Sections V.C and VI).

I have already invested time and resources in a U.S. degree. Applying computer science in supervised, degree-related practical training would complement that education. An additional charge imposed after enrollment could make that opportunity inaccessible. My concern is the loss of a meaningful educational option, not a guarantee of employment or permanent status.

DHS's proposed 60-day transition does not allow enrolled students to undo substantial educational commitments. Nor does the cited one-year share of F-1 students in higher education participating in OPT establish how graduating cohorts relied on practical training. OPT need not be the sole reason for enrollment to have materially influenced educational planning. DHS should justify imposing the fee on current students despite their different reliance interests from future applicants who can choose a program knowing the new costs.

3. Test affordability and costs to U.S. stakeholders (Sections VII.A.3.b and VII.A.5.b).

DHS should test scenarios with substantial participation losses among STEM students as well as other students. The possibility that OPT creates benefits greater than the fee does not establish that a student, university, and employer can jointly raise the money before a recommendation. Benefits can be delayed and shared broadly, while each party faces cash and coordination constraints. Please test those constraints and quantify, where feasible, foregone research, employer productivity, university enrollment, and costs passed to American students. Treating an unpaid fee as a proxy for lost social benefits needs empirical justification and sensitivity analysis.

4. Compare feasible alternatives and adopt a clear safeguard (Section IV.C).

DHS discusses alternatives such as site visits and training plans. Please compare their total costs and effectiveness with the proposed fees, including risk-based audits, employer verification, and sanctions for proven misconduct. Ease of collecting a fee is not sufficient evidence that it best protects workers or program integrity. Any alternative fee should have a transparent statutory basis and a proportionate, documented rationale.

Please withdraw this proposal. If DHS proceeds with a revised measure, exempt students already enrolled when the proposal was published from the new fees for otherwise eligible OPT and STEM OPT associated with their current degree. This safeguard would preserve existing eligibility and compliance requirements while allowing future students to plan under known conditions.

Please address these specific evidentiary questions and the grandfathering alternative in any final rule.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed fees because the analysis fails to establish that charges distinguish fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Opposition to Optional Practical Training Fees - Student Debt and Affordability
Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fees because they would impose an unreasonable financial barrier to degree-related practical training, particularly for students who have already borrowed to finance their education. This comment addresses the student cost impacts discussed in Sections IV.C and VII.A.

Students who finance tuition and living expenses with education loans may reach graduation with substantial debt and little remaining access to credit. Rent, food, health insurance, transportation, and loan obligations continue during the transition from study to practical training. Requiring another large payment at this stage could force otherwise qualified students to take on unaffordable debt or abandon the opportunity to apply their education.

Although schools would make the payments to the government, the proposal expressly allows costs to be passed on to students. Naming the school as the payer therefore does not resolve student affordability. If a school cannot absorb the charge and a student cannot finance it, the practical consequence may be the loss of access to OPT.

The proposal compares the fees with the cost of one or two years of U.S. education. That comparison does not establish affordability. For a student who borrowed to pay those original costs, it describes another major financial burden. The ability to finance a degree does not demonstrate the ability to produce an additional $70,000 before beginning practical training.

For perspective, if the full $70,000 initial fee were passed to a student seeking 12 months of OPT, the charge would be equivalent to approximately $5,833 for each month of potential training, before any financing costs. This would be additional to existing educational debt and necessary living expenses. The payment would be required before the school recommends OPT, so DHS cannot simply assume that future training income will cover the upfront cost.

Neither a suitable position nor a particular level of earnings is guaranteed. Additional borrowing could therefore expose students and any family co-signers to substantial financial risk without ensuring that the student can repay the new debt. Losing access to training would not erase the original educational loans; it could instead leave graduates with continuing obligations and fewer opportunities to develop the professional skills for which they studied.

Access to legitimate educational practice should not depend on whether a student has wealthy relatives or can obtain another large loan. Academic ability, compliance with program requirements, and the educational value of the training are more appropriate considerations. Making practical learning financially inaccessible to otherwise eligible borrowers would undermine its educational purpose.

I urge DHS to withdraw these proposed fees. Before proposing any replacement, DHS should evaluate existing educational debt, necessary living expenses, access to credit, interest costs, realistic training earnings, and the effects of passing institutional charges to students. Any revised approach should use proportionate fees supported by a transparent justification and include meaningful financial-hardship protections.

Students who have already made a substantial investment in their education should have a financially realistic opportunity to pursue lawful, degree-related practical training. They should not have to jeopardize their ability to meet basic needs or incur another major debt merely to access that opportunity.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the fees due to unreasonable financial barriers and student debt impacts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; Section VII.A.5.b, 91 FR 64588–64589.**

I oppose the proposed rule's reliance on unpaid OPT fees as a proxy for the social opportunity cost of lost participation. DHS acknowledges that actual benefits may exceed the fee but assumes affected parties could collectively finance participation when benefits are sufficiently large. That assumption needs support before it can anchor the regulatory analysis.

First, the proposal itself identifies practical obstacles to that financing. Initial OPT applicants need not already have an employer, and Section VII.A.5.d recognizes additional budgeting, funding, and transaction burdens. An unidentified future employer cannot necessarily commit funds before the school must pay. The ability to pool sufficient funds therefore cannot simply be presumed.

Second, a student's liquidity, a university's recoverable return, an employer's private benefit, and benefits to U.S. society are different quantities. Research spillovers and benefits to other workers or consumers may not be recoverable by the parties required to finance the fee. Even a project with social benefits above $70,000 can disappear when its participants cannot capture or finance those benefits. OMB Circular A-4 discusses externalities, transaction costs, and public goods, including basic scientific research; it does not assume that private bargaining always captures social value.[1]

Third, behavioral effects require explicit incidence assumptions. Clemens's 2026 working paper separately models effects when the economic burden falls on students, universities, or employers.[2] Its estimates are conditional projections, with substantial limitations; they are not observed effects of this proposed rule. They nevertheless illustrate why DHS should test financing and participation responses rather than infer social losses from a chosen fee alone.

DHS reasonably acknowledges that valuation is uncertain and that alternative workers may replace some OPT participants. Those considerations justify transparent ranges, rather than establishing that the fee is an appropriate ceiling or unbiased proxy. This objection does not establish whether the proposal's aggregate cost estimate is too high or too low, and fee transfers should not be double-counted as resource costs.

Please withdraw this unsupported assumption, or publish a revised analysis distinguishing private returns, financing constraints, coordination costs, and domestic spillovers. Include sensitivity and break-even analyses for replacement rates, participation, and unquantified effects, with an opportunity for supplemental comment before finalization.

[1] OMB, Circular A-4 (Sept. 17, 2003), pp. 2–4: https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/CircularA-4.pdf

[2] Michael A. Clemens, IZA Discussion Paper 18933 (Sept. 2026), Sections 1–4 and 6: https://docs.iza.org/dp18933.pdf
comments.reason: Opposes the proposed rule's economic assumptions regarding unpaid OPT fees and financing burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100; Section IV.C, 91 FR 64574–64576.

I oppose the proposition that the proposed uniform fee reliably distinguishes lawful, educationally valuable OPT participation from abuse. Fraud prevention is a legitimate objective. The missing step is evidence that this price-based mechanism improves compliance sufficiently to justify its exclusion of otherwise eligible participants.

First, Section IV.A describes serious cases, but the evidence has different statuses. Convictions, ongoing investigations, and students associated with highly suspect employers are not interchangeable. These materials establish reasons for investigation; without a sampling frame, denominators, case dispositions, and overlap checks, they do not establish a program-wide fraud rate or the relative effectiveness of a $70,000 charge. Please disclose the evidence needed to evaluate those inferences.

Second, fewer participants do not necessarily mean a lower fraud rate among those remaining. A well-financed violator may pay while a verified, lawful participant at a financially constrained institution cannot. This is a possible mechanism, not a claim that adverse selection will necessarily occur. Moreover, DHS expressly permits schools to pass the charge to students, other students, or employers. Nominal payment by a school therefore does not establish that the school bears the economic stake on which the proposed screening mechanism relies.

Third, GAO-19-297 identifies specific controls, including fraud-risk assessment, network analysis, school recertification, and fraud-specific DSO training.[1] Subsequent implementation updates show that several recommendations have been implemented. DHS should identify the residual risks after those measures and compare targeted improvements with the uniform charge. The proposal does discuss and reject expanded visits and other procedures; my objection is to the adequacy of that comparison, not an assertion that alternatives were ignored entirely.

DHS may reasonably argue that a smaller program reduces oversight burdens even if the fraud rate does not fall. It should quantify or otherwise substantiate that separate claim and explain the associated loss of legitimate training. Because the receipts go to the Treasury and are not retained by ICE, they cannot be assumed to finance additional oversight under this rule.

Please withdraw the uniform charge unless its relative screening effect is adequately supported. Evaluate targeted employer verification, risk-based reviews, and other feasible controls using common outcomes: substantiated violations prevented, compliant participants excluded, remaining fraud risk, and total public and private costs.

[1] GAO-19-297, findings, recommendations, and implementation updates: https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-297
comments.reason: Opposes the uniform fee as a reliable fraud prevention mechanism and criticizes the evidence used.

comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule that would charge universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one. I want to talk about a kind of fairness this proposal ignores: a flat fee is not a fair fee. The same $70,000 means something entirely different depending on which school is asked to pay it, and the schools asked to pay the most, relative to what they have, are the ones that serve the students this country can least afford to abandon.

Consider a regional public university — the kind that anchors a small city, educates first-generation students, and runs on state funding that has not kept pace with costs. Recommending OPT for sixty graduating international students would cost $4.2 million in a single year. That is not a rounding error. It is several faculty positions, a year's worth of need-based aid, or the budget of an entire academic department. A wealthy private university with a multibillion-dollar endowment can treat the same fee as an inconvenience and carry on. The regional school cannot, and it will not try: it will cap or suspend OPT recommendations, because there is no third option.

What disappears next is not only international enrollment. At many regional and minority-serving institutions, international students paying full tuition are what keep small graduate programs, language departments, and specialized STEM tracks viable at all. Lose those students, and the programs close — for American students too. The domestic student who loses a graduate seminar, a research assistantship, or a scholarship funded by international tuition is a casualty of this rule just as surely as the international graduate who loses OPT.

DHS applied this fee uniformly, as if uniformity were neutrality. It is not. A charge that a rich school absorbs and a modest school cannot is a policy that sorts opportunity by wealth, state by state and campus by campus, until OPT survives only where it was always easiest to keep. That is not a defensible way to regulate a national program, and it is not a burden the schools doing the hardest work in American higher education should be asked to carry. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket ICEB-2026-0100
RIN 1653-AB01
Re: Optional Practical Training Fees, 91 Fed. Reg. 64566 (October 8, 2026)

I oppose the proposed rule and request its withdrawal. Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives. DHS must nevertheless establish statutory authority for this particular assessment and reasonably explain its amounts, screening mechanism, economic assumptions, and transition provisions.

First, authority to administer OPT does not automatically resolve authority to impose this monetary assessment on educational institutions. Please explain how 8 U.S.C. 1184(a)(1) authorizes the proposed payer, amounts, and refund restrictions, and identify a limiting principle. Congress separately addressed student-information fees in 8 U.S.C. 1372 and adjudication-service fees in 8 U.S.C. 1356(m). Those provisions do not necessarily foreclose every additional charge, but their relationship to this assessment requires explanation. The requirement to deposit receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302 does not independently authorize their collection.

Second, the proposal should distinguish reducing participation from improving compliance. A uniform charge may reduce total investigations by shrinking the program. That does not establish that payment ability identifies more honest participants or more valuable educational opportunities. A compliant student or institution may lack financing, while a well-financed violator may pay. Because schools may transfer the economic burden to students or employers, nominal school payment also does not establish the institutional financial stake on which the proposal relies. Please explain these mechanisms and why $70,000 and $30,000 reasonably address them.

State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), requires a rational connection between relevant facts and the agency's choice. This objection does not demand perfect data or a new experiment. It requests a reasoned explanation addressing specific weaknesses in the proposed mechanism.

Third, evaluate targeted controls against the same objectives. GAO-19-297 identifies risk assessment, network analysis, school oversight, and DSO training. Its July 2026 updates show that mandatory DSO and fraud-specific training recommendations remained partially addressed. Please compare completing these measures, verifying high-risk employers, targeted reviews, and lower assessments using effectiveness, implementation costs, residual risk, and exclusion of compliant participants. The proposal discusses alternatives; the issue is whether its comparison adequately supports the selected approach.

Fourth, strengthen the reliance and transition analysis. DHS has addressed reliance, but an annual participation share does not establish a graduating cohort's eventual OPT use or how OPT availability influenced enrollment decisions. Educational quality and practical training can jointly influence substantial, irreversible commitments.

DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1, 30-33 (2020), requires meaningful consideration of relevant reliance interests without guaranteeing an unchanged policy. Preserving earlier recommendations and providing 60 days may offer little practical adjustment for students already enrolled who cannot yet receive recommendations. The transition can also impose the initial $70,000 assessment on a future STEM recommendation where that assessment has not previously been paid. Please compare protection through an existing student's current degree and associated OPT/STEM sequence, phased implementation, and a longer transition.

Fifth, test the financing and opportunity-cost assumptions. Liquidity, willingness to pay, private returns, and benefits to U.S. society are different quantities. Future employers may be unidentified when payment is required. Research spillovers and benefits to other American workers or consumers may not be recoverable by the parties funding the fee. An unpaid assessment is therefore not a demonstrated ceiling on forgone value. Please evaluate alternative participation scenarios, including STEM reductions, financing constraints, pass-through, replacement workers, and uncertainty. Do not double-count fee transfers as social resource costs.

Finally, worker effects require differentiation. Demirci (2020), Canadian Journal of Economics, DOI 10.1111/caje.12478, reports adverse employment effects for recently graduated native master's recipients alongside earnings gains for experienced native master's recipients in the same field. Such evidence supports examining affected groups, rather than assuming a uniform institutional charge is appropriately targeted.

Please withdraw the assessment. If DHS proceeds, address these objections, substantiate the statutory and analytical basis, evaluate significant alternatives, provide a reasoned transition, and publish objective refund criteria, timelines, written reasons, and error-correction procedures before implementation.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed rule and requests its withdrawal due to lack of statutory authority and justification.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I submit this comment as a U.S. citizen, engineer, and member of the public. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)) and urge DHS to withdraw them. The notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) doesn't explain its fee amounts, doesn't measure the problems it claims to address, and shifts billions in costs onto schools and students, including American students, without accounting for them.

1. DHS never explains how it arrived at $70,000.
The NPRM identifies no cost of administering OPT or investigating fraud. DHS says only that the fee is “comparable to the fee for H-1B visas” and “on par with the educational costs that foreign students incur” (NPRM § IV.C), neither of which reflects any government cost. Students already pay a USCIS filing fee for adjudication (§ VII.A.2.a). Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), which DHS itself cites (§ VI), an agency must rationally connect the facts to its choice. DHS never explains why these amounts are necessary.

2. DHS identifies an enforcement resource shortage, then proposes a fee that provides no resources.
DHS states that OPT’s growth “has exponentially outpaced the number of companies that DHS is able to effectively review and investigate,” and that “agency compliance resources are not scaled to (or keeping pace with) the size of the program” (§ IV.A), with roughly 60 field representatives covering about 6,186 schools. Yet ICE cannot retain the fee revenue because “the statute does not provide legal authority” to do so (§ IV.C). The rule shrinks participation to fit DHS’s capacity rather than resourcing oversight, even though the fraud DHS cites was uncovered through site visits and investigations (§ IV.A), the very tools DHS dismissed as “reactive” (§ IV.C).

3. DHS never quantifies the fraud or the fee’s effect on it.
Despite fraud being its primary justification, DHS never estimates fraud’s prevalence or how much the fee would prevent, listing monetized benefits as “Not Estimated” (§ VII.A.1, Table 1). Its central evidence is inconsistent; the preamble cites “more than 10,000 F-1 nonimmigrant students” at “highly suspect employers” (§ IV.A), while the supporting footnote describes “10,000 highly suspected employers”. Either way, it reflects suspicion, not confirmed fraud.

4. DHS projects billions in losses but never measures the worker benefits it claims.
DHS justifies the fee as protecting U.S. workers, yet lists the rule’s “Effects on wages” and “Effects on growth” as “N/A” (§ VII.A.1, Table 1), while estimating annualized costs of up to $8.2 billion, driven largely by “opportunity costs from the lost OPT participation”. DHS asks the public to accept billions in measured losses for wage gains it never estimated.

5. DHS invites schools to pass the fee onto American students without accounting for them.
DHS twice states schools may pass the fee onto “F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers,” presenting this as a way to “mitigate their budgetary impact” (§§ IV.C, VI), yet its deterrence rationale addresses only F-1 students and employers (§ IV.C). U.S. students cannot participate in OPT or commit the fraud DHS describes. Despite estimating $8.7 to $16.9 billion in annual transfers from schools, DHS never mentions tuition increases and omits domestic students from its reliance interests analysis (§ VI). A rule meant to “place the United States’ interests first” (§ IV.B) should not shift billions onto American students without justification.

6. DHS should reject charging $70,000 at each degree level.
DHS requests comment on reapplying the initial fee at each higher degree level (§ V.A). Though DHS says the rule targets “the most promising” and “high achieving” students (§§ IV.C, VI), this alternative would penalize exactly those students: a graduate earning three U.S. degrees could owe $210,000 in initial fees alone.

Requested changes
I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees in their entirety. If DHS proceeds, it should at minimum base any fee on a documented analysis of OPT’s actual administrative and oversight costs; pursue targeted enforcement, such as expanded employer site visits, instead of a blanket fee; publish estimates of fraud prevalence and the rule’s effect on U.S. wages before finalizing; prohibit schools from passing any fee onto students who do not participate in OPT; and reject the alternative of charging the initial fee at each degree level.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As a university instructor, one of my biggest concerns about the proposed OPT fees is something that has received far too little attention: the potential consequences for American students.

Universities are already under considerable financial pressure. Faculty positions, academic programs, student support services, and scholarships all depend on limited institutional resources. International students are an important part of that financial picture, particularly at institutions where international enrollment contributes significant tuition revenue.

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could make American universities considerably less attractive to prospective international students.

For many students, the opportunity to gain practical experience after graduation is an important factor in choosing where to study. If that opportunity becomes financially uncertain, some may choose universities in other countries instead.

What concerns me is what happens afterward.

When a university loses tuition revenue, the financial consequences do not simply disappear. Administrators must find ways to balance their budgets. That may mean reducing academic offerings, limiting scholarships, postponing faculty hiring, or increasing tuition.

American students could ultimately bear part of that burden.

Smaller private universities and regional institutions may be especially vulnerable because they often lack the financial reserves available to major research universities. In communities where a university is also a significant employer, prolonged financial difficulties could affect local jobs as well.

I am not suggesting that every institution would raise tuition or that this proposal would necessarily cause university closures. However, these are foreseeable economic risks that deserve serious consideration before such substantial fees are implemented.

My objection is specifically to the proposed fee provisions under 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2).

I ask DHS to evaluate how these fees could affect international enrollment, university finances, and the cost of education for American students. Any final decision should account for those indirect consequences rather than treating OPT fees as an isolated immigration issue.

Protecting American interests should include protecting access to affordable, high-quality education for American families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposed OPT fees raise a broader question about America's long-term economic competitiveness.

The United States has spent decades building an extraordinary system of universities, research institutions, technology companies, and startup ecosystems. One of the strengths of this system is its ability to attract talented people from around the world and provide opportunities to turn academic knowledge into useful technologies.

OPT is one part of that system.

In fields such as artificial intelligence, semiconductor engineering, biotechnology, and advanced computing, professional development does not end when a student receives a diploma. Practical training allows graduates to work with complex systems, participate in research and development, and acquire experience that universities alone cannot provide.

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could weaken this connection between education and industry.

The concern is not simply that fewer international students might remain in the United States. It is that talented students may increasingly decide not to study here in the first place.

Countries competing with the United States for scientific and technical talent have their own universities, research institutions, and technology industries. When qualified graduates choose to build their careers elsewhere, their future research contributions, entrepreneurial activities, and technological innovations may also occur elsewhere.

These effects are difficult to measure immediately. A lost research collaboration or a startup that is never founded may not appear in short-term employment statistics.

Yet such outcomes matter when evaluating a policy's long-term economic consequences.

DHS should therefore examine whether the proposed fees would reduce the attractiveness of American universities and limit the availability of highly trained graduates to domestic employers.

The analysis should also consider whether any anticipated employment benefits for American workers would outweigh possible losses in research productivity, innovation, and business formation.

Preventing immigration fraud is a legitimate objective. However, a broad financial requirement does not necessarily distinguish legitimate training opportunities from fraudulent arrangements.

I request that DHS withdraw the proposed fees under § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2) and evaluate more targeted compliance measures.

A policy affecting the future supply of scientific and technical talent deserves an economic analysis that extends beyond immediate immigration enforcement outcomes.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Who actually benefits if international students stop coming to American universities?

This is the question I would like DHS to answer before moving forward with the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees.

International students don't just attend classes. They rent apartments, buy groceries, eat at local restaurants, use transportation, and spend money in the communities surrounding their universities.

That spending supports American businesses and American jobs.

According to NAFSA's economic analysis, international students contributed approximately $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year.

Those numbers represent real economic activity, much of it benefiting people who have nothing to do with immigration policy.

If OPT becomes too expensive or uncertain, some prospective students may decide to study in Canada, Europe, or elsewhere.

The financial consequences would not stop at university campuses.

Landlords could lose tenants. Local restaurants could lose customers. University towns could experience declining demand for services. Institutions facing enrollment losses might reduce staffing.

And many of the people affected would be American citizens.

I understand the argument that OPT should not undermine employment opportunities for American graduates. That concern deserves attention.

But shouldn't DHS also consider the American jobs that depend on international education?

Reducing one category of foreign employment authorization does not automatically produce a net increase in American employment.

I am not claiming that every international student would leave or that every community would suffer equally. I am asking DHS to measure the potential losses before implementing fees of this magnitude.

My request is straightforward: withdraw the proposed fee provisions in 8 CFR § 214.13(i)(1) and (i)(2), and conduct a comprehensive assessment of their potential impact on American businesses, local employment, and university communities.

If the purpose is to protect American workers, the analysis should account for all American workers who may be affected, not just those competing for OPT-eligible positions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Alexandra Tabachnikova
comments.commentText:
I am writing to urge the DHS to withdraw proposed rule No. ICEB-2026-0100. I am a PhD Candidate in the department of Immunobiology at Yale University working on Long COVID and other chronic diseases. I am scheduled to defend my thesis on January 15th of next year and am planning to pursue further postdoctoral research at another US institution after I graduate. I have a lot of flexibility in deciding on what type of research I plan to pursue, in which lab and university, and when I plan to being my postdoctoral work. This flexibility means that I can pursue the most challenging and competitive career that will help me become a professor at a leading institute myself. 

Currently, international students in the United States have the same kind of flexibility in choosing their postdoctoral careers and contributing to the growing innovation in biological sciences in the United States. A huge reason for this flexibility is due to the Optional Practical Training program and STEM OPT extension, which allows an extension on visas for up to 3 years while obtaining additional postgraduate training. However, these proposed changes would make it prohibitively expensive for international workers to pursue this option, since no student worker could possibly have access to $70,000 or an additional $30,000 for the extension. My current salary is a little over $50,00 a year, so it would take 2 full years of pay to cover this cost. 

Multiple members of my lab are on OPT or OPT STEM extension and are conducting life-changing research that will help people with debilitating illness in the aftermath of the COVID pandemic. Without these key coworkers, the chronic disease field and our understanding of Long COVID, will suffer tremendously. Additionally, we are able to recruit the most talented new postdocs to work on this unmet need with needed expertise in neuroscience, microscopy, and autoimmunity, because they have the option of easily and affordably extending their student visas.

OPT allows the US economy and leading universities and pharmaceutical companies to retain talent that has been trained in the US to continue working in the country and contributing to our nation's status as a leader in healthcare and technological innovation. As a scientist, I would like to cite some studies which have been conducted on the impact of OPT on the US economy. Kwon et al (https://bse.eu/research/working-papers/the-effect-of-retaining-high-skilled-international-graduates-evidence-from-the-stem-opt-extension) use an economic analysis method called synthetic difference-in-differences (SDID) and demonstrated that OPT stimulates the creation of new businesses and start-ups and increased demand for not only international workers, but also for native high-skilled workers with high degrees. 

Another study by Madeline Zavodny (https://nfap.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/International-Students-STEM-OPT-And-The-US-STEM-Workforce.NFAP-Policy-Brief.March-2019.pdf) at the National Foundation for American Policy analyzed data from 2008 to 2016 to ask whether OPT has an impact on competing native workers. This study found that "unemployment rates are lower in areas with larger numbers of foreign students doing OPT as a share of workers in STEM occupations," showing that the economic boost of OPT helped hire native workers and provide MORE work opportunities, not less. Thus, the assertion made in this rule change that it will protect US workers is clearly false. 

Clearly the impact of OPT is very good for the US economy, and for ALL workers, not just international workers. This proposed rule change will essentially eliminate this option for international workers due to the extreme financial burden on international workers, principle investigators, or the university. With this in mind, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Opposition to the Proposed $100,000 Fee

I am an international graduate student at Yale University pursuing a PhD in biology. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed $100,000 fee, which I believe would have serious and long-lasting consequences for American higher education, scientific innovation, economic competitiveness, and global leadership.

For decades, the United States has been a global leader in scientific research and technological innovation, in large part because of its ability to attract talented students, researchers, and professionals from around the world. American universities have become centers of scientific excellence through the contributions of both domestic and international scholars. Imposing such a substantial financial barrier would discourage talented international students from pursuing advanced training and research careers in the United States, potentially driving them toward countries with more welcoming immigration policies.

This concern is particularly significant in STEM fields, where international graduate students and researchers make essential contributions to scientific discovery, technological development, and public health. As a PhD student working in biology, I have witnessed firsthand how international collaboration and diverse scientific perspectives accelerate research and innovation. Scientific progress depends on attracting the brightest minds, regardless of nationality. Policies that discourage talented researchers from remaining in the United States risk weakening the country's research institutions and its long-term ability to compete globally.

Furthermore, international students and highly skilled researchers should not be viewed simply as competitors for existing American jobs. They also contribute to the creation of new opportunities through scientific discoveries, entrepreneurship, technological innovation, and the development of new industries. Their contributions help expand the economy and create employment opportunities for American citizens. Restricting access to international talent may therefore undermine, rather than strengthen, the American workforce.

International students also make substantial economic contributions through tuition payments, living expenses, and participation in local economies. More importantly, those who pursue advanced research and remain in the United States contribute to the nation's long-term economic growth and technological leadership. Discouraging these individuals from building their careers in America could result in a significant loss of human capital and future innovation.

The United States has maintained its global leadership not by limiting access to talent, but by creating an environment in which talented individuals from around the world can contribute to shared progress. I fear that policies such as this one could gradually erode that advantage, with consequences extending far beyond the individuals directly affected.

I respectfully urge policymakers to reconsider this proposal and carefully evaluate its long-term effects on American universities, scientific research, job creation, and economic competitiveness. Protecting opportunities for American workers and maintaining America's ability to attract global talent are not mutually exclusive goals. In fact, they are deeply interconnected.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly support the proposed $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 fee for extensions. This cumulative $100,000 framework is an economically justified mechanism to protect qualified American workers and recent graduates during a severe tech economic contraction.
The necessity of this fee is supported by documented data and structural program exploits:
• Deviation from Statutory Intent: The F-1 visa is strictly an academic student visa, never intended to allow international students to work legally in the U.S. Permitting full-time employment decoupled from campuses for up to three years creates a massive guest-worker program under an educational guise.
• Demographic Monopolization: According to IIE data across 2023-2026, nationals from India (49%) and China (21%) consistently monopolize nearly 70% of all active OPT participants and 68% of STEM OPT extensions, operating as a localized corporate pipeline [International Students - IIE Open Doors].
• Protecting Workers Amid Tech Layoffs: The tech sector faces historic layoffs, with 245,953 workers cut in 2025 and 197,123 in 2026 to date. Massive contractions hit major entities like Oracle (21,000 jobs) and Amazon (16,000 jobs). Flooding this market with entry-level guest workers directly harms displaced citizens.
• Historical Escalation of OPT Permits: While domestic job openings plummeted, annual active OPT volume from IIE reveals an unchecked upward trajectory: 184,686 (2022); 198,793 (2023); 242,551 (2024); jumping to 294,253 (2025), with 2026 remaining at this 294,000 peak [International Students - IIE Open Doors].
• The Multi-Year Backdoor to H-1B Caps: Congress set a strict annual cap of 85,000 visas for the H-1B lottery. Because there is no restriction on the number of OPT allocations or applicants each year, corporations use it as a workaround. Combining a 12-month initial period and 24-month STEM extension gives three consecutive years of full-time work to enter the lottery repeatedly while remaining on domestic soil.
• No Minimum Wage Floor: Unlike the H-1B visa, there is no minimum prevailing salary requirement enforced for OPT applicants. Employers face no wage flooring, allowing corporations to depress entry-level technical wages by hiring foreign graduates at below-market rates.
• Corporate Tax Subsidies: Employers hiring OPT workers are exempt from FICA taxes, giving them an immediate 7.65% financial discount over identically qualified American citizens. A substantial fee balances this artificial distortion.
When extensive domestic layoffs occur, policy must prioritize the economic security of American citizens. DHS must adjust fee structures to reflect these realities. I urge the Department to finalize this rule as proposed. Putting the American people and their families first in the United States of America. Thank you, President Trump.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly supports the fees as an economically justified mechanism to protect American workers.

I strongly oppose this proposed fee. comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my opposition to the proposed rule, “Optical Practical Training Fees”, which would impose a fee of $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for a subsequent OPT recommendation.

As a PhD student conducting biomedical research, I have dedicated the last 5 years to advancing scientific knowledge, developing scientific skills, publishing research in prestigious journals like Science and Nature, and contributing to the U.S. research enterprise. As a researcher studying lung biology and inflammation to viral infection, I recognize the importance of sustained investment in scientific research. Advancing our understanding of infectious diseases and immune responses requires highly trained scientists who can translate fundamental discoveries into potential therapeutic applications.

After graduating, I wish to pursue a post-doctoral training and become an academic researcher and teacher. This is my way of passing on my knowledge, train the new generation of scientists, continue advancing science that could help develop therapeutics to treat patients, and give back to the community in the U.S. which I have called home for the last few years.

The proposed fees would could make it substantially more difficult for research institutions to recruit qualified graduates. If University lab employers respond by reducing opportunities for international researchers, the United States risk losing scientific talent and weakening the research capacity and advancement that supports biomedical discovery, workforce development, and innovation. My experience illustrates practical training opportunities are important for international students transitioning from universities with their advanced degrees to become independent researchers and finally an academic principal investigator ultimately, bringing talent to the American Universities, research institutions, healthcare, and the broader U.S. economy.

Moreover, the proposed fees would create an unreasonable financial barrier to employment. It would impose an extraordinary financial burden on the universities and other research institutions seeking to employ international graduates for conducting research and advancing science. As graduate students with high inflation, increasing gas prices and rising housing costs, we are already rent-burdened and barely surviving. Although, the proposal places the payment obligation on the universities, it permits the institutions to recover this cost from students, which will cause us to undergo substantial debts and make already difficult life even worse.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposed rule and pursue more targeted and reasonable alternatives towards visa abuse and illegal immigration without imposing disproportionate financial burdens on universities, employers, and students who comply with program requirements. As students in biomedical researchers pursuing advanced degrees, we are only here to pursue one dream- conduct and advance science to be able to identify and develop therapeutics to treat patients and improve our community’s health.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Annonymous Annonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 — Optional Practical Training Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. My primary concern is the harm these fees would cause to students who have invested years of effort and substantial financial resources in their education.

Practical training is an important part of students’ professional development. It allows graduates to apply classroom knowledge, develop specialized skills under supervision, and gain experience that cannot be replicated through coursework alone. In research settings, this can include learning to implement studies, analyze complex data, collaborate across disciplines, and translate findings into practical benefits. Losing access to these experiences would diminish the educational opportunities available to otherwise eligible students.

The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT would create an extraordinary financial barrier. Although the payment obligation would fall on institutions, students would experience the consequences if institutions could not or would not pay. Students could lose training opportunities regardless of their academic accomplishments, qualifications, or compliance with program requirements.

This would create an inequitable system in which access to practical training depends on financial resources. Two students with the same qualifications could face very different futures simply because one has access to an institution or another source of funding able to cover the fee. Students from less affluent backgrounds would be especially vulnerable. Academic achievement and eligibility should determine access to educational training opportunities.

The consequences could be particularly severe for students already pursuing degrees in the United States. These students have made consequential decisions about tuition, borrowing, housing, and years of study within an existing educational framework. Introducing a prohibitive financial barrier after they have made those investments could disrupt carefully developed training plans and substantially reduce the value of their education. Students approaching graduation would have limited time and resources to find alternatives.

The uncertainty itself could also cause harm. Students need to plan their training, finances, and next steps well before graduation. If access to OPT depends on whether an institution can secure a very large payment, students may be unable to make reliable plans even when they have met every academic and program requirement. That uncertainty could compound the financial and emotional pressures they already face.

Domestic students could also lose valuable learning opportunities. University research and training often depend on collaborative teams that include international graduates. When a trained team member cannot continue, projects may be delayed, mentoring relationships interrupted, and opportunities for other students reduced. These effects would extend beyond the individual OPT participant to classmates, research assistants, and the communities that benefit from their work.

I support appropriate oversight and efforts to prevent fraud. However, the ability to secure a large payment does not establish that a training opportunity is legitimate, and inability to pay does not indicate misconduct. DHS should address documented abuses through targeted oversight rather than impose a financial barrier that could exclude students and institutions that follow the rules.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and preserve meaningful access to practical training. At a minimum, DHS should fully assess the consequences for students, including unequal access, disruption of existing educational plans, financial hardship, and lost opportunities for both international and domestic students. Students who have worked hard and complied with the requirements should not find an important part of their education placed beyond reach by a prohibitive new fee.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the proposed OPT fees create financial barriers and urges DHS to withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Alicia Ci
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training fee rule under DHS Docket No. ICEB–2026–0100, particularly the proposed $70,000 fee for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations.

I understand and support DHS’s legitimate interest in preventing fraud and abuse in the OPT program. However, I do not believe that imposing an extremely large fee on educational institutions for each student recommended for OPT is a reasonable or well-targeted way to achieve that objective.

First, the proposed fee does not distinguish between legitimate students and employers and those engaged in fraud. The examples of abuse discussed in the proposed rule include fraudulent employers, nonexistent or staged worksites, false employment arrangements, and other forms of noncompliance. These are serious problems, but a blanket fee imposed whenever a school recommends an otherwise eligible student for OPT does not directly identify or prevent such conduct. The ability of a university, student, or employer to absorb a $70,000 fee is not evidence that an OPT placement is legitimate, just as an inability to absorb that fee is not evidence of fraud.

Second, the proposed rule would effectively transform access to practical training from an eligibility- and compliance-based determination into a financial selection mechanism. DHS states that the fee may cause schools to become more selective about which students they recommend for OPT. But financial selectivity is not the same as compliance screening. A qualified student participating in genuine practical training directly related to his or her field of study should not become less eligible simply because the student’s university cannot justify paying tens of thousands of dollars for the recommendation.

The proposal would also substantially alter the expectations under which international students make long-term educational decisions in the United States. Students often commit several years and substantial financial resources to U.S. undergraduate, master’s, and doctoral programs. Practical training related to their academic field has long been an important component of the F-1 educational framework. A fee of this magnitude could sharply reduce access to that training for students who have complied fully with immigration requirements and completed legitimate academic programs.

I am also concerned that the proposed fee could harm U.S. universities, research institutions, and employers without effectively addressing the underlying sources of fraud. Universities may be forced to absorb substantial new costs, pass those costs on to students, or decline to recommend otherwise qualified students for OPT. The result may be fewer international students choosing U.S. institutions and fewer graduates contributing their U.S.-acquired skills to American research, engineering, technology, and other industries.

DHS should instead prioritize measures that are directly connected to the conduct it seeks to prevent. These could include targeted employer verification, increased site visits for high-risk employers, stronger enforcement against fraudulent employment arrangements, improved data matching, and enhanced reporting or auditing requirements. Such measures would distinguish legitimate participation from fraud rather than imposing the same extraordinary financial barrier on both.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees. If DHS determines that additional program-integrity measures are necessary, I urge the Department to adopt targeted, evidence-based compliance and enforcement mechanisms that address fraudulent conduct directly while preserving practical training opportunities for students who follow the rules.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed high OPT fees, arguing they are an unreasonable mechanism to prevent fraud.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I'm writing to oppose the proposed fee on Optional Practical Training. I'll be direct about why: this is a small revenue measure with large, compounding costs, and the people who will absorb those costs are American universities, American employers, and American workers whose jobs depend on companies choosing to build here rather than somewhere else.

It makes American higher education a worse product.

International students pay full tuition, and often more. They subsidize in-state students, keep graduate programs in engineering and the physical sciences solvent, and staff the research labs that produce the patents universities license back to American industry. None of that happens because the United States has uniquely beautiful campuses. It happens because a U.S. degree has historically come with a credible path to real work experience, and OPT is the mechanism that makes that path credible.

Canada, the U.K., Australia, and Germany have all spent the last decade building post-study work pathways specifically designed to pull this population away from us. They advertise it. Adding a fee — on top of SEVIS fees, visa fees, application costs, and tuition — does not just raise a price. It sends a signal, and the signal is that the United States is becoming a more hostile and more expensive bet. Enrollment responds to signals like this quickly. Regional public universities and smaller private colleges, the ones already operating on thin margins, will feel it first and hardest. Some will cut programs. Some will cut faculty.

It raises the cost of hiring the people American companies are actually competing for.

Employers in technology, semiconductors, biopharma, advanced manufacturing, and finance use OPT as the bridge between a graduate's degree and a longer-term work authorization. It is how a company tries out a new Ph.D. before committing to an H-1B petition and the legal expense that comes with it. Narrow that bridge, add tolls to it, and the result is predictable: fewer tryouts, fewer hires, and more roles that get filled by opening an office in Toronto, Bangalore, or Warsaw instead.

Startups will be hit worst. A large firm can absorb another line item in its immigration budget. A fifteen-person company working on protein folding or chip design cannot, and that company is often precisely where the breakthrough work is happening. The founders of a meaningful share of America's billion-dollar companies arrived here as international students. We should be unusually careful about taxing the front door they came through.

The second-order effects reach further than immigration policy.

American technology and biopharma leadership is not a natural resource. It is the product of a talent pipeline that other countries would very much like to redirect. Semiconductor fabs, AI labs, and drug development programs all run into the same bottleneck, which is people with specialized training, and that training is concentrated in U.S. graduate programs full of international students. Constrict the supply and you get slower hiring, delayed projects, and research that relocates.

Those outcomes eventually show up in earnings, in capital expenditure decisions, and in the market valuations that rest on the assumption that American firms will keep winning the competition for the best researchers and engineers in the world. Investors are not pricing in a United States that makes it harder and costlier to hire the top of each graduating class. Policy should not quietly make that assumption false.

What I'm asking for.

OPT is not a subsidy. Participants pay taxes, pay tuition, and generate economic activity well in excess of the administrative cost of the program. If the agency's concern is genuinely about covering processing expenses, that case should be made transparently with cost data, and the burden should not be placed on a population that already pays substantially into the system.

The federal government should not impose a fee on Optional Practical Training. I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed OPT fee, arguing it harms universities, employers, and U.S. competitiveness.

During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. I ask you to rescind this proposed rule. Miranda Goldsteinmggoldst@uci.eduIrvine, California 92617

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT recommendations.

My primary concern is that this proposal would significantly undermine the international competitiveness of American higher education, ultimately harming not only international students but also U.S. universities, employers, and the broader American economy.

1. Undermining the competitiveness of U.S. universities

One of the major advantages of pursuing higher education in the United States is the opportunity to combine world-class academic instruction with practical experience in American industries. OPT provides an important bridge between these two experiences.

International students make substantial financial and personal investments when choosing where to study. The availability of post-graduation practical training is an important consideration in that decision. The proposed fees could severely restrict this opportunity, making American universities substantially less attractive compared with institutions in other countries.

Although the fees would technically be paid by educational institutions, universities may be unable or unwilling to absorb such extraordinary costs. They may instead restrict OPT recommendations, transfer some costs to students, or reconsider international enrollment strategies.

2. Negative consequences for the U.S. economy and innovation

According to the Institute of International Education's Open Doors 2025 report, U.S. institutions hosted approximately 1.18 million international students during the 2024–2025 academic year. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 jobs during that academic year.

These figures demonstrate that international education provides economic benefits extending well beyond individual students. Reduced international enrollment could negatively affect university revenue, local employment, and the talent pipeline supporting American research and industry.

The United States has historically benefited from attracting talented students from around the world. Restricting access to practical training risks weakening this advantage and encouraging prospective students to pursue educational and professional opportunities elsewhere.

3. Insufficient consideration of enrollment and institutional impacts

In Section VII.A.5.b of the proposed rule, DHS acknowledges that the fees could discourage international enrollment and cause educational institutions to lose tuition revenue. However, DHS also acknowledges that it cannot precisely quantify these opportunity costs.

I believe this uncertainty deserves substantially greater consideration before imposing fees of this magnitude. In particular, the analysis should more thoroughly evaluate the effects on international enrollment, universities with limited financial resources, students from less affluent backgrounds, and U.S. economic competitiveness.

Furthermore, currently enrolled students have already committed significant resources to their education under the existing regulatory framework. A short transition period may not adequately address the disruption to their educational and professional plans.

American higher education is not only an educational resource but also a major source of economic competitiveness, innovation, and international influence. Policies affecting international students should carefully account for these broader national interests.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed OPT fee structure and pursue more proportionate, evidence-based measures that protect program integrity without substantially diminishing the attractiveness of American universities to international talent.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition due to negative impacts on higher education competitiveness.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed OPT fees of $70,000 for initial applications and $30,000 for subsequent applications.

As an educator who works with international students, I have seen firsthand how much these students contribute to American universities and communities. Many have already invested their families’ savings into obtaining a U.S. education. Imposing such enormous fees would make practical training opportunities accessible only to the wealthy, regardless of talent, academic achievement, or qualifications.

This proposal would also discourage talented students from choosing American universities, weaken our ability to attract global talent, and hurt U.S. employers who rely on skilled graduates.

Preventing immigration fraud is important, but financially punishing students who have followed the rules is neither fair nor effective. I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue more reasonable, targeted measures.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yu-Chieh Tu
comments.commentText:
I want to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, Optional Practical Training Fees (ICEB-2026-0100), which would require educational institutions to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent OPT recommendations.

As an international student pursuing higher education in the United States, I believe this proposal would create an enormous barrier to accessing professional opportunities after graduation. OPT is an essential pathway for international students to apply the knowledge and skills acquired through their education, gain practical experience in their fields of study, and contribute to the U.S. workforce.

The proposed fees could make OPT inaccessible to qualified international students, regardless of their academic achievements or professional qualifications. Although the fees would formally be imposed on educational institutions, universities may be unable or unwilling to absorb such extraordinary costs for individual students. As a result, students who have worked hard to earn their degrees and secured legitimate employment opportunities could be denied the opportunity to gain professional experience simply because their universities cannot justify the financial burden.

This proposal is particularly concerning because international students face strict immigration timelines after graduation. Unlike domestic students, we cannot freely postpone our career plans or remain in the United States indefinitely while waiting for better opportunities. Our ability to work is subject to immigration requirements, and our post-graduation plans must be made within a limited period. If our universities decline to recommend us for OPT because of the proposed fees, we may have little time to find alternatives before being forced to leave the country. Years of investment in American education could end without the opportunity to gain the professional experience we came here to pursue.

The financial burden is also disproportionate to the circumstances of recent graduates. International students have often already paid substantial tuition and living expenses throughout their education. We are at the beginning of our careers and may not have the financial resources to absorb additional costs. If universities pass these fees on to students or employers, the proposal could make it prohibitively expensive for graduates to access employment opportunities. If universities absorb the costs instead, they may reduce the number of students they recommend for OPT or restrict access to the program altogether.

I recognize the Department's stated objectives of combating fraud, strengthening the integrity of the immigration system, and protecting U.S. workers. However, imposing fees of this magnitude on educational institutions for each individual OPT recommendation may prevent legitimate students from participating in the program without necessarily distinguishing them from those who engage in fraud or abuse. Stronger oversight, verification of employment, and enforcement against fraudulent participation would be more targeted approaches that would not place such an extraordinary burden on qualified graduates.

International students contribute to American universities, research, innovation, and the economy. We invest in our education with the expectation that we will have a fair opportunity to apply what we have learned. OPT provides a structured means of obtaining practical experience directly related to our fields of study. Creating substantial financial obstacles to this opportunity risks discouraging talented students from studying in the United States and preventing graduates who have already completed their education here from contributing their skills to the American workforce.

I respectfully urge the Department to withdraw the proposed fees or substantially revise the proposal to avoid imposing costs that could make OPT inaccessible to legitimate international students. If the Department determines that additional oversight is necessary, it should pursue proportionate measures that address fraud directly without undermining access to professional experience for qualified graduates.

For international students like me, the time immediately following graduation is not a period in which we have the freedom to indefinitely reconsider our plans. Our immigration status imposes real deadlines and constraints. A policy that makes OPT financially or institutionally inaccessible could fundamentally alter our career prospects with little opportunity to adapt.

Please consider the substantial consequences this proposal could have for international students, educational institutions, employers, and the long-term competitiveness of the United States.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the rule as it creates unreasonable barriers for international students.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT periods. I urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal.

First, the proposed fees would undermine U.S. economic competitiveness. The fees would substantially increase the cost of hiring international graduates, particularly in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields. Employers facing these additional costs may choose to relocate positions overseas, outsource technical work, or forgo hiring altogether. These outcomes would undermine the proposal’s stated objective of protecting U.S. workers by potentially reducing domestic employment opportunities and investment.

Second, the proposal would discourage international students from pursuing U.S. education and careers. International students contribute to American universities, research institutions, and innovation-driven industries. Many invest years and substantial financial resources in U.S. education with the expectation that they can obtain practical experience related to their studies. Imposing extraordinary fees on OPT participation would weaken the United States’ ability to attract and retain highly skilled graduates, potentially benefiting competing economies instead. The burden would be especially concerning for startups, smaller employers, and research institutions with limited budgets.

Third, DHS should provide stronger evidence that these fees are necessary and proportionate. The Department should demonstrate how the proposed amounts were calculated, how the fees relate to the actual costs of administering and monitoring OPT, and why less restrictive alternatives would not adequately address fraud and compliance concerns. DHS should also fully assess the proposal’s effects on universities, employers, students, and the broader U.S. economy before proceeding.
