comments.title: MM2 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I vehemently oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis. This proposal benefits no one besides the abusers of the system and aims to end a program that allows the United States to thrive as one of the global leaders in innovation. Please consider the following: 

1. Cherry-picked evidence (Sec. IV.A)
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests in 2020, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video cited by timestamp. The text says the video found 10,000 students working for suspect employers; footnote 56 says 10,000 suspect employers. Either way, suspicion is not a finding, and 10,000 is about 3% of 2024's ~290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants. The cases mostly involve employer fraud uncovered by existing site visits and prosecutions, yet the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." No fee would have stopped the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

2. Inconsistent data
To claim STEM OPT "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of ~92,000 by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, DHS cites 165,524 participants. Its own regulatory analysis counts 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, which is in line with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study of 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not any analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires commensurate wages (Form I-983).

3. A price is not a screen (Sec. IV.C)
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students." A fee sorts by ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS concedes schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Schemes that already sell job letters can price it in; honest students without $70,000 cannot. DHS offers no evidence that any fee level reduces fraud.

4. A tax, not a fee
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, with transfers of $8.7-16.9 billion a year. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must recover costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no cost; it is pegged to an H-1B fee to deter participation. That is a tax Congress has not authorized (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)), and INA 214(a)'s "time and conditions" power cannot support a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources not keeping pace with the program, and none of this money funds compliance. DHS also says it may shut down OPT without the fees, yet admits it cannot keep the money.

5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)
Benefits are unquantified while costs reach $8.2 billion a year. DHS caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee because parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. That is circular: much of OPT's value (innovation, taxes, local spending) goes to the public, not to whoever would pay the fee. DHS also never models enrollment losses, the omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

6. Alternatives dismissed
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as slower and costlier, though those tools uncovered the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, which DHS also cites, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative ease is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

7. Reliance and perverse incentives
DHS calls reliance speculative because only ~20% of F-1 students use OPT, but that is about 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt around it. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000 versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, which penalizes integrated work-study. Refund denials cannot be appealed.

8. Small entities and states
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS rejects relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then that it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, though 1,044 state institutions would pay.

9. Process and baseline
DHS gives 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days on a 5-minute paperwork burden. It relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) for its baseline and for vetting without noting that the rule is postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted enforcement against fraudulent employers.
comments.reason: Opposes the fees and urges DHS to withdraw the rule, criticizing its flawed data and cost-benefit analysis.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposed rule in Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100. I recently completed my PhD in chemistry at Yale University, where I also served as a graduate worker and volunteer organizer with Local 33. I am submitting this comment in my personal capacity.

[Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2) and 214.2(f)(11)(ii)–(iii)]

The proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent fee would place an extraordinary financial barrier between international graduates and opportunities to apply their education. Requiring universities to pay before recommending students would make access depend on institutional resources and willingness to pay. Passing the expense to students or employers would shift that barrier without resolving it.

During my PhD, I worked alongside international researchers and mentored visiting students from abroad. My work required electrochemistry, chemical synthesis, analytical measurements, and collaboration across areas of expertise. Research like this depends on people developing specialized skills over years and sharing what they learn with others. Losing a trained researcher can interrupt experiments, weaken mentorship, and leave colleagues without expertise that takes substantial time to replace.

I would expect these fees to make universities and employers less willing to support international graduates, particularly when research budgets are already committed. Prospective students would also have reason to reconsider studying here if gaining practical experience afterward required such a large payment. In green chemistry, that could weaken the teams working to develop cleaner manufacturing processes and alternatives to fossil-derived chemicals.

[Section VII.A.5(b), Opportunity Costs]

I ask DHS to evaluate research losses beyond the immediate earnings or position of an individual OPT participant. A researcher’s contribution can include training colleagues, maintaining experimental continuity, and helping a team solve problems. Those benefits extend across projects and years. An institution’s inability to fund a large upfront fee does not demonstrate that a researcher’s work has limited value.

My own research focused on converting carbon dioxide into useful chemical feedstocks. Moving such work toward practical applications requires sustained investment in people. Restricting opportunities for graduates trained at U.S. universities risks losing the expertise that investment helped develop.

[Section IV.A, Combating Fraud and Abuse of OPT]

DHS should address documented misconduct through targeted oversight and enforcement. Ability to pay a large fee is a poor measure of whether a training opportunity is legitimate. I urge the agency to explain why existing compliance tools cannot address specific violations before imposing a financial barrier on lawful participants.

My experience organizing graduate workers also informs my opposition. I want international colleagues to have fair pay, safe working conditions, and the ability to raise concerns without jeopardizing their careers. DHS should pursue worker protections directly, including measures against employer exploitation and retaliation.

International academic workers are colleagues, mentors, and contributors to research that benefits the public. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and preserve accessible OPT and STEM OPT opportunities.
comments.reason: Commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule due to the extraordinary financial barrier it creates.

comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed Optional Practical Training fee rule and request its withdrawal.

Access to legitimate practical training should depend on academic preparation, eligibility, and compliance. A financial barrier of this magnitude risks making access depend instead on institutional wealth and a student's ability to absorb additional costs. Two equally qualified students could face entirely different opportunities simply because their schools have different financial resources.

Students make educational decisions years before graduation. They commit tuition, relocate, and choose programs partly on the basis of available opportunities to apply what they learn. Recognizing these commitments does not mean guaranteeing employment or freezing immigration policy indefinitely. It means giving serious weight to decisions that cannot easily be reversed.

The proposed transition should therefore be evaluated against the length of an educational program, not merely the time needed to announce a new payment requirement. A student approaching graduation cannot readily change institutions, recover tuition, or redesign years of academic preparation.

I ask DHS to withdraw these fees. If the agency nevertheless proceeds with changes, it should protect students already enrolled and provide a meaningful transition covering their remaining studies and associated practical training. Any revised policy should preserve access for qualified students regardless of family income or institutional resources.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jeff Ma
comments.commentText:
DHS should withdraw this proposal because its economic consequences require a more convincing assessment.

The relevant question is whether restricting practical training would produce a net benefit for American workers and communities. A reduction in OPT participation does not, by itself, demonstrate an equivalent increase in employment for U.S. workers. Employers may respond by reducing activity, postponing projects, automating tasks, or moving work elsewhere. The analysis should test these possibilities instead of assuming that each unavailable OPT participant creates a job that will be filled domestically.

The agency should also examine how graduates contribute to teams. In research, engineering, and other specialized work, employees can complement one another's skills. Losing one team member may affect the productivity and opportunities of American colleagues. These effects deserve evaluation alongside any evidence of displacement.

Requiring schools to make substantial payments also creates budget choices with consequences beyond international students. Institutions may reduce services, limit training recommendations, or seek additional revenue. DHS should examine who ultimately bears those costs, including domestic students.

Protecting American workers is a legitimate objective. It calls for evidence about wages, working conditions, and actual hiring outcomes. I urge DHS to pursue targeted labor protections and enforcement, and to reject a fee structure that could undermine productive activity without establishing corresponding benefits.
comments.reason: Commenter urges DHS to withdraw this proposal because of its negative economic consequences.

comments.commentText: Secretary Markwayne Mullin,By submitting this comment, I am expressing my opposition to this proposed rule. America’s higher education programs are considered among the best in the world and attract the best and brightest from across the globe. During the program or after graduating, F-1 scholars who utilize Optional Practical Training (OPT) make major contributions to US innovation in many areas from medical breakthroughs to advancements in agriculture and energy that improve quality of life, create jobs and grow the economy. The proposal to increase OPT fees to $70,000 for initial approvals and $30,000 for renewals is unreasonable and harmful to workers. International and domestic workers alike are in need of policies that protect and lift standards for all workers, safeguard their rights in the workplace, and prevent employers from suppressing wages and benefits or pitting workers against each other. The proposed rule does nothing to achieve these ends – instead it punishes students and workers. I am concerned the rule could  damage the ability for the United States to attract and retain top-tier global talent, limit important professional and academic opportunities to only the wealthy, and negatively impact the academic and professional experiences for all students and workers. This is a step in the wrong direction and would harm the nation’s higher education system, global leadership in science, and the economy. I ask you to rescind this proposed rule. Raghava  Sunkararaghava.sunkara@mssm.eduNew York, New York 10029
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fee hikes as unreasonable, harmful to workers, and damaging to U.S. higher education and innovation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jenny Bao
comments.commentText:
I object to the proposed fee structure because willingness or ability to pay is an unreliable measure of compliance.

A legitimate student or institution may be unable to afford a large fee. A well-financed fraudulent operation may be able to pay it. Payment does not establish that an employer exists, that training relates to a student's degree, or that reported employment actually occurs. DHS should demonstrate why this financial screening mechanism would distinguish lawful participation from misconduct.

The agency should also separate two different outcomes: reducing the number of participants and reducing the rate of fraud. Fewer participants could produce fewer detected violations even if the program became no better at identifying misconduct. An effective evaluation should measure compliance outcomes and the exclusion of legitimate participants, not simply declining enrollment in OPT.

Before adopting this approach, DHS should compare its expected results with risk-based audits, verification of suspicious employment records, targeted site inspections, and sanctions against proven violations. That comparison should explain the costs, enforcement capacity, and likely effectiveness of each option.

I request withdrawal of the proposed fees. Any replacement should have measurable objectives, a transparent evidentiary basis, and a proportionate relationship to the specific conduct it seeks to address. Broadly pricing qualified participants out of a program is not sufficient evidence that the program has become more trustworthy.
comments.reason: Objects to the proposed fees and requests withdrawal of the rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed policy.

International students invest an enormous amount of money, time, and effort to pursue higher education in the United States. We come here not only to receive an education, but also to gain professional experience, broaden our perspectives, and build better futures for ourselves. Imposing additional financial burdens without sufficient justification would unfairly deprive young graduates of opportunities to grow, pursue their careers, and contribute to this country.

International students come from all over the world, bringing diverse perspectives, exceptional talents, creativity, and ambition. We are not simply seeking opportunities for ourselves. We want to use the best years of our lives to contribute something meaningful to the world, to the United States, and to our home countries.

Imagine how much innovation, productivity, and talent the world would have lost if similar barriers had prevented generations of international graduates from pursuing their potential over the past ten or twenty years.

By making it increasingly difficult for international students to build their careers, the United States risks losing talented individuals who could otherwise contribute to its economy, industries, research, arts, and communities.

Is driving away the very talent this country has attracted and educated really the outcome this policy intends to achieve?

I strongly urge policymakers to reconsider this proposal and protect the opportunities that allow international graduates to contribute to American society and the wider world.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed policy and additional financial burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and an additional $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorization.

This proposal would severely undermine America’s ability to attract, educate, and retain talented researchers and engineers. It would ultimately harm the American innovation ecosystem that has made the United States a global leader in science and technology.

First, this proposal would weaken American technological competitiveness. The United States has benefited enormously from attracting talented students and researchers from around the world. International graduates contribute to scientific discoveries, develop new technologies, and support American companies. OPT provides an essential bridge between American higher education and professional experience. Imposing fees of up to $100,000 would effectively eliminate this opportunity for many qualified graduates, pushing highly trained talent toward competing countries.

Second, the proposed fees would place an unreasonable financial burden on American universities. Most universities cannot afford to pay tens of thousands of dollars for each international graduate seeking OPT. Research universities already face significant financial constraints. These fees would force institutions to restrict OPT recommendations, divert resources from education and research, or reduce opportunities for international students. Ultimately, American universities and their research missions would suffer.

Third, this proposal would discourage talented international students from choosing the United States. International students make substantial financial and personal commitments to pursue American higher education. Post-graduation practical training is an important part of that decision. If this opportunity becomes financially inaccessible, future students will increasingly choose countries with more predictable and welcoming pathways. The United States would lose talented future workers, tuition revenue, research contributions, and broader economic benefits.

Fourth, excessive fees are not an effective substitute for targeted immigration enforcement. Preventing fraud and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives. However, charging extraordinary fees to legitimate students and universities does not directly address fraudulent conduct. A more reasonable approach would strengthen oversight, verify legitimate employment, and enforce existing requirements against actual violations without penalizing students who follow the rules.

Finally, this proposal would undermine America’s long-term investment in STEM education and innovation. The United States invests substantial resources in educating and training international graduate students, particularly in critical scientific and engineering fields. Preventing these graduates from contributing their expertise to American industries would waste that investment and potentially transfer the benefits of American education to economic competitors.

America’s global leadership has been built in part on its openness to exceptional talent from around the world. Policies that make it prohibitively expensive for highly skilled graduates to participate in the American economy would weaken, rather than strengthen, the nation’s economic and technological competitiveness.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety and pursue more targeted, proportionate, and evidence-based measures to maintain the integrity of the OPT program.

Thank you for considering this public comment.
comments.reason: Expresses strong opposition to the proposed OPT fees.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Public Comment on DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100: Proposed OPT Fees

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT participation. These extraordinary fees are disproportionate to the stated objectives, insufficiently justified by the available evidence, and likely to impose substantial costs on legitimate students, educational institutions, employers, and the U.S. economy.

1. The evidence of fraud does not justify these specific fees.

DHS cites examples of fraud, shell companies, and questionable employment arrangements. However, evidence that fraud exists does not establish its prevalence across the overall OPT population or demonstrate that imposing enormous fees on all participants is an effective solution.

DHS should provide verified data on the percentage of OPT participants involved in confirmed fraud, distinguish proven violations from suspected cases, quantify the resulting harm, and explain how these specific fees would prevent future violations. Without this evidence, the proposed policy risks penalizing legitimate participants for misconduct they did not commit.

2. The proposed fee amounts lack adequate justification.

Why $70,000 and $30,000? DHS should provide a transparent explanation of how these amounts were calculated and how they relate to actual administrative costs, enforcement expenses, or measurable reductions in fraud.

If the primary purpose is to discourage participation, DHS should acknowledge that the policy may exclude legitimate students and explain why this outcome is necessary and proportionate. A policy should not be considered justified merely because an extraordinarily high price discourages people from participating.

3. The policy is poorly targeted at the actual problem.

The proposed fees apply regardless of whether a student, employer, or educational institution has engaged in misconduct. Legitimate students and compliant institutions could face the same financial barriers as those associated with fraudulent arrangements.

If DHS’s concerns involve shell companies, nonexistent jobs, and false employment records, targeted investigations, employer verification, compliance audits, and stronger penalties for proven violations would address these problems more directly. DHS should demonstrate why a blanket fee is more effective than these alternatives.

4. The economic analysis acknowledges significant uncertainty.

DHS acknowledges uncertainty about how much OPT participation would decline and the difficulty of precisely quantifying the resulting opportunity costs. Nevertheless, the proposed fees could fundamentally change hiring decisions, university recommendations, and students’ employment opportunities.

The analysis should rigorously assess the potential effects on international student enrollment, employer recruitment, small businesses, research, innovation, productivity, and U.S. competitiveness. A decline in OPT participation should not automatically be treated as a policy success if it also means lost employment opportunities, reduced economic activity, and qualified graduates taking their skills elsewhere.

Where substantial uncertainty exists, DHS should provide transparent sensitivity analyses and explain how its conclusions change under different assumptions about participation, employer demand, and cost-sharing arrangements.

5. DHS has not adequately demonstrated why less burdensome alternatives are insufficient.

The agency should compare the effectiveness and costs of the proposed fees against risk-based audits, enhanced employment verification, stronger oversight of institutions with documented compliance problems, and penalties for confirmed fraud.

Administrative convenience is not sufficient justification for imposing extraordinary financial burdens on legitimate participants. DHS must demonstrate that the proposed fees would produce meaningful improvements in program integrity that could not be achieved through more targeted enforcement measures.

6. The proposal could harm U.S. workers and the broader economy rather than benefit them.

DHS identifies protecting U.S. workers as an objective, but reducing OPT participation does not automatically create additional employment opportunities for American workers. Employers might instead reduce hiring, delay projects, abandon research, or move investment and talent elsewhere.

DHS should provide evidence of the specific labor-market harms it seeks to address and demonstrate that the proposed fees would improve employment outcomes for U.S. workers. It should also assess the consequences for universities, local economies, and the country’s ability to attract international talent.

Conclusion

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees in their current form.

Fraud prevention and protection of U.S. workers are legitimate objectives, but they do not justify a policy without a convincing evidentiary foundation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Feihua Fang
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent fees on Optional Practical Training (OPT). I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

1. The fee is prohibitive and bears no relation to administrative cost. Existing OPT-related fees are modest and tied to processing. A charge of up to $100,000 per student is hundreds of times larger and cannot be justified as cost recovery. Whatever its stated purpose, its practical effect is to shut the door on the international graduates the U.S. has spent decades attracting and training.

2. It undermines America's long-term interests. OPT is the main bridge between a U.S. education and a U.S. career. International graduates, especially in STEM fields, found companies, fill critical roles and drive research. If the U.S. makes it prohibitively expensive to employ them, they will take their skills to Canada, the UK, Europe or Asia, and our competitors will gain the talent we trained.

3. It will cause direct economic harm. International students pay tuition, rent, and buy food, transportation and services throughout their studies and their time working here, and many universities rely on that revenue. Because the fee falls on schools, many institutions simply cannot absorb it. Economic Innovation Group has estimated that a $100,000 charge per OPT graduate could cut international master's enrollment by at least 35 percent. Lost enrollment means lost tuition, lost local spending and lost jobs in college towns.

4. DHS lacks the authority to impose it. The power to tax belongs to Congress. In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the executive's power to regulate does not include a power to tax. Applying that reasoning, a federal court in Massachusetts struck down the $100,000 H-1B payment as an unauthorized tax, and the First Circuit declined to revive it. A fee set far above any cost of administering the program is a revenue-raising tax in substance, and Congress has not clearly delegated that power to DHS.

5. Fraud concerns call for targeted tools. If the concern is program integrity, DHS already has better options, such as employer reporting, SEVP audits and enforcement against abusive actors. A blanket six-figure fee penalizes the overwhelming majority of compliant students and schools.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposed rule.

The proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent Optional Practical Training (OPT) fees raise significant concerns regarding proportionality, regulatory effectiveness, and unintended consequences for American educational institutions and workforce development.
Preventing immigration fraud, maintaining program integrity, and protecting domestic workers are legitimate regulatory objectives. However, imposing substantial uniform fees on educational institutions may restrict legitimate practical training without meaningfully addressing the underlying causes of fraudulent employment arrangements.

1. Financial barriers should not replace effective oversight.
The proposed fees do not distinguish institutions with strong compliance records from those presenting documented regulatory risks. Financial capacity is not a reliable indicator of institutional integrity or employer legitimacy.
Universities, research hospitals, and nonprofit institutions may lack the financial resources to absorb these expenses, potentially discouraging legitimate employment and disrupting research continuity. Such consequences could undermine the return on substantial American investments in higher education, scientific research, and workforce training.

2. Adopt risk-based institutional and employer verification.
DHS should prioritize compliance resources using objectively documented risk indicators rather than imposing uniform financial barriers.
Potential measures include enhanced employer verification, targeted audits of suspicious employment arrangements, periodic confirmation of qualifying employment, and stronger enforcement against substantiated violations.
Institutional oversight should account for demonstrated compliance history, with appropriate opportunities to correct administrative errors and appeal adverse findings.
This approach would focus enforcement on identifiable misconduct while preserving legitimate training opportunities.

3. Establish proportionate, cost-based administrative fees.
If additional revenue is required, DHS should adopt fees reasonably related to documented processing, monitoring, and enforcement expenses.
A transparent cost analysis should distinguish routine administrative expenses from investigative and enforcement costs. Reduced fees or exemptions should be considered for qualifying nonprofit educational institutions, research hospitals, and federally supported research programs.
Subsequent OPT recommendations should not automatically incur substantial additional fees without evidence of corresponding administrative costs.

4. Strengthen accountability through measurable approaches.
Rather than relying primarily on financial deterrence, DHS may establish measurable compliance objectives, including verified fraud detection rates, investigation outcomes, administrative costs, and impacts on legitimate OPT participation.
Employer verification, targeted investigations, and proportionate sanctions for demonstrated misconduct would provide more direct mechanisms for improving program integrity.
DHS should publish periodic evaluations comparing the effectiveness and financial consequences of these approaches.

5. Protect reasonable reliance interests and educational continuity.
Major regulatory changes should account for individuals and institutions that made multi-year educational and financial commitments under existing rules.
Students enrolled in lengthy graduate programs may have reasonably anticipated access to practical training upon graduation. Abruptly introducing substantial institutional fees could disrupt established professional pathways and reduce the value of prior investments in education and research.
DHS should consider appropriate grandfathering protections, extended implementation timelines, and transitional exemptions for students already enrolled when the final rule is issued.

Conclusion
The proposed fee structure risks imposing significant costs on compliant institutions without demonstrating that financial deterrence is more effective than targeted oversight.
DHS should reconsider the proposed fees and conduct a comparative assessment of alternatives emphasizing risk-based verification, proportionate administrative costs, targeted enforcement, and transitional protections.
Such measures could better advance program integrity while preserving legitimate practical training and the competitiveness of American education and research.

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Evelyne Francois
comments.commentText:
As a U.S. citizen, I recognize that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has legitimate governmental interests in deterring fraud, protecting U.S. workers, and preserving the integrity of the immigration system. However, I oppose the proposed fees because their excessive cost may undermine these objectives rather than advance them.
First, the proposed fees are not a sufficiently targeted means of combating fraud. DHS could pursue less restrictive alternatives, such as strengthening institutional oversight, conducting more rigorous background checks, and requiring institutions to verify that students and their employment opportunities satisfy established eligibility requirements. If academic achievement is relevant to the purpose of OPT, objective criteria such as GPA or class ranking could also be considered where appropriate. Imposing a prohibitive fee, however, risks penalizing genuinely qualified students rather than effectively deterring those who engage in fraud. Moreover, individuals or organizations determined to circumvent the law may not be deterred by financial penalties alone. Meanwhile, students who lack the financial resources to overcome this barrier may be discouraged from pursuing legitimate opportunities. The result could be that the proposed rule places its greatest burden on those attempting to comply with the law, while doing little to eliminate the underlying sources of fraud.
Second, the proposed fees do not adequately demonstrate how they would protect U.S. workers. If the concern is that OPT participants may displace American workers or create unfair competition, DHS should consider measures that address those concerns more directly. For example, stronger employer oversight and appropriate wage requirements could help prevent employers from using OPT participants to undercut the compensation of U.S. workers. Simply making OPT prohibitively expensive could drive international students away from the United States without addressing the incentives that may lead employers to seek cheaper labor. Furthermore, in an increasingly global economy where remote work is possible, some employers could continue hiring foreign workers abroad, potentially at lower wages and without creating employment opportunities in the United States. Consequently, the proposed fees may fail to protect U.S. workers while discouraging international students from contributing to the U.S. economy.
Finally, the proposed fees may discourage institutions from recommending students for OPT rather than incentivize them to exercise greater diligence. Requiring institutions to pay $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent recommendation could expose them to substantial financial liability, regardless of whether they have acted responsibly. Faced with this burden, institutions may simply stop recommending students for OPT instead of assuming the financial risk. This outcome would undermine the program without necessarily reducing fraud. It could also discourage prospective international students from studying in the United States, leading them to pursue comparable opportunities in other countries. Because the stated objective is to prevent fraud and protect U.S. workers—not to discourage international students from studying in the United States—such an outcome would be counterproductive.
For these reasons, I urge DHS to consider a more narrowly tailored approach that directly addresses fraud, strengthens institutional oversight, and protects U.S. workers without imposing excessive financial barriers on legitimate OPT participants. Effective regulation should target the conduct it seeks to prevent while preserving lawful opportunities for qualified students and the institutions that serve them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) proposed rule imposing a $70,000 fee for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) recommendations and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations, including STEM OPT extensions.

While some proponents argue that penalizing universities with $70,000 to $100,000 fees will lower tuition or protect opportunities for U.S. students, economic data proves the exact opposite. This punitive fee is a de facto ban on experiential learning that will raise tuition for American students, devastate university budgets, and drive top innovators to global competitors.

1. International Students Subsidize Domestic Education Rather Than Draining Aid
A common misconception in comments supporting this rule is that universities divert financial aid from U.S. citizens to fund international students. In reality, international students are legally ineligible for U.S. federal aid (like Pell Grants and federal loans), and the vast majority pay full, unsubsidized tuition. At public universities in Michigan, California, and nationwide, they pay two to three times the in-state tuition rate.

National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) studies show that revenue from full-paying international students cross-subsidizes domestic students—keeping tuition lower for U.S. citizens and funding campus financial aid. DHS itself acknowledges colleges may pass this new $70,000-$100,000 fee on to the general student body. Furthermore, NAFSA data shows international students contribute over $40 billion annually to the U.S. economy and support 378,000+ U.S. jobs. Driving them away will force universities to hike tuition for working-class and first-generation American students.

2. OPT Creates American Jobs Rather Than Taking Them
The labor market is not a zero-sum game. Studies by the Business Roundtable and the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP) confirm there is no correlation between OPT participation and U.S. worker unemployment. High-skilled OPT participants fill acute shortages in STEM, healthcare, and manufacturing, expanding domestic operations and creating downstream jobs for Americans. Without OPT, U.S. companies will simply offshore R&D and engineering roles to Canada, Europe, or Asia.

3. What America Stands to Lose: The Track Record of F-1 and OPT Alumni
According to NFAP, nearly 25% of U.S. billion-dollar startups ("unicorns") have a founder who first came to America as an international student, creating hundreds of thousands of U.S. jobs:
- Elon Musk came to UPenn as an international student before founding SpaceX and Tesla, which now employ over 100,000 Americans.
- Satya Nadella (CEO of Microsoft) and Sundar Pichai (CEO of Alphabet/Google) arrived as F-1 students, gained early experience through practical training, and now lead trillion-dollar U.S. enterprises.
- AI pioneers like Aravind Srinivas (Perplexity AI) and Ali Ghodsi (Databricks) transitioned from U.S. university research to building foundational American tech companies.
- Thousands of biomedical researchers and healthcare professionals also rely on OPT for life-saving work at U.S. hospitals and labs.

Had a $70,000-$100,000 fee existed when they graduated, no school or startup could have afforded to recommend them for OPT, and the jobs they created would belong to another country today.

4. Harm to Public Universities and Small Businesses
A $100,000 fee does not regulate billionaire endowments; only a few ultra-wealthy private colleges could ever absorb it, while regional public universities and small businesses will be completely priced out. Using a $100,000 blanket fee instead of targeted SEVIS audits is arbitrary, capricious, and exceeds reasonable regulatory fee authority.

I urge DHS to withdraw Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100 in its entirety.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Member of the Public
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed OPT fees, calling them a de facto ban on experiential learning.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Sections IV–V — the proposed fee is not a targeted anti-fraud measure.

DHS considered extending the safeguards that already exist for STEM OPT — Form I-983 training plans, employer site visits, and enhanced reporting — to OPT generally, and rejected them because a fee "can be implemented quickly," requires no "significant additional resources" from the government, and imposes "minimal administrative burdens on the government" (91 FR 64566). That reasoning concedes the point: the fee was chosen because it is easy for DHS, not because it detects fraud. It detects nothing. It is imposed before any individualized finding of ineligibility, on every participant at every accredited school, and the refund — available only at SEVP's discretion, and only before the EAD issues — offers no meaningful process to a student wrongly priced out.

The fee also creates a conflict of interest for schools. DHS says the charge is meant to make institutions "more selective and deliberate." In practice, a school with $70,000 at stake per student will deny meritorious cases to avoid financial risk, and will favor students who can repay it. Academic eligibility decisions should be made on academic criteria, under published standards — not on a university's willingness to absorb a five-figure federal levy.

If fraud in OPT is the problem, the remedy is enforcement against the fraudulent: risk-based audits and site visits, employer verification, action against diploma mills and shell companies selling jobs, and prosecution of organizers — tools directed at the small population actually abusing the program, rather than a blanket charge on the compliant majority. DHS should withdraw the fee proposal and, if it acts further, propose measures rationally connected to identifying actual fraud.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fees, arguing they are not targeted anti-fraud measures and cause harm.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Section VII (Regulatory Analyses) — I oppose the proposed fees.

DHS's own analysis is the strongest case against this rule. DHS estimates annualized costs with a primary estimate of $4.1 billion and 10-year costs of $35.1 billion (discounted at 3 percent), alongside transfers to the federal government with a primary estimate of $12.8 billion per year / $109.4 billion over 10 years. It counts 2,478 affected schools, of which roughly 56 percent are small entities, and it considered — and rejected — an exemption for small institutions. DHS should explain what public benefit justifies costs of this magnitude, because the NPRM identifies none that is quantified: the asserted benefits are qualitative, while the costs are admitted and enormous.

The predictable institutional response is rationing. Faced with $70,000 per first recommendation, schools will recommend fewer students, favor programs and students who can reimburse the fee, and in many cases exit OPT participation altogether. DHS acknowledges the cost may instead be spread to "all students" — i.e., a tuition increase for U.S. students who will never use OPT. International students pay tuition, fund research laboratories, and cross-subsidize domestic enrollment; driving down their enrollment does not protect U.S. workers, it shrinks the universities and labs that employ them.

Nor does pricing out foreign graduates create jobs for Americans. It moves the work: employers who cannot train and hire STEM graduates in the United States will expand research and engineering operations in Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and elsewhere. DHS must address this offshoring effect, and the loss to U.S. research competitiveness, in the administrative record — the current analysis assumes lost OPT participation as an "opportunity cost" without confronting where that activity goes.

I ask DHS to withdraw the proposed fees.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees, highlighting massive costs and predictable institutional rationing.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorizations. As an international doctoral student and researcher at a U.S. public university, I urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal and pursue more targeted, evidence-based approaches to ensuring program integrity.

First, the proposed fees are disproportionate to their stated objectives. I recognize the importance of preventing immigration fraud, ensuring regulatory compliance, and protecting American workers. However, imposing a $70,000 fee does not establish whether a student, university, or employer is complying with OPT requirements. Financial capacity is not a reliable measure of program integrity. The proposed approach risks restricting legitimate participation without adequately distinguishing compliant institutions and students from those engaged in misconduct.

Second, the proposal would impose substantial financial burdens on American universities and their students. Although the rule formally places payment responsibility on educational institutions, DHS explicitly acknowledges that institutions may transfer these costs to students or employers. For public universities operating under constrained budgets, the proposed fees could make supporting OPT financially impractical. For international doctoral students, whose education often involves years of research, teaching, and scholarly contributions, such costs could effectively eliminate access to authorized practical training regardless of academic achievement, professional qualifications, or compliance history.

Third, the proposal could undermine American research capacity and international competitiveness. U.S. universities invest substantial resources in educating and training international graduate students, many of whom contribute to federally funded research, classroom instruction, technological development, and scientific innovation. OPT provides an important opportunity to translate this specialized education into practical experience. Restricting access through exceptionally high fees could weaken universities' ability to attract international talent and reduce the return on investments already made in graduate education and research. These consequences deserve particular attention in fields where research projects, technical expertise, and institutional knowledge develop over multiple years.

Fourth, the rule raises serious concerns about equity and reliance interests. International students make substantial educational, financial, and professional commitments when entering U.S. degree programs. Students already enrolled in multiyear programs have reasonably planned their educational trajectories under an existing regulatory framework. Although DHS proposes prospective implementation, the rule would still affect currently enrolled students who have not yet received an OPT recommendation. A 60-day transition period does little to address the substantial disruption these students and their universities may experience. Moreover, the ability to participate in OPT should not depend primarily on a student's personal wealth or an institution's willingness to absorb extraordinary fees.

Fifth, DHS's own regulatory impact analysis raises questions about proportionality and alternatives. The proposed rule estimates approximately $4.1 billion in annualized costs and $12.8 billion in annualized fee transfers under its primary estimates at a 3 percent discount rate. DHS also acknowledges uncertainty regarding reduced participation and associated opportunity costs. These substantial projected consequences warrant stronger evidence that the proposed fee amounts would meaningfully reduce fraud and that less burdensome alternatives would be insufficient.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 and $30,000 OPT fees. Any future regulatory changes should be grounded in demonstrated program-integrity risks, supported by transparent evidence, proportionate to the administrative and enforcement objectives pursued, and carefully evaluated for their effects on U.S. universities, research institutions, students, and employers.

Protecting the integrity of the immigration system and preserving America's capacity to attract, educate, and retain highly qualified international talent should be mutually reinforcing objectives, not competing priorities.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the proposed rule, citing disproportionate fees and substantial financial burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, Sections III–IV and proposed 8 CFR 214.13 — the proposed charge exceeds DHS's statutory authority and is arbitrary and capricious.

1. By the NPRM's own admission, this is revenue-raising, not a user fee. DHS states that the amounts collected "would be deposited in the Treasury of the United States as a miscellaneous receipt pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 3302," that "ICE would not maintain or use the funding collected," and that INA 214(a) "does not provide legal authority for ICE to retain the funds collected" (91 FR 64566). A fee must bear a reasonable relationship to the cost of a service provided to the payer. Here there is no service and no cost nexus: the underlying acts — a DSO entering a recommendation in SEVIS and USCIS adjudicating Form I-765 — are already charged for, at $470 (online I-765 filing). DHS estimates annual transfers of $8.7–$16.9 billion (primary estimate $12.8 billion), orders of magnitude above any processing cost it identifies. A levy of that scale, sent to the general Treasury, is a tax, and only Congress may impose one.

2. The amount was not derived from cost at all. DHS explains that it set the initial fee to "closely align with the H-1B fees" in Presidential Proclamation 10973 in order to deter participation — that is, the number is a deterrent penalty aimed at a different visa category, not a measurement of anything OPT costs the government.

3. It fails reasoned decision-making. A flat charge cannot distinguish fraud from compliance: a fraudulent operator selling fake jobs can pass $70,000 on to its victims, while a fully compliant doctoral student at an accredited nonprofit university is priced out entirely. DHS concedes it "cannot confidently predict the extent of any reduction in participation." A rule whose stated purpose is to target abuse, but whose mechanism screens solely on ability to pay, lacks a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.

DHS should withdraw the proposal. At minimum, it must identify the statutory provision that authorizes a revenue measure of this size, and reconcile the amount with the actual cost of the service.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fees, arguing they exceed statutory authority and lack reasoned decision-making.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100, proposed 8 CFR 214.13 — I oppose the proposed OPT fees and ask DHS to withdraw them.

I am an F-1 student pursuing a graduate degree in a STEM field at a U.S. university. Like many F-1 students, I expect to seek practical training directly related to my field of study during and after my program: an internship on pre-completion OPT, a period of post-completion OPT, and, if eligible, the STEM OPT extension.

Under this proposal, my university would have to pay $70,000 before a DSO could even enter the first of those recommendations in SEVIS, then $30,000 more for the next recommendation and another $30,000 for the STEM extension — up to $130,000 for one student who has complied with every rule. No university can rationally pay that, and DHS itself acknowledges that schools "may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee onto F-1 nonimmigrant students, all students, or employers" (91 FR 64566). If the fee is passed to students, it is simply unpayable on a graduate student's stipend. If it is not, eligibility for training that is part of a degree will turn not on academic standing or compliance, but on a department's budget.

DHS defends the amount by saying it is "on par with the educational costs that foreign students incur for one or two years of education." That is a reason to reject the fee, not to adopt it: it more than doubles the cost of the education for the students least able to pay, and it prices out exactly the rule-following students the program exists for. OPT is not a loophole; it is supervised, time-limited practical training directly related to the student's major, authorized only after a DSO recommendation and USCIS adjudication of Form I-765, for which students already pay a filing fee.

Please withdraw the proposed fees. If DHS proceeds, it must explain how a student mid-degree, with a concrete, degree-related training plan, is supposed to participate at all, and why the answer should depend on wealth rather than eligibility.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed OPT fees, requesting that DHS withdraw them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Making universities pay $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for STEM extensions is a massive mistake that will backfire on the American economy and cost us the next generation of builders and job creators.

When we talk about international students and OPT, we aren't talking about people taking away opportunities. We are talking about the exact pipeline that brought some of the biggest job creators in modern American history to our shores. Think about Elon Musk, who came to the United States as a college student at the University of Pennsylvania before staying here to build Tesla and SpaceX. Those two companies alone employ well over 100,000 Americans today and keep the U.S. ahead in space and manufacturing. Look at Satya Nadella at Microsoft or Sundar Pichai at Google, or the founders of major AI and cloud companies like Databricks, Perplexity, and Stripe. Nearly a quarter of all billion-dollar startups in the U.S. were founded by people who first arrived here on student visas.

None of these people started out as billionaires. When they graduated, they were just smart, ambitious twenty-somethings who needed a legal way to get early work experience and start building. If a $70,000 or $100,000 OPT tax had been in place back then, no university or fledgling startup would have paid that kind of money for an entry-level graduate. They would have packed their bags and built their companies in Canada, Europe, or Asia instead. 

That is exactly what will happen if DHS finalizes this rule. Brilliant engineering, medical, and computer science graduates won't stop inventing things just because we price them out of OPT. They will simply take their patents, their startups, and the hundreds of thousands of jobs they would have created for American workers to countries that actually welcome them. Even established U.S. companies have made it clear that when they cannot hire STEM talent domestically, they don't magically create more local jobs—they just open R&D offices offshore.

On top of losing future innovators, this fee will hurt regular American college students. International students already pay two to three times the in-state tuition rate at public universities, which helps subsidize tuition and programs for domestic students. If we slap a $100,000 post-graduation penalty on their degrees, international enrollment will collapse, and everyday American families will be left paying higher tuition to cover the budget shortfall.

Please withdraw this proposed rule before we permanently hand our technological and economic lead to our competitors.
comments.reason: The commenter argues the fees are a massive mistake that will backfire on the economy and drive away talent.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees because their consequences could fall unevenly across American communities, placing regional universities, smaller employers, and less wealthy areas at a particular disadvantage.

A uniform fee does not create a uniform burden. The proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee could be more difficult for a regional institution with limited resources to absorb than for a wealthy university. If institutions pass these costs to students or seek support from employers, the financial barrier remains; it simply shifts to another participant.

This matters for communities that rely on local colleges and universities to develop their workforce. A graduate who has studied in a region has already established connections there and may be prepared to contribute to a local business. If the proposed fees prevent that graduate from accessing practical training, the surrounding community could lose an opportunity to retain someone it helped educate.

The effects could be especially significant for smaller employers. A company outside a major metropolitan area may have fewer applicants with specialized skills and fewer resources for recruiting nationally. Losing access to a qualified local graduate could delay a project, limit expansion, or increase recruitment costs. DHS should evaluate these possibilities rather than assume that another suitable worker will always be immediately available in the same location.

The proposal could also concentrate opportunities in institutions and businesses with the greatest financial resources. Wealthier organizations may be better positioned to absorb or arrange payment of the fees, while smaller institutions and firms reduce participation. That would risk making access to practical training depend more heavily on institutional wealth and geography than on the quality of the training itself.

For the United States, this is a question of balanced regional development. Communities seeking to build new industries and retain educated residents should not face unnecessary barriers to connecting local education with legitimate practical experience. A policy that concentrates talent and opportunity in a smaller number of well-resourced locations could work against those communities’ efforts.

Before proceeding, DHS should provide a geographically differentiated assessment of the proposal’s effects. National totals alone may obscure substantial local losses. The analysis should consider differences in institutional resources, employer size, local recruitment conditions, and the availability of realistic alternatives when a graduate cannot participate in OPT. It should also examine whether the proposed fees would concentrate participation among wealthier institutions without improving the quality or integrity of training.

I support effective oversight of OPT. However, preventing misconduct does not require imposing a financial barrier that could disproportionately weaken legitimate education-to-employment connections in less wealthy American communities. Targeted verification and enforcement would address actual violations more directly.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and preserve accessible, accountable practical training opportunities that allow a broad range of American communities—not only the wealthiest institutions and regions—to benefit from the graduates they educate.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the OPT fees due to uneven negative consequences on regional universities and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed OPT fees because they risk weakening a central source of American technological strength: the ability to attract talented people from around the world and bring them together in American universities, laboratories, and companies.

In artificial intelligence, national competitiveness depends on more than computing infrastructure and investment. It also depends on researchers and engineers who can develop new methods, test systems, and turn discoveries into useful products. The United States should make it attractive for talented graduates educated here to contribute their skills here.

Consider a typical pathway: an international student studies machine learning at an American university, develops specialized expertise through research, and then seeks practical training with an American AI company. This is an illustrative example, not a claim about a particular person. If a prohibitive OPT fee prevents that transition, the student’s skills do not disappear. Those skills may instead become available to an employer or research institution outside the United States. The relevant policy question is therefore not simply whether fewer foreign graduates will work here, but where their future contributions will occur.

AI development also relies on teams with complementary expertise. A researcher, an infrastructure engineer, and a specialist in a scientific application may each make the others more productive. Restricting access to one member of such a team can affect the work of the entire group, including American colleagues. DHS should examine these complementary relationships rather than assume that excluding an international graduate necessarily creates an equivalent opportunity for a domestic worker.

The proposed fees could also send a damaging signal to prospective students: the United States welcomes their tuition and academic work but may make the practical application of that education financially inaccessible. Students choosing where to study can consider opportunities in multiple countries. Even if the immediate effects appear limited, repeated decisions to study and build careers elsewhere could gradually weaken the networks of expertise that sustain American technological leadership.

I am particularly concerned that a very large fee measures access to money more directly than it measures talent, educational value, or compliance. A promising AI researcher at a less wealthy institution may face greater barriers than a less qualified applicant with substantial financial support. That is a poor basis for deciding which graduates can receive practical training in fields important to American competitiveness.

DHS should evaluate how the proposal could affect the retention of AI researchers and engineers, university-to-industry collaboration, and the location of future research and business activity. The analysis should distinguish short-term changes in participation from longer-term effects on the United States’ ability to remain a destination for global talent.

Fraud prevention is necessary, but enforcement should focus on actual misconduct and the legitimacy of training arrangements. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure and preserve an accessible, accountable OPT program that helps American institutions turn education into innovation within the United States.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed fees for weakening American technological strength and talent attraction.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As a U.S. citizen and taxpayer, I am writing to oppose this proposed rule (ICEB-2026-0100). On the surface, charging a $70,000 fee for initial OPT and $30,000 for extensions might sound like a way to "put Americans first," but when you actually look at how our universities and job market work, this policy ends up hurting everyday Americans the most.

First, let's be honest about who pays the bills at our state universities. International students don't get federal financial aid or Pell Grants—they pay full out-of-state tuition, often two or three times what my family or my neighbors pay. That money is what keeps tuition somewhat affordable for American kids and keeps science and engineering programs funded at public colleges. DHS even admits in the text of this proposal that universities might deal with this $70,000 to $100,000 fee by passing the cost on to the rest of the student body. Why should American families and first-generation college students get stuck with higher tuition bills just to cover a ridiculous new government fee?

Second, as someone who works in the U.S. economy, I know that companies don't magically hire more people here if you cut off their access to specialized graduates. When American tech, healthcare, or manufacturing companies can't fill tough STEM roles locally, they don't leave those jobs in the U.S.—they move the whole engineering department to Canada, India, or Europe. When that happens, American workers lose out on the management, sales, operations, and support jobs that surround those teams. Plus, international students and recent grads spend over $40 billion a year right here in our local towns—renting apartments, buying groceries, and paying taxes. Driving them away hurts American landlords, small business owners, and college towns across the country.

Finally, some of the biggest employers of American workers today—companies like Tesla, SpaceX, Google, and Microsoft—were built or led by people who first came to the U.S. as international students and stayed to work after graduation. We want the brightest minds in the world building their companies, paying taxes, and hiring Americans right here in the United States, not doing it for our competitors overseas.

This $100,000 fee doesn't help American workers or students; it just punishes our own schools and ships future jobs abroad. Please drop this proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT. I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted measures to address fraud while preserving legitimate, accessible practical training.

My concerns relate particularly to the proposal’s rationale in Section IV, its fee requirements and transition provisions, and its economic analysis. Fees of this magnitude risk making OPT financially inaccessible to many students and institutions. Although the proposal does not formally eliminate OPT, it could substantially reduce access to the program, with consequences for the American economy and the nation’s long-term talent pipeline.

First, DHS should fully account for the economic value that international students bring to American communities. NAFSA estimates that international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported 355,736 jobs during the 2024–2025 academic year. These figures describe international education overall, rather than the incremental contribution of OPT alone. Nevertheless, they demonstrate the scale of economic activity potentially affected if restrictions on practical training make American education less attractive. DHS should evaluate how the proposed fees could affect enrollment, tuition revenue, housing demand, local businesses, and employment connected to universities.

Second, sharply reducing OPT participation could impose immediate costs on American employers. Practical training allows graduates to apply knowledge acquired at U.S. institutions in work directly related to their studies. If otherwise qualified graduates become unavailable because their institutions cannot afford the fees, employers may face disrupted projects, additional recruitment costs, and the loss of people they have already trained. Smaller businesses, startups, and research organizations may have fewer resources to absorb these disruptions. DHS should assess these effects rather than assume that each reduction in OPT participation produces an equivalent employment opportunity for a U.S. worker.

Third, the proposal could weaken America’s long-term ability to attract and retain talent. The United States benefits when people educated in its universities can contribute their skills to American research, product development, and business formation. Making practical training prohibitively expensive could encourage talented students to choose other countries or take their U.S.-acquired skills elsewhere after graduation. The potential cost extends beyond immediate hiring: it includes future research capacity, entrepreneurial activity, professional networks, and the development of specialized expertise.

The National Science Foundation’s 2026 science and engineering indicators report that STEM employment is projected to grow faster than overall employment between 2024 and 2034. This does not establish that every STEM occupation faces a shortage, but it reinforces the need for a careful, occupation-specific assessment of future workforce needs before sharply restricting a pipeline of U.S.-educated talent.

Fourth, the proposal risks selecting participants based on financial resources rather than educational merit or compliance. A large fee does not itself establish that a training opportunity is legitimate, that a student is highly qualified, or that an employer protects American workers. Institutions with fewer financial resources could be unable to support otherwise deserving students. If costs are passed to students, access could depend primarily on personal wealth. DHS should explain why these outcomes are necessary and evaluate less restrictive alternatives.

Preventing fraud and protecting U.S. workers are legitimate objectives. More closely targeted approaches could include verifying actual training activity, auditing high-risk employers and institutions, enforcing applicable wage and training requirements, and imposing meaningful consequences on proven violators. DHS should compare the costs and effectiveness of these alternatives against the proposed fees.

Finally, DHS should give substantial consideration to students who enrolled and invested in American education under the existing framework. A short transition period may not adequately address the reliance interests of students already pursuing multi-year degrees. At minimum, any material change should include meaningful protections for currently enrolled students and existing training arrangements.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fee structure. Preserving accessible, well-supervised OPT would better support American businesses, local economies, higher education, and long-term competitiveness while allowing targeted enforcement against abuse.

Speaking from the perspective of university scientific research and laboratory operations, the proposal to charge $70,000 for initial OPT and $30,000 for STEM extensions will cripple academic research across the United States. The people who drafted this rule clearly do not understand how university laboratories are funded or how modern scientific breakthroughs actually happen.

In STEM fields—whether it is cancer biology, semiconductor engineering, artificial intelligence, or materials science—our research labs run on competitive grants from agencies like the NIH, NSF, and the Department of Energy, alongside tight departmental budgets. Every dollar of a research grant is strictly accounted for: it goes toward lab equipment, reagents, clinical trials, and modest stipends for graduate researchers and postdocs. There is zero line item in an NIH or NSF grant—and zero surplus in a state university department budget—to pay a $70,000 to $100,000 regulatory tax just to keep a freshly trained scientist in the lab after they defend their thesis.

It takes four to six years of intensive mentorship and American research funding to train a Ph.D. student to operate specialized instrumentation and lead complex experiments. OPT and the STEM extension are the critical period when these researchers finally transition from trainees to peak productivity—finishing multi-year clinical studies, publishing flagship papers, patenting university inventions, and training the next cohort of incoming American undergraduate and graduate students. 

If DHS imposes a $70,000 fee at graduation, our labs will be forced to let these scientists walk out the door the moment they become most valuable. Multi-year experiments will be abandoned mid-stream. Worse yet, American taxpayers and universities will have spent years training top scientific minds, only to force them to take that expertise straight to competing labs and biotech hubs in Europe, Canada, or Asia.

Furthermore, prospective Ph.D. and master's candidates are not going to commit years of their lives to U.S. university labs if they know a $100,000 wall awaits them at graduation. When top international researchers stop applying to American graduate programs, our laboratories shrink, our grant competitiveness drops, and American undergraduate students lose the lab mentors and teaching assistants they rely on for their own STEM education.

This rule does not protect American science; it actively dismantles it from the inside. I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this destructive proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01) establishing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for any subsequent OPT for F-1 nonimmigrant students. I urge DHS to finalize the rule as proposed.Combating Fraud and Strengthening Program Integrity
OPT has become a high-volume pathway that is frequently abused. Schools, students, and employers have used the program in ways inconsistent with its original educational purpose, including as a prolonged work authorization vehicle that feeds directly into the H-1B system. Significant fees will create meaningful financial accountability, discourage low-quality or “visa mill” institutions from recommending students indiscriminately, and incentivize greater oversight by Designated School Officials before they enter OPT recommendations in SEVIS. This aligns with DHS’s stated goals of combating fraud and abuse and ensuring the program is used consistent with applicable regulatory requirements.
Addressing the Pipeline into H-1B Abuse and Nepotism
OPT serves as a primary feeder into the H-1B program. The well-documented problems of fraud, misrepresentation of job duties, wage undercutting, and nepotistic hiring practices in segments of the H-1B program are enabled in part by the large volume of OPT participants who transition into temporary worker status. By imposing substantial fees on the front end of this pipeline, the proposed rule will reduce the volume of participants who view OPT primarily as a bridge to longer-term employment authorization rather than genuine practical training related to their field of study. This is a necessary and proportionate step to protect the integrity of both programs.
Protecting American Workers
The current structure of OPT allows large numbers of foreign students to enter the U.S. labor market with employment authorization that is not subject to the same labor-market protections or numerical limits as other temporary worker categories. This depresses opportunities and wages for American workers, particularly recent graduates and mid-career professionals in STEM and other fields. Requiring schools to pay significant fees before recommending students for OPT will reduce the supply of low-cost foreign labor entering the job market through this channel and help restore a more level playing field for U.S. citizens and permanent residents.
Promoting Accountability Among Educational Institutions
Under the proposed rule, SEVP-certified schools must pay the fee before a Designated School Official can recommend a student for OPT, and USCIS will not grant employment authorization without confirmation of payment. This places the financial responsibility where the recommendation decision is made and encourages institutions to exercise greater selectivity and diligence. Schools that treat OPT as a marketing tool to attract international students, rather than a limited educational benefit, will face real costs. Collected fees deposited in the U.S. Treasury further support broader government efforts to maintain immigration system integrity.
Balancing Legitimate Use with Necessary Reform
The rule does not eliminate OPT. It simply attaches a meaningful cost to participation so that the program is no longer effectively unlimited and cost-free for the institutions that drive volume. Legitimate students and high-quality programs can still participate; the fees will primarily deter abuse and excessive reliance on foreign student labor. Efficiency and volume should not override the statutory and policy imperative to protect U.S. workers and maintain program integrity.

Conclusion
I strongly urge DHS to finalize the Optional Practical Training Fees rule as proposed, without reducing the fee amounts or creating broad exemptions that would undermine its effectiveness. Significant fees are a direct and appropriate response to documented fraud, abuse, and the role OPT plays as a pathway into problematic H-1B practices. Finalizing this rule will combat fraud, strengthen oversight, reduce the flow of cheap labor into the American job market, protect U.S. workers, and restore public confidence in the integrity of the F-1 and related nonimmigrant programs.
